A Full Year of Grade 1 Language, at Home

This guide covers all 63 specific expectations of the Ontario Grade 1 Language curriculum (2023) in 51 lessons, a daily Word Lab phonics spine, and a year plan from September to June. You do not need to be a teacher. Every lesson tells you what to say, what to watch for, and how to know your child really understands.

The promise of Grade 1: by June, your child should be reading simple books on their own, writing their own short stories, opinions and instructions, and talking about ideas with confidence and curiosity.

How this guide works

📦 One lesson = 3 sessions

Each lesson has 9 parts. Spread them over three 45–60 minute sessions: (1) Wonder Hook, Objectives and The Lesson; (2) Think challenges and Classwork; (3) Assignment and review. Homework happens in between.

🔤 Word Lab is daily

Phonics must be practised every day, in short bursts. Work through one Word Lab lesson over about 3 weeks: teach it in 3 sessions, then use its Classwork and word lists for a 15-minute daily warm-up until the Progress items are solid.

🗓️ A typical week

Mon–Thu: 15 min Word Lab + one main-lesson session (A, B, C or D).
Friday: 15 min Word Lab + Author’s Chair (child reads their writing aloud) + library/free reading.
Every day: 20 minutes of being read to, and 10 minutes of your child reading a decodable book to you.

💾 Saving work

Everything typed into the boxes and every ticked progress item is saved automatically in this browser. Use the same device and browser. Much of the work also belongs in a real notebook — handwriting matters in Grade 1.

🧑‍🏫 Colour code

🔊 Read it to me

The “Read it to me” button in each Lesson section uses your device’s built-in voice. The Lesson text is written slightly above Grade 1 level on purpose: read it together, and let your child read the words they can.

The daily routines (the secret sauce)

1 · Read aloud to your child — 20 min

The biggest single predictor of vocabulary. Read books above their reading level: picture books, then chapter books like Frog and Toad, Mercy Watson, My Father’s Dragon. Stop now and then to ask “What do you think will happen?” and “Why did she do that?”

2 · Your child reads to you — 10 min

Use decodable books that match the phonics they have learned (ask your library, or search “free decodable passages”, e.g. UFLI Foundations). Guessing from pictures is NOT reading — gently point back to the letters: “Look at the letters. Sound it out.”

3 · Word Lab warm-up — 15 min

5 min sounds (blending/segmenting out loud) · 5 min reading word lists from the current Word Lab lesson · 5 min spelling 3–5 words from dictation. Short, brisk, fun.

4 · Write something real — daily

A sentence in a journal, a note to Grandma, a grocery list, a label for a drawing. Accept their spelling attempts of untaught patterns; correct only patterns already taught.

Year plan: September to June

About 4 main lessons a month plus one Word Lab lesson running daily. Click any lesson to open it. Adjust freely: if a lesson needs more time, take it.

If your child is…

🐢 Finding it hard

Slow down, never skip Word Lab. Shorten sessions, keep them daily. Use real objects and movement. If after several months your child still cannot blend three sounds, or letters/sounds do not “stick”, talk to your family doctor about a speech-language or learning assessment — early help works best.

🐇 Racing ahead

Do not rush to the next lesson. Go deeper: use the ⭐⭐⭐ Brain-benders, Keep Wondering questions, longer writing, and harder read-alouds. Depth, not speed, is the goal.

😣 Frustrated or tired

Stop while it is still fun. Say “This is hard — that means your brain is growing.” Return tomorrow. Celebrate effort out loud. A 10-minute happy session beats a 60-minute battle.

Lesson 1 of 9

My Seven Learning Superpowers

Discover the seven “transferable skills” — superpowers you carry into every subject, every game, and every conversation.

A1.1A1.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

If you could only take ONE thing with you to a brand-new planet where nobody speaks your language — a backpack of toys, a tablet, or your brain’s skills — which would help you most, and why?

Let your child argue for their answer for at least two minutes. There is no wrong choice — push them to give a reason for each claim ("because…"). Then ask: "What skills would your brain need on that planet?" Write their ideas on a sticky note and keep it; you'll return to it at the end of the lesson.

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A1.1 name the seven learning superpowers and give an example of using each one when I read, listen, watch, or write
  • A1.2 explain how one of my superpowers helps me share my ideas (my voice) and stay interested in learning
  • A1.1 notice which superpower I am using in the middle of a real task

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

The 2023 Ontario Language curriculum asks children to understand seven "transferable skills" — skills that transfer (move) from one subject to another. Researchers and employers agree these matter as much as reading itself. Your job today is not to have your child memorize a list, but to help them notice themselves using these skills.

The seven skills (official name → kid name)

  • Critical thinking and problem solving → The Puzzle-Solver 🧩
  • Innovation, creativity, and entrepreneurship → The Inventor 💡
  • Self-directed learning → The Self-Starter 🚀
  • Collaboration → The Team Player 🤝
  • Communication → The Communicator 💬
  • Global citizenship and sustainability → The World Helper 🌎
  • Digital literacy → The Tech Explorer 💻

How to teach it (about 20 minutes of talk before reading)

  1. Ask your child to tell you about something hard they figured out recently (a Lego build, a game level, tying shoes). Listen fully.
  2. Replay it back using superpower words: "When you tried three different ways, that was your Puzzle-Solver superpower."
  3. Read the lesson together. Pause after each superpower and ask, "When did YOU use this one this week?"
  4. Make the superpower cards in Classwork. They will be used all year — put them somewhere visible.
💬 You can say

"A superpower isn't something you're born with. It's something that grows every time you use it — like a muscle."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often think "being smart" means already knowing answers. Gently redirect: the superpowers are all about what you do when you DON'T know yet. Praise the process ("You kept trying!") rather than the person ("You're so smart!"). Psychologist Carol Dweck's research found that praising effort helps children take on harder challenges.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can, without the cards, name at least 4 superpowers and tell you a real moment from their own life for at least 2 of them.

💡 Teaching tip

For the rest of the year, when you catch your child using one of these skills in ANY subject, name it out loud. This one habit is the whole point of Expectation A1.

📚The Lesson

Did you know you have superpowers? Not flying or turning invisible. These are learning superpowers — skills your brain uses every single day. Scientists and teachers call them transferable skills. Transfer means "to move from one place to another." These skills move with you everywhere: into reading, into math, onto the playground, and one day into your grown-up job.

There are seven of them. Let's meet them.

🧩 1. The Puzzle-Solver (critical thinking and problem solving)

The Puzzle-Solver asks, "Why?" and "How do I know?" When a word in a book doesn't make sense, the Puzzle-Solver doesn't give up. It says: "Let me look at the picture. Let me reread the sentence. Let me sound it out again." Every time you ask "Is that really true?", you are using this superpower.

💡 2. The Inventor (innovation, creativity, and entrepreneurship)

The Inventor makes something new that did not exist before — a new story, a new game, a new way to build a fort. When you make up a funny ending to a story, that's the Inventor.

🚀 3. The Self-Starter (self-directed learning)

The Self-Starter can say, "I want to learn about sharks," and then goes and finds a shark book — without anyone telling them to. The Self-Starter also knows how to say, "I'm stuck. What can I try next?"

🤝 4. The Team Player (collaboration)

The Team Player works with other people. Taking turns, listening to a friend's idea, and saying "What if we put your idea and my idea together?" are all Team Player moves.

💬 5. The Communicator (communication)

The Communicator shares ideas so other people understand — with words, pictures, faces, and hands. Reading and writing are communication. So is a hug, a wave, or a thumbs-up!

🌎 6. The World Helper (global citizenship and sustainability)

The World Helper thinks about other people and about the Earth. "Is this fair for everyone?" "How can we waste less?" "What is life like for kids in other places?"

💻 7. The Tech Explorer (digital literacy)

The Tech Explorer knows how to use tablets, computers and apps safely and wisely — and knows when to turn them off!

🤯 Did You Know?

The Inuit people of the Arctic have built snow houses (igloos) for hundreds of years. A good igloo is built in a spiral so every block leans on the one before it — and it can be so strong that a grown-up can stand on top! Building one takes Puzzle-Solving (how do the blocks stay up?), Team Playing (often two people build together), Communicating (passing on the knowledge from Elders to children) and caring for the World (using only snow, which melts back into the Earth). One skill is never alone — superpowers work as a team.

Superpowers help your VOICE

Your voice is not just the sound coming out of your mouth. Your voice is your ideas, your feelings, and your opinions. When you use your superpowers, your voice gets stronger. The Communicator helps you say what you think. The Puzzle-Solver helps you give good reasons. The Inventor helps you say it in a way nobody else ever has.

🧠 Brain moment

When you learn something new, tiny paths in your brain called connections get stronger — like a path in the snow that gets easier to walk on every time you walk it. That's why practice works!

Meet a real Puzzle-Solver

Sequoyah was a Cherokee man who lived about 200 years ago. His people did not yet have a way to write their language. People told him it couldn't be done. Sequoyah didn't give up. He spent about twelve years working on it, and he made a set of symbols — one for each syllable in Cherokee. It was so clever and easy to learn that thousands of Cherokee people learned to read and write within just a few years! Sequoyah used the Puzzle-Solver, the Inventor, the Self-Starter, and the World Helper — all at once.

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

Your friend is building a block tower and it keeps falling. Which superpower would help most? Why? Could a second superpower help too?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Sequoyah spent twelve years on one invention. Which superpower do you think he needed the MOST? Is there a superpower he needed that isn't on the list? Invent a name for it!

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Can you use a superpower in a bad way? (Hint: could someone be a great Communicator but say unkind things? Could someone be an Inventor of a trick that hurts people?) What does that tell us about superpowers?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Create a set of seven Superpower Cards and test them on a real task.

Materials

  • 7 index cards or paper rectangles
  • crayons or markers
  • a small, slightly tricky task: a 24–48 piece puzzle, a paper-airplane challenge, or a simple Lego build

Steps

  1. On each card, write the kid name of one superpower (a grown-up can print it lightly for your child to trace) and draw a symbol for it.
  2. Do the tricky task together.
  3. Every time one of you uses a superpower, hold up the card and say its name. Put a tally mark on the back of the card.
  4. When finished, count the tally marks.

Observation recording

SuperpowerHow many times we used itOne moment we used it

📝Assignment

Complete all three parts. Your child may dictate longer answers for you to write; they should print at least one sentence themselves.

Part 1 — Match it (recall)

For each situation, name the superpower: 1. Maya asked the librarian for a book about volcanoes. 2. Jonah and his sister shared the crayons and made one big poster together. 3. Priya noticed the recycling bin was full and made a sign that said "Please squish your boxes!" 4. Leo read a word wrong, noticed it didn't make sense, and fixed it.

Part 2 — My Superpower Story (thinking)

Draw a picture of a time YOU used a superpower. Then write or say: "I used my ___ superpower when I ___."

✏️ Draw your superpower story in your notebook

Part 3 — My voice (original thinking)

Finish this sentence three different ways: "Something I want people to know about me is ___." Then tell a grown-up which superpower helped you say it.

🏠Homework

  1. Superpower Spotting. Watch a grown-up in your family do a job (cooking, fixing something, paying bills, gardening). Which superpowers did they use? Ask them: "What was the hardest part?" Tell your teacher-parent about it next session.
  2. Put the cards to work. Keep your Superpower Cards on the fridge. Each evening this week, move one card to a "Used today!" spot and say how you used it.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Do animals have learning superpowers? Which ones might a crow, a beaver, or an octopus use?
  2. If you could give a superpower to a robot, which one would be the hardest to teach it — and why?
  3. Is there a superpower that grown-ups are often worse at than kids?
Lesson 2 of 9

Who Am I? Stories of Me, Stories of We

Explore identity, family, community and belonging — and discover that everyone’s story is worth telling.

A3.2A1.2C2.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Your name was chosen for you before you could talk. Someone thought hard about it. What secret story might be hiding inside your name — and how could you find out?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A3.2 describe some parts of my own identity (name, family, languages, food, places, things I love) and listen to someone else's
  • A3.2 explain what it feels like to belong and name things that help people feel they belong
  • A1.2 use my voice to tell the story of my name and something important about me
  • C2.5 connect a story to my own life and to another person's life

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

Expectation A3.2 asks children to explore identity, self, and a sense of belonging through texts that reflect many people's lives, including people in Canada. Children who see their own lives in books — and who meet lives different from theirs — become stronger, kinder readers.

Recommended read-alouds (library)

- The Name Jar by Yangsook Choi — a Korean girl new to the U.S. thinks about changing her name. - Alma and How She Got Her Name by Juana Martinez-Neal. - My Heart Fills with Happiness by Monique Gray Smith (Cree, Lakota and Scottish author). - Hair Love by Matthew A. Cherry. If you can't get these, use the original story in The Lesson.

How to teach it

  1. Before the lesson, prepare the true story of your child's name: who chose it, why, what it means, any family or cultural connections, nicknames. If you don't know, that becomes a homework interview!
  2. Read the lesson story aloud. Stop at the question marks and let your child answer.
  3. Share your child's name story in a special voice — make it a gift.
  4. Talk about belonging: "Where do you feel like you really belong? What makes it feel that way?"
💬 You can say

"Everybody's story matters — yours, mine, and people who are very different from us. When we listen to other people's stories, our world gets bigger."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

A child may say that another person's name, food, or clothing is "weird." Don't shame them — get curious together: "It's new to you. To that person, it's normal and special. What might your lunch look like to someone from far away?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can tell the story of their own name in 3+ sentences AND ask a thoughtful question about someone else's identity.

💡 Teaching tip

Identity can include tender topics (adoption, separated families, a family member who has died). Let your child share only what they want to share.

📚The Lesson

Everybody is a story. You are a story too! The things that make you you are called your identity. Your identity includes your name, your family, the languages you hear at home, the food you love, the places you have lived, what you look like, what you believe, and what makes you laugh.

📖 Amara's Name

On the first day at her new school, the teacher called, "Ah-MAR-ah?"

Amara felt her cheeks get hot. "It's AM-ah-rah," she said quietly.

At lunch, a boy named Theo asked, "What does your name mean?"

Amara smiled. "My grandma chose it. In the language of her family, it means grace. It also means forever."

"Whoa," said Theo. "My name is from my great-grandpa. I don't know what it means. I'm going to ask!"

The next day, Theo ran in. "It means gift from God in Greek!"

The teacher had an idea. The whole class made a Name Tree. Every leaf had a name and its story.

Amara looked up at the tree. Her leaf was right next to Theo's. She felt like she belonged.

Why do you think Amara's cheeks got hot? How did she feel at the end? What changed?

What is belonging?

Belonging is the warm feeling that you are welcome, you are wanted, and you are part of the group — just as you are. People feel like they belong when others: - say their name correctly - listen to their ideas - are curious about their culture instead of laughing at it - include them in games - notice when they are missing

Many people, many stories

Canada is home to people from almost every country on Earth. More than 200 different languages are spoken in Canadian homes! The first languages spoken on this land were the languages of First Nations, Métis, and Inuit peoples — like Cree, Ojibwe, Mohawk, Michif, and Inuktitut — and many families still speak them today.

🤯 Did You Know?

In many First Nations and Inuit families, a baby may receive a name from an Elder or be named after a relative who has passed away. In some Inuit traditions, the person who shares your name (your sauniq) is thought to share a special connection with you — so a little girl named after her grandfather might be lovingly called "grandpa" by her family!

Your identity can grow

Some parts of your identity stay the same, like your birthday. Other parts grow — you learn new languages, try new foods, and discover new favourite things. You are not finished — you are becoming!

🧠 Brain moment

When you hear your own name, even in a noisy room, your brain notices it. Scientists call this the "cocktail party effect." Your name is so important to your brain that it's always listening for it!

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

Amara's teacher said her name wrong. What are two things a person can do to make sure they say a new name correctly?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Theo didn't know what his name meant. Then he found out. How did learning his name's story change how he felt? Why do you think it mattered to him?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Can a person belong to more than one group at the same time — like a family, a team, a country, and a culture? Can you belong somewhere and still feel a little different there? Explain with an example.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Build an "All About Me" Identity Map and compare it with a family member's.

Materials

  • large paper (or two sheets taped together)
  • markers or crayons, family photos (optional)

Steps

  1. Draw yourself in the middle of the page.
  2. Draw 6 lines coming out like sun rays. At the end of each line, draw or write one part of your identity: my name, my family, languages I hear, food I love, places that matter to me, something I'm great at.
  3. Ask a grown-up to make a map about themselves too (quickly!).
  4. Put the two maps side by side. Look for things that are the same and things that are different.

Observation recording

Part of identityMeMy grown-upSame or different?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Remember (recall)

Answer in full sentences: 1. What does the word identity mean? 2. What are two things that help someone feel they belong?

Part 2 — The Story of My Name (writing)

Write (or dictate, then copy one sentence) the story of your name: - Who chose my name? - Why was it chosen? - What does it mean, or who is it from? - How do I feel about my name?

Part 3 — A Welcome Plan (original thinking)

A new kid named Kiona is joining your class. She just moved from far away. Plan three things you could do on her first day so she feels she belongs. Draw your favourite idea.

🏠Homework

  1. Name Interview. Interview a family member about THEIR name. Ask: Who named you? What does your name mean? Do you have a nickname? Have people ever said your name wrong? Bring back their answers.
  2. Belonging Hunt. Over the next few days, notice one time you felt like you belonged and one time you felt left out. What made the difference? Tell your grown-up at bedtime.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If you could choose a new name for yourself, would you? What would you lose if you changed it?
  2. Can a place — like a forest, a kitchen, or a grandma's house — make you feel like you belong? Why?
  3. Do pets know their names, or do they just know the sound?
Lesson 3 of 9

Safe Explorers: Being a Good Digital Citizen

Learn the rules of the online world: asking permission, keeping private things private, and being a kind digital citizen.

A2.1A2.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Imagine you wrote a message with a marker that can NEVER be erased, and then it got copied a thousand times and blew away in the wind. Where could it end up? That is a little bit like posting something online. Why?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A2.2 explain why I always ask a trusted grown-up for permission before going online, downloading, or clicking something new
  • A2.2 sort information into “private” (keep secret online) and “OK to share with permission”
  • A2.1 describe my rights and responsibilities online, and explain what a digital footprint is
  • A2.1 choose actions online that make me — and others — feel safe and respected

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

Even 6-year-olds use tablets, video apps and games. The curriculum (A2.1, A2.2) asks them to understand permission, privacy, and responsibility online. The goal is not fear — it's confident, careful habits that will protect them for life.

Your family rules (decide these BEFORE the lesson)

Write down 4–5 simple rules. Suggested: 1. I ask a grown-up before I go online, download, or click on something new. 2. I keep my private information private: full name, address, school, phone number, passwords, photos of me. 3. If something online makes me feel scared, confused or yucky, I stop, close the screen, and tell a grown-up. I will NOT be in trouble. 4. I only talk online to people I know in real life, with permission. 5. I am kind online, just like in person.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: do the "marker that can't be erased" thought experiment. Let your child imagine where the message could go.
  2. Read the lesson together. Play the "Private or OK to share?" sorting game (Classwork).
  3. Role-play: pretend a game pops up saying "You won a prize! Type your address!" What does your child do?
💬 You can say

"If anything online ever makes you feel worried — even if you clicked something you weren't supposed to — tell me. You will never be in trouble for telling me. My job is to help you."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often believe that people online are who they say they are, and that "deleted" means gone forever. Also, many children think a "stranger" looks scary — explain that online, a stranger can seem very friendly.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can list 3 private things, explain "Stop, close, tell," and explain in their own words what a digital footprint is.

💡 Teaching tip

Post your family's rules next to the device. Revisit them monthly.

📚The Lesson

The internet is like a huge city with billions of buildings — some are libraries, some are playgrounds, some are shops, and some are places kids should never go. A digital citizen is someone who lives in that online city and follows its rules, just like a good citizen of a real town.

Rule 1: Ask permission first

Before you go online, download a game, or click on something new, you ask a trusted grown-up. This is called permission. It's like asking before you cross a busy street. Grown-ups can see dangers that kids might not see yet.

Rule 2: Keep private things private

Some information is private — it belongs only to you and your family. Private information online can help a stranger find you. Keep these private: - your full name - your address and your school's name - your phone number - your birthday - your passwords (only share with your grown-up!) - photos of you or your house

Rule 3: Stop, Close, Tell

If you see or hear something online that makes you feel scared, sad, confused, or "yucky inside" — Stop what you're doing. Close the screen or turn the device over. Tell a trusted grown-up right away. You will not be in trouble.

Your digital footprint

When you walk on sand, you leave footprints. When you do things online, you also leave tracks. Every photo, comment, like, and search can leave a mark. This is called your digital footprint. Unlike sand footprints, digital footprints may never wash away. Someone can copy a picture or a message and share it again and again.

That's why good digital citizens ask: "Would I be happy for my grandma, my teacher, and my future self to see this?"

Rights AND responsibilities

Online, you have rights — things you deserve: to be safe, to be treated kindly, to have your privacy respected. You also have responsibilities — things you should do: be kind, ask permission, don't share other people's photos without asking them, and tell a grown-up when something is wrong.

🤯 Did You Know?

The very first website ever made went online in 1991 — probably before your parents were grown-ups! It was made by a scientist named Tim Berners-Lee. He did not make money from his invention — he gave it away free so everyone in the world could use it.

🤯 Did You Know?

A lot of games and apps have an age rule. Many popular apps say you must be 13 or older to have an account. These rules exist to help protect children's privacy.

🧠 Brain moment

Scientists have found that the part of your brain that stops and thinks, "Wait — is this a good idea?" (right behind your forehead) keeps growing until you're about 25 years old! That's why even teenagers still need grown-ups to help them online.

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

A game says: "Type your name and city to get 100 free coins!" What should you do? Which rule helps you?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Your friend took a silly photo of you making a funny face. They want to share it online. What are YOUR rights? What would a good digital citizen do?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If you drew a picture on paper, you could rip it up. Why is it so much harder to "rip up" something online? Where might it be hiding?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Sort information into PRIVATE and OK-TO-SHARE (with permission), then create a family "Digital Citizen Promise."

Materials

  • 12 slips of paper, two bowls or boxes labelled 🔒 PRIVATE and ✅ OK to share (with permission)
  • markers

Steps

  1. A grown-up writes one item on each slip: my favourite colour, my address, my password, my favourite animal, my school's name, a drawing of a dragon, my phone number, my birthday, what I ate for breakfast, a photo of my house, my first name only, my favourite book.
  2. Read each slip together. Decide which bowl it goes in. Explain WHY.
  3. Some are tricky! Put tricky ones in the middle and talk about them.
  4. Write a family Digital Citizen Promise with 4–5 rules. Everyone signs it — grown-ups too!

Observation recording

🔒 Private✅ OK to share (with permission)🤔 Tricky — why?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Words to know (recall)

Explain in your own words: permission, private, digital footprint.

Part 2 — What would you do? (applying)

For each problem, write or tell what you would do and which rule helps: 1. A video starts playing that shows something scary. 2. Someone in a game you don't know asks, "What school do you go to?" 3. You want to download a new drawing app.

Part 3 — Make a safety poster (creating)

Make a poster to teach a younger child Stop, Close, Tell. Use a picture, a title, and at least one sentence you print yourself.

✏️ Plan your poster here or in your notebook

🏠Homework

  1. Family Tech Tour. Ask your grown-up to show you where the privacy or parent settings are on one device at home. What does each setting do? (Grown-up: choose settings together.)
  2. Footprint Detective. With a grown-up, search your family's name online (grown-up does the typing). Is anything there? Talk about how it got there.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Should kids have the right to say “Don't post that picture of me” — even to their own parents?
  2. When you're 30 years old, what do you want your digital footprint to show about you?
  3. If the internet disappeared tomorrow, what would change in your family's life?
Lesson 4 of 9

Information Detectives: Where Do Facts Come From?

Learn to gather information, ask “How do we know?”, and compare different people’s ideas about the same thing.

A2.3A3.1D1.3
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

A website says, “Goldfish only remember things for 3 seconds!” Your cousin swears it's true. How could you — a six-year-old — find out if it really is?

(Spoiler for grown-ups: it's a myth. Scientists have trained goldfish to push levers and respond to sounds, and they remember for months.) Don't reveal it yet — let your child suggest ways to check.

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A2.3 gather information about a question from a book, a video, or a person, with a grown-up's help
  • A2.3 ask “How do we know this is true?” and notice when two sources say different things
  • A2.3 listen to different people's opinions about the same topic and explain how they are different
  • A3.1 use my reading and listening skills to learn something in science or social studies

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

A2.3 asks children to gather, evaluate, and use information, considering various perspectives. Grade 1 children can absolutely learn that not everything they hear or see is true — and that we check by looking at more than one source and asking who made this and how they know.

How to teach it

  1. Start with the goldfish hook. Let your child guess, then ask: "How could we find out?"
  2. Read the lesson. Introduce the three detective questions: Who made this? How do they know? Does another source agree?
  3. Do the Classwork investigation with a real question your child cares about.
  4. End by reading the goldfish fact together and celebrating the "myth-busting."
💬 You can say

"Good detectives don't believe the first thing they hear. They look for clues and check with more than one witness."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Kids (and adults!) often trust whatever sounds confident or has a nice picture. Also, children may think a fact is false just because it's surprising. Teach that surprising ≠ false and confident ≠ true.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child spontaneously asks "How do they know?" or "Is that true?" about a claim, and can name two different kinds of sources (book, expert, video, website, observation).

💡 Teaching tip

Keep a "Myth or Fact?" jar all year. Whenever someone at home hears a surprising claim, write it on a slip for weekend investigation.

📚The Lesson

A fact is something that is true and can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels — and different people can have different opinions. "A goldfish is a fish" is a fact. "Goldfish are the best pets" is an opinion.

Sometimes people say things that sound like facts but aren't true at all. These are called myths. Detectives use clues to find out what's really true. You can be an Information Detective!

Where can a detective find information?

Information comes from sources. A source is where information comes from. Some sources are: - 📚 books — especially non-fiction books from the library - 🧑‍🔬 experts — people who study a topic for a long time (a vet knows about animals, a nurse knows about bodies) - 👀 your own eyes — observing carefully - 💻 websites and videos — some are great, some are not - 👵 people with experience — a grandparent who grew up on a farm knows about farm life!

The Three Detective Questions

  1. Who made this? Is it an expert? A company trying to sell something? A random person?
  2. How do they know? Did they study it, see it, or just guess?
  3. Does another source agree? If two or three good sources say the same thing, it's more likely to be true.

Different people, different views

Sometimes information depends on who you ask. Ask a farmer about rain and they may say, "Rain is wonderful — my crops need it!" Ask a kid with a birthday party outside and they may say, "Rain is terrible!" Both are telling the truth about how they see it. That's called a perspective. A good detective listens to many perspectives.

📖 The Goldfish Mystery

People used to say goldfish forget everything in three seconds.

Scientists wanted to check.

They played a sound every time they fed the goldfish.

Soon the fish swam to the food spot when they heard the sound — even with no food!

Months later, the fish still remembered the sound.

The three-second story was a myth!

🤯 Did You Know?

Scientists in Australia trained fish to swim to the feeding spot when they heard a sound — and the fish remembered it five months later. Some goldfish have even learned to push a lever to get food!

Detective skills help in every subject

In science, you check ideas by observing. In social studies, you ask older people how life was different. In math, you check your answer another way. Reading and listening carefully makes you better at everything. That's what cross-curricular means — skills that cross between subjects.

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

Fact or opinion? (a) Dogs have four legs. (b) Dogs are cuter than cats. (c) Snow is cold. (d) Winter is the best season.

⭐⭐ Stretch

A toy company's ad says, "This is the BEST toy in the world! Every kid loves it!" Use the Three Detective Questions. Should you believe it? Why might the company say this?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If two books say different things about the same animal, how could you decide which one to trust? Think of at least two ways.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Investigate one real question using two different sources and compare what they say.

Materials

  • one non-fiction library book on an animal your child chooses
  • a short, grown-up-chosen kids' video or website on the same animal (e.g., a national geographic kids page)
  • paper and pencil

Steps

  1. Your child chooses a question, such as "How long do octopuses live?" or "What do owls eat?"
  2. Guess first! Record the guess.
  3. Look in Source 1 (book). A grown-up reads aloud; the child listens for the answer.
  4. Look in Source 2 (video/site). Listen again.
  5. Compare: Do they agree? Did one give extra information?

Observation recording

My questionMy guessSource 1 saidSource 2 saidDo they agree?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What are the Three Detective Questions? What is a source? Give two examples.

Part 2 — Sort it (thinking)

Make two columns in your notebook: FACT and OPINION. Write or draw 3 of each about your favourite food.

Part 3 — Myth Buster Mini-Report (creating)

Choose one surprising claim (from your Myth or Fact? jar, or pick: "Bats are blind" — hint: they're not!). With help, check it in two sources. Write 2–3 sentences: What was the claim? What did you find? Is it a myth or a fact?

🏠Homework

  1. Ask an Expert. Interview someone who knows a lot about something (a grandparent's job, a neighbour who gardens). Prepare 3 questions in advance. Write down one thing you learned.
  2. Perspectives at dinner. Ask everyone at dinner: "What's the best season and why?" Notice how everyone's answer depends on their perspective.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Is it possible for something to be true for one person and not true for another?
  2. Why do myths spread so fast, even when they're not true?
  3. How did people check facts before there were books or the internet?
Lesson 5 of 9

How Media Talks to Us: Ads, Shows & Screens

Become a media detective: every ad, cereal box and video was made by someone, for someone, with a message.

A2.4A2.5C3.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Why do cereal boxes for kids have cartoon animals with their eyes looking DOWN — while cereal boxes for grown-ups have people looking straight ahead? Who planned that, and why?

(For grown-ups: a Cornell University study found characters on kids' cereal boxes tend to look downward — toward children's eye level in the store, which is usually low on the shelves. Walk down a cereal aisle and check!)

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A2.4 name different forms of media (ads, videos, posters, packages, websites) and some tricks they use: colour, music, big letters, happy faces
  • A2.5 explain who made a media text, who it is for (audience), and what it wants me to think or do (message)
  • C3.5 notice how a media text is trying to influence people like me

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

A2.4 and A2.5 ask children to understand that media texts are made on purpose: someone creates them, for an audience, with a message, using techniques. This is called media literacy, and it protects children from being manipulated by advertising.

The Big Three Media Questions

  1. Who made this? (the creator)
  2. Who is it for? (the audience)
  3. What does it want me to think, feel, or do? (the message)

How to teach it

  1. Gather 3–4 real media texts: a cereal box, a toy catalogue page, a flyer, a short kids' toy ad (preview it yourself first).
  2. Read the lesson together.
  3. Analyze the media texts with the Big Three questions and the "tricks" list.
  4. In Classwork, your child becomes the creator.
💬 You can say

"Every ad was made by someone who wants something from you. That's OK — but you get to decide, not the ad."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Young children often believe ads are just "information" or that the toy will really do what the ad shows. Point out things like slow-motion, special lights, music, and kids who are "actors" paid to look excited.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can look at an unfamiliar ad and answer all three Big Questions, and name at least one "trick."

💡 Teaching tip

Make "What do they want us to do?" a family catch-phrase during commercials and while shopping.

📚The Lesson

Media is any way of sending a message to lots of people at once: TV shows, videos, ads, posters, websites, games, cereal boxes, magazines, even the words on a T-shirt! Each one is a media text. Every media text was made by someone, for someone, for a reason.

Media Detectives ask three big questions

  1. Who made it? — the creator
  2. Who is it for? — the audience
  3. What does it want me to think, feel, or do? — the message

Tricks media makers use

Media makers use techniques (special tricks) to catch your attention: - 🎨 bright colours — kids' toys often use red, yellow and blue - 🎵 catchy music — a song that gets stuck in your head - 🔠 BIG, bold letters — "NEW!" "FREE!" "BEST!" - 😄 happy faces — kids laughing and having the most fun ever - 🐯 cartoon characters — a friendly tiger or monkey you trust - 🔁 repeating — saying the name again and again so you remember it - ✨ special effects — slow motion, sparkles, and camera tricks that make toys look bigger or faster

Form, message and audience fit together

The form is the type of media. A message for little kids might be a cartoon video. A message for grown-ups might be a newspaper ad. The creator chooses the form that the audience will notice most.

📖 Two Ads for the Same Juice

Ad 1 shows a cartoon orange doing a silly dance. It says: "SUPER SLURPY JUICE! Kids go BANANAS for it!"

Ad 2 shows a calm kitchen with a sunny window. It says: "100% juice. No sugar added. Good choice, parents."

Same juice. Two very different ads!

Who is Ad 1 for? Who is Ad 2 for? How can you tell?

🤯 Did You Know?

The word emoji comes from Japanese: e means "picture" and moji means "letter or character." It is NOT related to the word "emotion" — it's a coincidence! The first set of emojis was made in 1999 by a designer named Shigetaka Kurita, and it had just 176 tiny pictures.

🤯 Did You Know?

In the province of Quebec, it has been against the law since 1980 to make most TV and online ads aimed directly at children under 13. People decided kids deserved protection from advertising.

Media is also good!

Not all media is trying to sell you something. Some media teaches (a nature show), some entertains (a cartoon), some keeps us safe (a stop sign or a fire-safety poster), and some helps people share their culture and stories. The Big Three Questions help with ALL media.

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

Look at a toy ad or a cereal box. Name two tricks it uses.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why do you think toy ads show kids laughing and cheering, and never show a toy that is broken or boring? What is the ad NOT telling you?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

The same message can be shown in different forms: a song, a poster, a video. If you wanted to teach little kids to wash their hands, which form would work best? Which would work for grandparents? Why might they be different?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Analyze real media texts, then create your own ad for an ordinary object.

Materials

  • 3 real media texts (cereal box, flyer, toy catalogue page)
  • paper, markers, a boring household object (a spoon, a sock, a rock)

Steps

  1. For each real media text, answer the Big Three questions out loud. A grown-up records answers.
  2. Now YOU are the creator! Choose your boring object. Choose an audience (kids? grandparents? dogs?!).
  3. Make a poster OR act out a 30-second TV ad to sell it. Use at least 3 tricks.
  4. Perform or show it. The grown-up must guess which tricks you used.

Observation recording

Media textWho made it?Who is it for?What does it want?Tricks used

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What are the Big Three Media Questions? What does audience mean?

Part 2 — Compare (thinking)

Look at the Two Juice Ads story again. Write or say 3 differences between the ads and explain why each is different.

Part 3 — Honest Ad (creating)

Make an HONEST ad for your favourite toy — one that tells the truth, including something the toy CAN'T do. Draw it and write at least one sentence. Would your honest ad make people want to buy it? Why or why not?

🏠Homework

  1. Supermarket Safari. At the grocery store, find: 1) a product with a cartoon character, 2) a product with the word "NEW!", 3) a product placed at kids' eye level. Who is each one for?
  2. Ad Count. With a grown-up, count how many ads you see or hear in one car ride, TV hour, or walk down a main street. Were you surprised?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If ads work so well, could we use ad tricks to make people do good things — like eat vegetables or recycle?
  2. Are YouTubers and game streamers a kind of ad? How could you tell?
  3. What would the world look like with no ads at all?
Lesson 6 of 9

Design Thinkers: Solving Real Problems

Use the design process — and simple digital tools like a camera or voice recorder — to solve a real problem at home.

A2.6A1.1A3.1
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Grown-ups built the whole world for grown-up-sized people. Look around your home: what's one thing that is annoying, hard, or impossible for a kid your size? What if YOU were the one hired to fix it?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A2.6 name the steps of the design process: Notice, Imagine, Plan, Make, Test, Improve
  • A2.6 use a digital tool (camera, voice recorder, drawing app) with permission to help me plan, make or share a solution
  • A1.1 use Puzzle-Solver and Inventor superpowers together to solve a problem
  • A3.1 explain how the design process could help in science, math or everyday life

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

A2.6 asks children to use digital and media tools to support the design process and to develop creative solutions to authentic, real-world problems. "Authentic" is the key word: the problem should be something your child actually cares about.

The design process (kid version)

  1. 👀 Notice a problem
  2. 💭 Imagine lots of ideas
  3. ✏️ Plan — pick one and draw it
  4. 🔨 Make it
  5. 🧪 Test it
  6. 🔁 Improve it

Digital tools in Grade 1

Keep them simple and supervised: taking photos of their problem and solution, voice-recording their explanation, or drawing a plan in a simple drawing app.

How to teach it

  1. Walk around your home together looking for kid-sized problems (can't reach the light switch, shoes are always lost, the dog's water spills).
  2. Read the lesson about Mary Anderson and the windshield wiper.
  3. Choose ONE problem and move through the design process across 2–3 sessions.
💬 You can say

"Real inventors' first ideas almost never work. The test-and-improve steps are where the magic happens."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children want to skip straight to "Make" with their first idea. Insist on at least 3 ideas in "Imagine" — quantity leads to quality. Also, children see a failed test as "I failed." Reframe: a test that doesn't work gives you information.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can explain their solution in order using the design process words, and describe one improvement they made after testing.

💡 Teaching tip

Save the photos and recordings — they become a "design journal" you can revisit at the end of the year.

📚The Lesson

Everything around you that humans made — your chair, your spoon, your shoes, your toothbrush — was designed by someone. Somebody noticed a problem and thought, "There must be a better way!"

Meet Mary Anderson

Over 100 years ago, in 1902, a woman named Mary Anderson was riding a streetcar in New York City on a snowy day. She noticed the driver had to open his window and reach out to wipe the snow off the glass — or even stop and get out! Everyone was cold and the streetcar was slow.

Mary thought, "There must be a better way." She went home and designed a handle inside the car that moved a rubber blade across the outside of the window. She had invented the windshield wiper! People laughed at her idea at first. Today, almost every car in the world has one.

The Design Process

Designers follow steps called the design process: 1. 👀 Notice — find a problem. "The streetcar driver can't see!" 2. 💭 Imagine — think of MANY ideas. Brainstorm means letting ideas pour out like rain, without saying "no" to any yet. 3. ✏️ Plan — choose one idea and draw it. Label the parts. 4. 🔨 Make — build a model called a prototype. A prototype is a first try. 5. 🧪 Test — try it out! Does it work? 6. 🔁 Improve — change it to make it better. Then test again!

The steps go around in a circle. Designers improve and test, improve and test, many times.

👀 Notice→💭 Imagine→✏️ Plan→🔨 Make→🧪 Test→🔁 Improve↺

Digital tools can help designers

- 📷 A camera can take a "before" photo of the problem and an "after" photo of your solution. - 🎙️ A voice recorder can save your ideas while you brainstorm, so you don't forget them. - 🖌️ A drawing app can help you plan and change your drawing easily. Always use devices with permission!

🤯 Did You Know?

James Dyson made 5,127 prototypes of his vacuum cleaner over five years before he got it right. Each one that didn't work taught him something new.

🤯 Did You Know?

Kids invent things too! Frank Epperson was 11 years old when he accidentally left a cup of soda with a stirring stick outside on a freezing night. The next morning — the first Popsicle!

Design helps in every subject

In science you design experiments. In math you design patterns. In gym you design games. At home you might design a better way to feed the cat. Design thinking goes everywhere!

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

Put the design process steps in order: Test, Notice, Make, Imagine, Improve, Plan.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why do you think people laughed at Mary Anderson's idea at first? What would you say to someone who laughed at YOUR invention?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

James Dyson's first 5,126 tries didn't work. Were those failures — or were they part of the success? Explain.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Solve a real kid-sized problem at home using the design process and at least one digital tool.

Materials

  • recycled materials: boxes, tubes, tape, string, paper cups, rubber bands
  • a device with a camera or voice recorder (with permission)

Steps

  1. Notice: Take a "before" photo of your problem.
  2. Imagine: Voice-record at least 3 ideas.
  3. Plan: Draw your best idea. Label 3 parts.
  4. Make: Build a prototype.
  5. Test: Try it 3 times. Record what happens.
  6. Improve: Change one thing. Test again. Take an "after" photo.

Observation recording

Test numberWhat I didWhat happenedWhat I'll change

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Name the six steps of the design process. What is a prototype?

Part 2 — Design Journal (explaining)

Using your photos, tell the story of your invention in order. Use the words First, Next, Then, Finally. Print at least two sentences yourself.

Part 3 — Design for someone else (thinking)

Think of someone in your family or community who has a problem (a grandparent who can't open jars, a baby who throws food). Imagine 3 solutions. Draw the best one.

🏠Homework

  1. Invention Hunt. Find 5 objects at home. For each, guess what problem it solves. (A clothes peg solves: "My laundry blows away!")
  2. Share your design. Show your invention to someone outside your home (in person or on a video call, with permission) and ask for one idea to improve it.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. What is something that hasn't been invented yet but SHOULD be?
  2. Can a problem have more than one right solution? How would you choose?
  3. What if animals could design things — what would a beaver or a bird invent next?
Lesson 7 of 9

Kind Connections: Talking Respectfully Online and Beyond

Practise communicating with people in different communities — online and face-to-face — with kindness, safety, and cultural respect.

A2.7A2.1A3.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

When you talk to someone face-to-face, they can see your smile, hear your voice, and see you were only joking. Online, most of that disappears. How could a message you meant as funny end up hurting someone?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A2.7 communicate with family, friends or community members using a digital tool, safely and with a grown-up
  • A2.7 show respect for people's cultures, languages and traditions when I talk, write or play with them
  • A2.1 choose words online that make others feel good, and explain what to do if someone is unkind
  • A3.2 learn about another family's traditions and share something about mine

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

A2.7 asks children to communicate and collaborate with various communities in a safe, respectful, responsible, and inclusive manner when using online platforms, and to show cultural awareness. Grade 1 children may video-call grandparents, send voice notes, or play games with others.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: act out a message two ways — "Nice drawing." said warmly, then said sarcastically. Then write it down. Ask: "When it's written, how do you know which way I meant it?"
  2. Read the lesson together.
  3. Plan the Classwork: a respectful video call or voice message to a relative or family friend from a different place or culture, prepared with real questions.
💬 You can say

"Before you send anything, ask THINK: Is it True? Is it Helpful? Is it Inspiring? Is it Necessary? Is it Kind?"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children may think that because they can't see the person, "it doesn't count." Also, children can confuse curiosity with rudeness. Model the difference: "What do you eat for holidays?" (curious, respectful) vs. "Your food looks gross" (hurtful).

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can explain THINK, and during a real call asks at least two respectful questions and listens to the answers.

💡 Teaching tip

Make the call real and meaningful — a grandparent in another country, a friend who celebrates a different holiday, or a local community member. Prepare them in advance.

📚The Lesson

A community is a group of people who share something — a place, a school, a language, a hobby, or a culture. You belong to lots of communities: your family, your street, your city, maybe a faith community, a sports team, or a group of friends who love the same game.

Today, people can connect with communities all over the world using digital tools: video calls, voice messages, emails, and games. That's amazing! It also means we need to be extra careful and kind.

Why online words can hurt more

When you talk face-to-face, people can see your face, hear your tone of voice, and watch your body. Online, a lot of that disappears. A joke can look mean. A short answer can look angry. So online, we choose our words extra carefully.

THINK before you send

  • T — Is it True?
  • H — Is it Helpful?
  • I — Is it Inspiring (does it make someone feel good)?
  • N — Is it Necessary?
  • K — Is it Kind?

What if someone is unkind to you online?

  1. Don't answer back with mean words.
  2. Stop, close, and tell a trusted grown-up.
  3. Grown-ups can help save the message, block the person, and report it.

Cultural awareness

Culture is the way a group of people lives: their language, food, clothes, music, stories, celebrations, and beliefs. When we meet someone from a different culture, we can be curious and respectful: - Ask kind questions: "What's your favourite holiday? How do you celebrate?" - Listen to the answer without saying "weird" or "gross." - Learn a greeting in their language!

HelloBonjour (French)Hola (Spanish)Salaam (Arabic)Aaniin (Anishinaabemowin/Ojibwe)Tansi (Cree)Ullaakkut — good morning (Inuktitut)Ni hao (Mandarin)
🤯 Did You Know?

In Canada, people speak more than 70 Indigenous languages. Some, like Cree, Inuktitut and Ojibwe, have tens of thousands of speakers. Many communities are working hard to teach their languages to children so they stay strong for the future.

🤯 Did You Know?

When you smile on a video call, the other person's brain often smiles back without even trying! Scientists call this mirroring. Kindness is contagious!

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

Use THINK to check this message: "Your drawing is ugly lol." Which letters does it fail?

⭐⭐ Stretch

A new friend online says their family eats with their hands at dinner. Someone else in the game types "EW." What could you say that is kind AND helps everyone learn?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Is it possible to be too careful online — so careful that you never talk to anyone? What's the right balance between staying safe and connecting with people?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Plan and hold a respectful video call or voice-message exchange with someone from a different community or place.

Materials

  • a device (grown-up sets up the call)
  • paper for questions

Steps

  1. Choose who to call with your grown-up (a relative far away, a family friend who celebrates different traditions).
  2. Write or dictate 4 respectful questions. Check each one with THINK.
  3. Practise your greeting — maybe in their language!
  4. Hold the call. Take turns speaking. Listen carefully.
  5. After the call, record what you learned.

Observation recording

My questionTheir answerSomething new I learned

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does each letter in THINK stand for? What should you do if someone is unkind online?

Part 2 — Fix the message (applying)

Rewrite each message so it passes THINK: 1. "That game is for babies." 2. "Why do you talk funny?" 3. "You lost AGAIN."

Part 3 — Share my culture (creating)

Make a small "postcard" about one tradition in YOUR family (a food, a celebration, a song, a saying). Draw it and write 2 sentences. You might send it to the person you called!

🏠Homework

  1. Greeting Collector. Learn to say "hello" and "thank you" in one new language this week — maybe a language spoken by a neighbour, classmate, or the First Peoples where you live. Teach your family.
  2. Kindness Message. With permission, send one kind message (voice note or card) to someone who might need it.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If everyone in the world spoke only one language, would that be better or worse? What would we lose?
  2. Why do you think kindness is contagious?
  3. Can you be friends with someone even if you don't speak the same language?
Lesson 8 of 9

Learning from the First Peoples: Land, Relationships & Stories

Explore big themes in First Nations, Métis and Inuit cultures — relationships, respect for the land, gratitude and family — through real stories.

A3.3A3.2C1.7
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Some First Nations teachings say we should make decisions by thinking about how they will affect people seven generations from now — that's about 150 years in the future! How would YOUR choices today change if you thought about kids who won't be born for 150 years?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A3.3 name some big themes in First Nations, Métis and Inuit cultures, such as relationships with the land and water, gratitude, family and community, and passing on knowledge
  • A3.3 understand that First Nations, Métis and Inuit are different peoples with many different nations, languages and ways of life
  • C1.7 listen to and talk about a text by a First Nations, Métis or Inuit creator
  • A3.2 name the First Peoples of the place where I live

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

A3.3 asks children to identify themes explored in First Nations, Métis, and Inuit cultures and to understand the varied identities, perspectives, relationships, legacies, truths, and ways of knowing, being, and doing. The key word is varied: there are more than 630 First Nations communities in Canada, plus Métis and Inuit peoples, each with distinct languages and traditions.

Before you teach

  • Find out whose traditional territory you live on (search "native-land.ca" together, or check your municipality's land acknowledgement). For example, St. Catharines and the Niagara region are the traditional territory of the Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe peoples, covered by treaties including the Upper Canada Treaties.
  • Borrow a book by an Indigenous creator. Excellent Grade 1 choices: Nibi's Water Song by Sunshine Tenasco (Anishinaabe); Sweetest Kulu by Celina Kalluk (Inuit); Fiddle Dancer by Anne Patton & Wilfred Burton (Métis); My Heart Fills with Happiness by Monique Gray Smith; We Are Water Protectors by Carole Lindstrom (Anishinaabe/Métis); Little You by Richard Van Camp (Tłı̨chǫ Dene).

How to teach it

  1. Start with the Seven Generations hook.
  2. Read the lesson; stop to talk about each theme.
  3. Read your chosen book. After, ask which themes you noticed.
  4. Take a respectful nature walk (Classwork).
💬 You can say

"First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples are still here today. They are doctors, artists, teachers, astronauts, and kids just like you — and they have been caring for this land for thousands of years."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

The most common misconceptions are (1) that Indigenous peoples existed only "long ago," (2) that all Indigenous peoples are the same, and (3) stereotypes like feather headdresses for everyone. Use present tense and specific nation names wherever possible.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can name at least two themes, say that First Nations, Métis and Inuit are different peoples, and name the First Peoples of their area.

💡 Teaching tip

Stories are sometimes owned by communities and told only at certain times (e.g., some stories are told only in winter). Books published by Indigenous creators are the respectful way to learn.

📚The Lesson

Long before there were cities or roads here, this land was home to First Peoples. They are still here today. In Canada we talk about three groups of Indigenous peoples: - First Nations — many different nations, like the Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee, Cree, Mi'kmaq, and hundreds more. Each has its own language and traditions. - Métis — a people with their own culture, language (Michif), music and art that grew from both First Nations and European families, especially on the prairies. They are famous for fiddle music, jigging, and colourful beadwork. - Inuit — people whose homelands are in the Arctic, where it is snowy for much of the year. Their language is Inuktitut (and related languages).

These are many different peoples, not just one. But some big ideas, or themes, appear in many of their stories and teachings.

Theme 1: Everything is connected

Many teachings say that people, animals, plants, water, and land are all relations — like a family. The Anishinaabe often say "all my relations." If you hurt the water, you hurt the fish, the birds, and yourself.

Theme 2: Respect for the land and water

The land and water are gifts to be cared for, not wasted. Anishinaabe women like Josephine Mandamin walked around all five of the Great Lakes — more than 17,000 kilometres over many years — carrying a copper pail of water to pray for the water and remind people to protect it.

Theme 3: Gratitude

Many ceremonies begin by giving thanks — to the water, the plants, the animals, the sun, the moon. The Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address thanks many parts of the natural world, one by one, before important gatherings.

Theme 4: Family and community

Elders, parents, aunties, uncles, and cousins all help raise children. Elders are respected because they carry knowledge and wisdom.

Theme 5: Passing on knowledge through story

For thousands of years, knowledge was passed on through oral storytelling — telling stories out loud. Stories teach lessons about how to live well. They are still told today.

🤯 Did You Know?

The Inuit language has words for many kinds of snow and sea ice — because knowing the difference could keep you safe on the land! For example, aputi means snow on the ground and qanik means falling snow.

🤯 Did You Know?

The Seven Grandfather Teachings of the Anishinaabe are: Wisdom, Love, Respect, Bravery, Honesty, Humility, and Truth. Each one is often connected with an animal — for example, the beaver for wisdom and the eagle for love.

Truth

There is also a hard truth in Canada's story. For many years, the government took many First Nations, Métis and Inuit children away from their families to schools where they were not allowed to speak their languages. It was very wrong. Today, people are working to tell the truth and to make things right. This is called reconciliation. Learning about First Peoples, respectfully, is one way to help.

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

"All my relations" means we are connected to animals, plants, water and land. Name one way YOU are connected to water.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Josephine Mandamin walked 17,000 km for the water. Why do you think she walked instead of just giving a speech? What does walking show that talking might not?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Think about the Seven Generations idea. What is one thing your family does that would be good for kids 150 years from now? What is one thing that might not be?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Take a "Gratitude Walk" and practise noticing relationships in nature.

Materials

  • clipboard or notebook, pencil, a bag for litter (and gloves)

Steps

  1. Find out together: Whose traditional land do you live on? Say it out loud.
  2. Walk in a park or yard for 20 minutes. Move slowly and quietly.
  3. Find 5 living things (a tree, a bird, an ant, grass, water). For each, say "thank you for ___" and name one way it helps other living things.
  4. Pick up some litter as a gift back to the land.
  5. At home, draw a "Web of Relations" connecting the 5 things.

Observation recording

Living thingThank you for…How it helps others

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Who are the three groups of Indigenous peoples in Canada? Name two big themes from the lesson.

Part 2 — Book Talk (connecting)

After reading a book by an Indigenous creator: What was the book about? Which theme did you notice? Draw your favourite part and write one sentence about it.

Part 3 — My Gratitude Circle (creating)

Draw a circle. Around it, draw 6 things in nature you are thankful for. Inside the circle, write: "Thank you, ___, for ___."

🏠Homework

  1. Place Names. Many places in Canada have names from Indigenous languages — Canada itself comes from the St. Lawrence Iroquoian word kanata, meaning "village" or "settlement." Ontario is often said to come from an Iroquoian word meaning "great lake" or "beautiful water." Find one more place name near you and learn its meaning.
  2. Elder Wisdom. Ask an older person in your family: "What is a lesson you learned from YOUR grandparents?" Write or record it.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. What would it be like to learn everything important by listening to stories instead of reading books?
  2. If the river could talk, what would it ask people to do?
  3. Who are the Elders in your life, and what knowledge do they carry that nobody else has?
Lesson 9 of 9

Language Everywhere: Reading and Writing in Real Life

Discover how reading, writing, listening and speaking help you in math, science, cooking, shopping, playing — everywhere.

A3.1A1.1A2.3
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Imagine you woke up tomorrow and every single letter in the world had vanished — from signs, cereal boxes, phones, books, money, and street names. What would go wrong first? What would be the most dangerous?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • A3.1 find at least 10 ways people use reading and writing in everyday life
  • A3.1 use my reading and writing skills in a science or math task
  • A1.1 explain which superpowers I use when I read signs, recipes, maps and instructions
  • A2.3 use information I read to do something real (like follow a recipe or a map)

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

A3.1 asks children to apply their language skills in other subject areas and to identify ways this learning is used in everyday life. This is the lesson that answers "Why do I have to learn to read?" in a way a child can feel.

How to teach it

  1. Spend 5 minutes on the "letters vanish" hook — let it get silly and serious.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Go on a Print Walk (Classwork) — at home and/or in your neighbourhood.
  4. Cook something simple together from a written recipe your child "reads" with support.
💬 You can say

"Reading isn't just for books. Reading keeps you safe, helps you cook, helps you play games, and helps you find your way."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Some children think "reading" only counts in books. Celebrate reading signs, logos, labels, and game screens: this is called environmental print, and it's real reading.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can list 10+ real-life uses of reading/writing and successfully follows a 4-step written procedure with support.

💡 Teaching tip

This lesson makes a wonderful close to the year — revisit it in June and compare lists!

📚The Lesson

Reading and writing aren't just school things. They are life things! Grown-ups read and write all day long, often without noticing.

Reading keeps you safe

🛑 STOP signs, ⚠️ "Wet Floor" signs, 🚫 "Do not touch," ☠️ labels on cleaning bottles, "EXIT" signs, and "Hot!" on the coffee cup. These words can protect you. The words you see around you on signs and labels are called environmental print.

Reading helps you do things

  • 🍪 A recipe tells you how to bake cookies.
  • 🧩 Instructions tell you how to build a Lego set or play a board game.
  • 🗺️ A map helps you find the playground or the washroom at the zoo.
  • 🛒 A shopping list helps you remember what to buy.
  • 📅 A calendar helps you know when your birthday party is!

Reading and writing in other subjects

  • Science: scientists write down what they observe so they don't forget. They read other scientists' work to learn more.
  • Math: math problems are written in words! "Sam has 3 apples. He gets 2 more…" You need to read to solve it.
  • Art and Music: songs have written lyrics; artists sign their names; museums have labels.
  • Gym: game rules are often written down.
  • Social Studies: we read old letters, maps and stories to learn about the past.
📖 How to Make a Fruit Kebab

You need: 1 wooden stick, 3 grapes, 2 strawberries, 1 banana.

First, wash your hands.

Next, ask a grown-up to cut the banana into circles.

Then, slide the fruit onto the stick. Make a pattern!

Last, eat your kebab. Yum!

This is a procedure — a text that tells you how to do something, in order. Notice the order words: First, Next, Then, Last.

🤯 Did You Know?

The first writing in the world was invented about 5,000 years ago in a place called Mesopotamia (today, mostly Iraq). And what did people write first? Not stories — lists and records of things like grain and sheep! Writing was invented to help people remember information.

🤯 Did You Know?

A grown-up reads around 200–300 words a minute when reading silently. When you started school, you knew a few words. By the end of Grade 1, many kids can read hundreds of words! Your brain is building a reading machine.

🧩Think Like an Explorer

⭐ Warm-up

Name 3 places at home where you can find words that are NOT in a book.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why do you think people first invented writing to keep track of sheep and grain instead of to write stories?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Some signs use only pictures and no words (like a washroom sign or a no-smoking sign). Why? When are pictures better than words? When are words better than pictures?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Go on a Print Walk and follow a real procedure.

Materials

  • clipboard and pencil (or a camera, with permission)
  • ingredients for fruit kebabs (or another simple recipe)

Steps

  1. Print Walk: Walk around your home (and outside if possible). Find 10 examples of words in real life. Take a photo or draw each one.
  2. For each, answer: What does it tell us? Why is it there?
  3. Follow a procedure: Read the fruit kebab recipe together, one step at a time. Point to each word as you read.
  4. Make and eat your kebab!

Observation recording

Where I found wordsWhat it saysWhy it's there

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is environmental print? What is a procedure? Give one example of each.

Part 2 — Sort it (thinking)

Sort your 10 Print Walk finds into groups: Keeps us safe · Helps us do something · Tells us information · Other. Explain one choice.

Part 3 — My Procedure (writing)

Write your own 4-step procedure for something you know how to do (brushing teeth, feeding a pet, making a sandwich). Use First, Next, Then, Last. Draw a picture for each step.

🏠Homework

  1. Grown-up Reading Diary. Ask one grown-up to keep a list for one day of everything they read and write — texts, emails, labels, signs, receipts. Count them together. Were you surprised?
  2. Cook with words. Help make a family meal using a written recipe. You are in charge of reading the ingredients list out loud.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If you invented a brand-new kind of writing, what would it look like?
  2. Will people still need to read in 100 years, or will computers do it all for us?
  3. What is the most important word you know how to read? Why?
Word Wall

Key Vocabulary

Read each card aloud together. Cover the definition and ask: “What does this word mean? Use it in your own sentence.” Revisit the cards at the start of every session in this strand.

transferable skills
Skills you can use in lots of different places and subjects — like learning superpowers.
“I used my transferable skills in math AND in soccer.”
voice
Your own ideas, feelings, and opinions, and the way you share them.
“My story showed my voice because it was full of my own ideas.”
identity
All the things that make you who you are: your name, family, languages, likes, and more.
“Speaking two languages is part of my identity.”
belonging
The feeling that you are welcome and part of a group.
“I felt a sense of belonging when my team cheered for me.”
digital citizen
A person who uses the internet and devices safely, kindly and responsibly.
“A good digital citizen asks permission before going online.”
permission
When a trusted grown-up says yes before you do something.
“I asked for permission before downloading the game.”
private
Belonging only to you or your family; not for sharing with strangers.
“My address is private information.”
digital footprint
The tracks you leave online with everything you post, search or share.
“I want my digital footprint to show that I am kind.”
source
Where information comes from, like a book, an expert or a website.
“We checked two sources to find out what owls eat.”
fact / opinion
A fact can be checked and proven true. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels.
““Cats have whiskers” is a fact; “Cats are the best” is an opinion.”
perspective
The way one person sees or thinks about something.
“From the farmer's perspective, rain is good news.”
media
Ways of sending a message to lots of people, like ads, videos, posters and websites.
“The cereal box is a kind of media.”
audience
The people a text or message is made for.
“The audience for that cartoon is young kids.”
design process
The steps inventors use: notice, imagine, plan, make, test, improve.
“We used the design process to build a better bird feeder.”
prototype
A first try at building an invention, made to be tested.
“My first prototype fell over, so I improved it.”
community
A group of people who share something like a place, language or interest.
“Our library is an important part of our community.”
culture
The way a group of people lives: their language, food, stories, music and celebrations.
“Music and dancing are an important part of Métis culture.”
First Peoples
The First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples, who have lived on this land for thousands of years.
“We learned the names of the First Peoples of our area.”
Elder
A respected person who carries knowledge and wisdom and shares it with the community.
“The Elder told a story about the moon.”
environmental print
Words and symbols we see around us in real life, like signs, labels and logos.
“The STOP sign is environmental print.”
