Lessons
Lesson 1 of 11

Whole-Body Listening

Listening is not just hearing. Discover how your eyes, body, brain and heart all help you listen.

B1.1B1.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Your ears never, ever turn off — not even when you're asleep. So why do grown-ups sometimes say you're “not listening”? What's the difference between hearing and listening?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B1.1 show whole-body listening: eyes watching, body calm, brain thinking, heart caring
  • B1.1 ask a question that is about what the speaker just said (a relevant question)
  • B1.2 use a strategy while listening, like making a picture in my mind
  • B1.1 explain the difference between hearing and listening

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B1.1 asks children to use effective listening skills, including listening attentively and asking relevant questions. Listening comprehension in Grade 1 is often years ahead of reading comprehension — it's how children learn most vocabulary and ideas this year. Strong listeners become strong readers.

How to teach it

  1. Hook experiment: Sit silently for 60 seconds with eyes closed. Count every sound you hear. Compare lists. Point out: "Your ears heard all those sounds before, but you weren't listening to them."
  2. Read the lesson. Practise each "body part" of listening.
  3. Play the listening games in Classwork.
  4. Practise "relevant questions": you tell a 1-minute story; your child must ask a question about your story (not about something else).
💬 You can say

"Hearing is what your ears do. Listening is what your brain does with it."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Whole-body listening is a tool, not a rule. Some children (especially neurodivergent children) listen better while moving, fiddling, or not making eye contact. The goal is understanding, not looking still. If your child listens best while doodling, that's fine!

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often ask "questions" that are really stories about themselves ("I have a dog too!"). Gently coach: "That's a connection. Can you turn it into a question about MY story?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

after a 2-minute read-aloud, your child can retell 3 details and ask one relevant question.

💡 Teaching tip

Model it! When your child talks, put down your phone, turn your body toward them, and ask a question about what they said.

📚The Lesson

Your ears are always hearing. Right now they can hear sounds around you — maybe a fridge humming, a car outside, or a bird. But listening is different. Listening means your brain pays attention to sounds and thinks about what they mean.

A great listener uses their whole body. This is called whole-body listening.

👀 Eyes

Your eyes look toward the speaker. You can see their face, which helps you understand their feelings.

👂 Ears

Your ears are ready and pointed toward the speaker.

🤐 Mouth

Your mouth is quiet while the other person talks. You'll get your turn!

🧍 Body

Your body is calm and turned toward the speaker. (If wiggling helps you listen, that's OK — just make sure it doesn't distract others.)

🧠 Brain

Your brain is thinking about what the speaker is saying — making pictures, wondering, and remembering.

❤️ Heart

Your heart cares about what the other person is saying. You want to understand them.

Asking a good question

When someone finishes talking, a great listener can ask a relevant question. Relevant means "connected to what was said." If your friend tells you about her trip to the beach, a relevant question is "Did you find any shells?" A question that is NOT relevant is "Do you want to play Lego?"

📖 The Lost Mitten

Kai lost his red mitten at the park.

He looked under the slide. He looked by the swings.

Then he heard a little bark.

A puppy was running across the snow — with a red mitten in its mouth!

What relevant questions could you ask about this story?

🤯 Did You Know?

You can hear sounds even while you are asleep — your ears never switch off! Your brain decides which sounds are important enough to wake you up. That's why many parents can sleep through a thunderstorm but wake up the moment their baby makes a tiny cry.

🤯 Did You Know?

Elephants can "hear" through their feet! They pick up rumbling sounds from other elephants that travel through the ground — from kilometres away.

🧠 Brain moment

Scientists say that people remember much more when they listen actively — asking questions and making pictures in their minds — than when they just let the words go by.

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Which of these is a relevant question after hearing "The Lost Mitten"? (a) What's your favourite colour? (b) Did Kai get his mitten back? (c) Can we have pizza?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Can someone look like they're listening but not really be listening? Can someone look like they're NOT listening but actually be listening well? How could you tell?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Dogs can "listen" to us — they understand some words. Are dogs good listeners? What can a dog do with its listening that a person can't? What can a person do that a dog can't?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Test and train your listening with four listening games.

Materials

  • a timer, a small bell or spoon and pot, paper and crayons

Steps

  1. Sound Map (3 minutes): Sit outside or by a window with eyes closed. Draw a map of every sound you hear and where it came from.
  2. Simon Says — Tricky Version: A grown-up gives 2-step instructions ("Touch your nose, then jump twice"). Then 3-step. Then 4-step! How many steps can you remember?
  3. Draw What I Say: A grown-up describes a simple picture without showing it ("Draw a big circle. Put a small triangle on top of it. Draw three dots inside the circle…"). You draw it. Compare!
  4. Story Questions: A grown-up reads a short story. You ask 2 relevant questions.

Observation recording

GameHow I did (⭐ to ⭐⭐⭐)What helped me listen

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Name the six parts of whole-body listening. What is the difference between hearing and listening?

Part 2 — Listening Detective (applying)

Listen to a grown-up read a short story or non-fiction page (3–5 minutes). Afterward: 1. Tell 3 things you remember. 2. Ask 2 relevant questions. 3. Draw the most important part.

Part 3 — Listening Poster (creating)

Make a poster called "How I Listen Best." Draw yourself listening. Label at least 3 things you do. Include one thing that helps YOU listen that might be different from other people.

✏️ Your listening poster

🏠Homework

  1. Dinner Listening Challenge. At dinner, listen to one person tell about their day. Then ask them a relevant question and tell them one thing they said. Watch their face — how do they feel when someone really listens?
  2. Nature Sound Hunt. On a walk, find 5 sounds made by nature and 5 made by people. Which were louder? Which were more interesting?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Can you listen to silence? What do you hear?
  2. Why do some sounds, like a favourite song, make us feel happy while others make us feel scared?
  3. If you could listen to what trees say to each other (scientists think they “talk” through their roots!), what do you think they would say?
Lesson 2 of 11

Listening Detectives: Before, During & After

Learn clever strategies to use before, during and after listening to understand and remember what you hear.

B1.2B1.1B1.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

If a friend whispers “I'm FINE” while crossing their arms and frowning, are they fine? How did you know — when their words said the opposite?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B1.2 use a BEFORE listening strategy: think about what I already know and what I want to find out
  • B1.2 use DURING listening strategies: make mind pictures, listen for key words, notice the speaker's face and voice
  • B1.2 use an AFTER listening strategy: retell, ask questions, or connect to my life
  • B1.4 use a speaker's tone of voice and gestures to help me understand the message

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B1.2 asks children to identify and use listening strategies before, during, and after listening, including understanding messages communicated non-verbally. These are the same strategies used later in reading comprehension (Strand C), so teaching them through listening first makes reading easier.

The strategies

  • Before: What is this about? What do I already know? What do I want to find out?
  • During: Make a movie in my mind. Listen for key (important) words. Watch the speaker's face and hands.
  • After: Retell it. Ask a question. Connect it to my life.

How to teach it

  1. Do the "I'm FINE" hook as a little skit.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Use a short non-fiction read-aloud or a kids' podcast (e.g., a 5-minute science podcast for kids) for Classwork. Stop the audio at planned spots.
💬 You can say

"Good listeners don't just wait for the talking to be over. They get their brain ready before, keep it busy during, and check it after."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often think retelling means repeating everything. Teach "the most important parts" — beginning, middle, end or 3 key facts.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can name one strategy for each of before, during and after, and uses at least two of them independently when listening to something new.

💡 Teaching tip

Use car rides for podcast listening practice; pause and ask "What's a picture in your mind right now?"

📚The Lesson

Good detectives don't just wait for clues to fall into their laps. They prepare, they watch closely, and they think afterwards. Good listeners do the same thing! These clever tricks are called strategies.

BEFORE you listen 🔍

  • Guess the topic. Look at the title, the picture, or ask "What is this about?"
  • Wake up what you know. "I'm going to hear about penguins. I already know they live where it's cold and they can't fly."
  • Wonder. "I want to find out how penguins stay warm."

DURING listening 🎬

  • Make a movie in your mind. Turn the words into pictures in your head. This is called visualizing.
  • Listen for key words. Key words are the most important words — words the speaker says loudly, says more than once, or says slowly.
  • Watch the speaker. Their face, hands and voice give you clues!

AFTER listening 💭

  • Retell the most important parts in your own words.
  • Ask a question about what you still wonder.
  • Connect — "This reminds me of…"

Listening with your eyes

People don't only talk with words. They also talk with their tone of voice (how the voice sounds), their face, and their body. This is called non-verbal communication.

If someone says "Great job!" in a cheerful, bouncy voice with a big smile, they mean it. If they say "Great job…" in a flat voice and roll their eyes, they might mean the opposite! When the words and the body don't match, the body often tells the truth.

📖 How Penguins Stay Warm

Emperor penguins live in Antarctica, the coldest place on Earth.

In winter, the wind is freezing. So the penguins huddle — they stand close together in a giant group.

The penguins in the middle get warm. The penguins on the outside get cold.

So they take turns! Slowly, the huddle moves, and every penguin gets a turn in the warm middle.

Which key words did you hear? What movie did your mind make?

🤯 Did You Know?

An emperor penguin huddle can have thousands of penguins, and the middle can get as warm as a warm summer day — about 37°C, even when it's colder than −40°C outside!

🤯 Did You Know?

Some scientists say a big part of a message's feeling comes from our face and voice, not just our words. When you're on the phone, you can even "hear" a smile — smiling changes the sound of your voice!

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Name one strategy for BEFORE, one for DURING, and one for AFTER listening.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why do you think the penguins take turns? What would happen if the middle penguins refused to move? Does this remind you of anything people do?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Say the sentence "I love broccoli" four different ways so that it means four different things (really love it, hate it, surprised, asking a question). What changed? The words — or something else?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Use before, during and after strategies while listening to a real non-fiction text or kids' podcast.

Materials

  • a short non-fiction read-aloud (library) or 5-minute kids' podcast/video (grown-up previews it)
  • paper folded into 3 columns: BEFORE · DURING · AFTER

Steps

  1. Before: Hear only the title. Write or draw: What do I know? What do I wonder?
  2. During: Listen. The grown-up pauses 3 times. Each time, draw the picture in your mind and say one key word.
  3. After: Retell the 3 most important parts. Ask one question. Make one connection.
  4. Tone Test: The grown-up says the same sentence ("We're going to the dentist") in 4 different voices. Guess the feeling each time.

Observation recording

BEFORE — I know / I wonderDURING — Key words & mind picturesAFTER — Retell / question / connection
How the grown-up said itThe feeling I guessedClue I used (voice, face, body)

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does visualizing mean? What are key words? What is non-verbal communication?

Part 2 — Penguin Retell (applying)

Retell "How Penguins Stay Warm" to someone who has never heard it. Use the words First, Then, Finally. Then write or dictate your retell and print one sentence yourself.

Part 3 — Feelings Detective (thinking)

Draw 4 faces showing: happy, worried, angry, surprised. Under each, write what the person's body might be doing (arms, shoulders, eyebrows).

✏️ Four feelings faces

🏠Homework

  1. Car Podcast Challenge. Listen to a short kids' podcast or audiobook chapter. Tell your family the 3 most important parts afterward.
  2. Mute Detective. Watch 2 minutes of a show with the sound OFF. Guess what is happening and how people feel, just from their faces and bodies. Then watch with sound. Were you right?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Can animals understand our tone of voice even if they don't understand our words?
  2. Is it possible to listen to a book? Is listening to a book “reading”?
  3. Why do some people talk with their hands a LOT and others hardly at all?
Lesson 3 of 11

Right Words, Right Time: Purpose & Audience

Discover why you talk differently to a baby, a best friend and a doctor — and learn when to speak, how to take turns, and how much to say.

B1.3B1.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

You probably talk to a baby, your best friend, and a police officer in three completely different ways — even if you're saying the same thing. Why? Who taught you to do that?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B1.3 identify the purpose of speaking (to tell, to ask, to explain, to persuade, to entertain) and who my audience is
  • B1.3 change the way I speak for formal and informal situations
  • B1.3 take turns, know when to speak, and know how much to say
  • B1.5 choose words that fit my audience

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B1.3 asks children to identify the purpose and audience for speaking in formal and informal contexts, and to use speaking strategies like taking turns, understanding when to speak, and knowing how much to say. These are called "pragmatic" language skills — the social rules of talking.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: act out saying "I'm hungry" to a baby, a friend, and a restaurant server. Laugh together.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Practise with the "Goldilocks Talking" game: too little, too much, just right.
  4. Role-play in Classwork — use props and hats!
💬 You can say

"Talking is like choosing clothes. You wear pajamas at home and fancy clothes to a wedding. You use different talking for different places too."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Some children talk a LOT (and struggle to stop), others give one-word answers. Both are normal at 6. Use visual cues: a "talking stick" for turns, and holding up fingers for "3 sentences, please."

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can switch between formal and informal language in role-play, and waits for a pause before speaking in a conversation at least most of the time.

💡 Teaching tip

Before real-world situations (doctor visit, ordering food, phoning Grandma), rehearse: "Who is our audience? What's our purpose? What will you say?"

📚The Lesson

Every time you talk, you have a purpose — a reason for talking. And you have an audience — the people who are listening.

Purposes for talking

  • 📣 To tell — "I saw a deer in the backyard!"
  • ❓ To ask — "Can I have a glass of water?"
  • 🧑‍🏫 To explain — "First you put the bread in the toaster…"
  • 🙏 To persuade (convince) — "Please can we go to the park? It's sunny!"
  • 😂 To entertain — telling a funny joke or story

Formal and informal

Informal talking is relaxed, like with family and friends. "Hey! Wanna play?" Formal talking is more careful and polite, like with a doctor, a principal, or when giving a speech. "Excuse me. May I please ask a question?"

Neither one is better. Smart speakers switch between them, like switching gears on a bike!

Talking rules

  1. Take turns. A conversation is like a game of catch — the ball goes back and forth. If you keep the ball, nobody else gets to play.
  2. Know when to speak. Wait for a pause. Don't talk while someone else is talking — unless it's an emergency!
  3. Know how much to say. Not too little ("Fine."), not too much (talking for 10 minutes without stopping). Just right, like Goldilocks!
  4. Stay on topic. If we're talking about dinosaurs, don't suddenly talk about socks!
📖 Maya Orders Lunch

Maya went to a restaurant with her dad.

The server smiled and asked, "What would you like?"

Maya said, "Hello! May I please have the grilled cheese and apple juice?"

"Of course," said the server.

Later, Maya ran to her cousin Leo. "Dude! The grilled cheese was SO good!"

How did Maya talk to the server? How did she talk to Leo? Why were they different?

🤯 Did You Know?

Babies start learning conversation turn-taking before they can even talk! When a parent coos to a baby and pauses, babies often "answer" with a coo of their own. Scientists call these back-and-forth moments serve and return, like tennis.

🤯 Did You Know?

In many First Nations traditions, people speak in a talking circle. A special object like a feather or a stone is passed around. Only the person holding it speaks — and everyone else listens with respect. Everyone gets a turn.

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Formal or informal? (a) Talking to your grandma at breakfast. (b) Asking the librarian for help. (c) Playing tag with friends. (d) Speaking at a school assembly.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Your friend talks and talks and never gives you a turn. How does it feel? What kind words could you use to get a turn?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Is it ever a good idea to interrupt someone? When? Think of at least two times.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Practise switching purpose and audience through role-play.

Materials

  • props or hats: a doctor's clipboard, a chef's hat, a crown, a baby doll, a talking stick (any stick or spoon)

Steps

  1. Same Message, Different Audience: Say "I need help finding my shoe" to: a baby, a friend, a store worker, the Queen/King. How does it change?
  2. Goldilocks Talking: The grown-up asks "What did you do today?" Answer three ways: too little, too much, just right. Which was best?
  3. Talking Circle: Sit in a circle with family. Pass the talking stick. Each person tells one thing they're thankful for. Only the holder talks.
  4. Real-world practice: Phone a relative OR order something at a store/café yourself (with a grown-up nearby).

Observation recording

AudienceWhat I saidFormal or informal?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Name the 5 purposes for talking. What is the difference between formal and informal?

Part 2 — Two Ways (applying)

Write two ways to ask for a cookie: one formal (to a neighbour you don't know well) and one informal (to your brother or sister). Print them yourself.

Part 3 — Conversation Comic (creating)

Draw a 4-box comic of two people having a good conversation — taking turns, asking questions, staying on topic. Add speech bubbles.

✏️ Your conversation comic

🏠Homework

  1. Purpose Spy. Listen to grown-ups talking this week. Find one example of each purpose: telling, asking, explaining, persuading, entertaining.
  2. Family Talking Circle. Hold a talking circle at dinner with the question "What was the best part of your day?"

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why do people use a special voice when they talk to babies and pets?
  2. Do you talk to yourself in your head? Is that a conversation? Who is the audience?
  3. If robots could talk, should they talk formally or informally to kids?
Lesson 4 of 11

Talking Without Words: Faces, Hands & Voices

Explore how expression, gestures and body language add meaning — and sometimes say more than words.

B1.4B1.2D3.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

A baby who can't say a single word can still tell you it's hungry, happy, scared, or wants to be picked up. How? How much could YOU say without any words at all?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B1.4 use my face, gestures and body to add meaning to what I say
  • B1.4 change my voice (loud/soft, fast/slow, high/low) to show feelings
  • B1.4 read other people's faces and bodies to understand their messages
  • B1.2 notice non-verbal clues while I listen

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B1.4 asks children to identify and use oral and non-verbal communication strategies, including expression, gestures, and body language. This is how children read social situations and how they bring life to reading aloud and presenting (D3.2).

Voice "dials"

Teach 4 dials you can turn on your voice: volume (loud/soft), speed (fast/slow), pitch (high/low), and pause (stopping for effect).

How to teach it

  1. Play "Baby Talk" — communicate a need without words.
  2. Read the lesson. Practise every gesture and expression.
  3. Play charades and "Emotion Voice" (Classwork).
  4. Read a picture book aloud together, each taking a character, using big expression.
💬 You can say

"Your face and body are like the pictures in a picture book. They help people understand your words."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Gestures differ across cultures. A thumbs-up is friendly in Canada but rude in some countries; nodding means "yes" in most places but "no" in a few (such as Bulgaria). Use this to build curiosity, not judgement.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can act out at least 5 emotions recognizably and uses voice changes when reading dialogue aloud.

💡 Teaching tip

Mo Willems' Elephant & Piggie books are perfect for expression practice — huge, clear emotions and speech bubbles.

📚The Lesson

People can talk without saying a single word! When you wave hello, shrug your shoulders, or smile, you are sending a message. This is non-verbal communication — "non" means not, and "verbal" means with words.

Three ways to talk without words

  • 😊 Facial expressions — what your face does. Eyebrows up = surprised! Eyebrows down = angry or thinking. A smile, a frown, a wink…
  • 👋 Gestures — moving your hands and arms to send a message: waving, pointing, thumbs-up, shaking your head.
  • 🧍 Body language — the way you hold your whole body. Standing tall can show you feel confident. Slumped shoulders might show you're sad or tired. Crossed arms might show you're upset — or just cold!

Your voice has dials 🎛️

Even when you use words, HOW you say them changes the meaning. - 🔊 Volume — loud or soft - 🐇 Speed — fast or slow - 🎵 Pitch — high or low - ⏸️ Pause — stopping for a moment... to make people wait!

Try saying "There's a spider on your head" in a calm, slow voice. Now say it FAST and LOUD and HIGH! Which one makes people jump?

When words and body don't match

If someone says "I'm not scared" but their voice is shaking and they're hiding behind the couch — which do you believe? Good listeners watch for clues.

Gestures around the world

Some gestures mean different things in different places: - 👍 In Canada, thumbs-up means "Good!" In some countries, it is rude. - 🙂↕️ In most places, nodding means "yes." In Bulgaria, a nod can mean "no"! - 🙏 In Thailand, people greet each other with a wai — palms together and a small bow. In Japan, people often bow. In many places, people shake hands or hug.

🤯 Did You Know?

Sign languages are full languages made with hands, faces and bodies. American Sign Language (ASL) and Quebec Sign Language (LSQ) are used in Canada. There's even an Indigenous sign language — Plains Sign Talk — that many First Nations of the plains used to talk between nations that spoke different languages!

🤯 Did You Know?

Your face has over 40 muscles, and people can make thousands of different expressions. Scientists have found that some expressions — like happy, sad, and surprised — are recognized by people all over the world.

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Without talking, show: "Come here," "I don't know," "Be quiet," and "Yay!" Which gestures did you use?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why might someone cross their arms? Think of 3 different reasons. Can body language be misunderstood?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Emojis are little faces and gestures we put in writing. Why do you think people invented them? Can an emoji be misunderstood like a real gesture?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Practise using and reading non-verbal communication and voice dials.

Materials

  • slips of paper with emotions (happy, sad, scared, excited, bored, angry, proud, confused), a small mirror

Steps

  1. Mirror Faces: Look in a mirror and make each emotion's face. Notice your eyebrows, eyes and mouth.
  2. Emotion Charades: Pick a slip. Act it out with NO words. The other person guesses.
  3. Voice Dials: Say "The cat is in the kitchen" 5 ways: whisper, shout, super-slow, super-fast, with a dramatic pause.
  4. Silent Story: Tell a tiny story ("I found a present, opened it, and it was a frog!") using only gestures and faces.
  5. Read-aloud theatre: Read an Elephant & Piggie book (or any dialogue book), each taking a character, with BIG expression.

Observation recording

EmotionWhat my face didWhat my body didDid they guess?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What are facial expressions, gestures, and body language? Name the 4 voice dials.

Part 2 — Feelings Chart (applying)

Draw a chart with 4 people showing 4 different feelings using only their faces and bodies. Label each feeling and one clue.

✏️ My feelings chart

Part 3 — Performance Plan (thinking)

Choose one page of a favourite picture book to read aloud to your family. Plan it: Where will you get loud? Soft? Where will you pause? What gesture will you use? Then perform it!

🏠Homework

  1. Learn 3 signs. Learn to sign "hello," "thank you," and "friend" in ASL (with a grown-up, using a kids' ASL video). Teach your family.
  2. Body Language Spy. At the grocery store or park, notice 3 people's body language. What do you think they were feeling? (Keep it private and kind!)

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Can animals read our faces? How does a dog know when you're sad?
  2. If you could only communicate with gestures for a whole day, what would be hardest to say?
  3. Why do we cry when we're very happy, not just when we're sad?
Lesson 5 of 11

Speaking Like a Storyteller: Word Choice & Linking Words

Swap boring words for brilliant ones, use your new vocabulary, and join your ideas with linking words so your talking flows.

B1.5B1.3B2.7
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

If you told a friend, “I went to the place and saw a thing and it was good,” would they have ANY idea what happened? What's missing — and how could you fix it with just a few words?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B1.5 choose interesting, exact words when I speak (not just “good,” “nice,” “said”)
  • B1.5 use new vocabulary words I've learned when I talk
  • B1.5 use linking words (first, then, because, so, but, finally) to join my ideas into a smooth retell
  • B1.3 tell a short oral story that is clear and in order

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B1.5 asks children to use appropriate word choice, including new vocabulary, grammar, and cohesive phrases and sentences when speaking. "Cohesive" means the ideas stick together — using linking words like first, then, because, so. Oral storytelling is the rehearsal for written storytelling (Strand D).

How to teach it

  1. Hook: say the vague sentence, then say the exact one: "I went to the aquarium and saw a giant octopus squeeze through a tiny hole and it was AMAZING!"
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Play "Boring Word Jail" (Classwork) — lock up tired words and replace them.
  4. Your child tells a 1-minute oral story using linking words; record it on your phone.
💬 You can say

"Words are like paint colours. 'Good' is plain grey. 'Delicious,' 'hilarious,' and 'enormous' are bright colours!"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

When children first learn linking words, they chain everything with "and then… and then… and then…" This is a normal developmental stage! Celebrate it, then introduce variety: next, after that, suddenly, finally, because, so.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

in an oral retell of their day, your child uses 3+ different linking words and at least one "vivid" word.

💡 Teaching tip

Pick a "Word of the Day" at breakfast (e.g., enormous, curious, furious, delicious). Everyone tries to use it before bedtime.

📚The Lesson

Great storytellers are word collectors. They choose words carefully, like picking the perfect crayon. This is called word choice.

Boring words vs. brilliant words

Some words are tired because we use them SO much: good, nice, bad, big, said, went, fun. They're not wrong — they just don't paint a clear picture. Look:

  • "The dog was big." → "The dog was enormous!" / "The dog was as big as a pony!"
  • "The pizza was good." → "The pizza was delicious — cheesy and crispy!"
  • "I went to the park." → "I raced to the park." / "I skipped to the park."
  • "She said." → "She whispered." / "She shouted." / "She giggled."

Each brilliant word gives the listener a clearer picture — and tells them how it felt!

Using your new words

Every time you learn a new word, try to use it three times that day. That's how it moves into your brain for keeps!

Linking words: the glue for ideas

When you tell a story or explain something, your ideas need to stick together. Linking words are the glue.

Time-order words: first, next, then, after that, suddenly, later, finally, at the end Reason words: because, so Different-idea words: but, or

Without glue: "I woke up. I ate. I went outside. It rained. I came in." With glue: "First, I woke up and ate breakfast. Then I went outside, but it started to rain, so I came back in. Finally, I built a blanket fort instead!"

Which one sounds like a storyteller?

📖 The Squirrel Thief

First, Grandpa put peanuts in the bird feeder.

Then a fluffy grey squirrel crept up the pole.

The squirrel stretched, but the feeder was too high.

Suddenly, it leaped from a branch and landed right on the feeder!

Finally, it munched every single peanut because it was starving.

Grandpa groaned. The birds squawked!

🤯 Did You Know?

The Oxford English Dictionary lists more than 600 different meanings for the word "run" — that's more than any other English word! Think: run a race, a run in your tights, a runny nose, run a business, the car runs…

🤯 Did You Know?

Scientists think kids learn about 8 to 10 new words every day, on average, during their early school years — many of them from listening to stories read aloud.

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Replace the boring word: "The cake was good." "The man said, 'Watch out!'" "The elephant was big."

⭐⭐ Stretch

Is "said" ALWAYS a boring word? When might a plain word be the best choice?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Some words sound like what they mean — slither sounds slippery, crunch sounds crunchy. Can you think of 3 more words that sound like their meaning? Why do you think words like this exist?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Replace tired words with brilliant ones and tell a smooth oral story with linking words.

Materials

  • a shoebox "jail," slips of paper, a picture book with lots of action, a phone to record (with permission)

Steps

  1. Boring Word Jail: Write good, nice, big, said, went, fun, bad on slips. "Lock them up!" For each, brainstorm 3 brilliant replacement words together. Make a "Brilliant Words" poster.
  2. Linking-word cards: Write First, Then, But, So, Because, Suddenly, Finally on cards.
  3. Picture Story: Look at a wordless picture book (e.g., Journey by Aaron Becker) or a sequence of 4 photos from your day. Tell the story out loud, flipping over a linking card for each part.
  4. Record your story. Listen back. Count your linking words and brilliant words!

Observation recording

Boring wordBrilliant word 1Brilliant word 2Brilliant word 3

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What are linking words? Name 5. What is word choice?

Part 2 — Glue it together (applying)

Add linking words to make this story flow: "I planted a seed. I watered it. I waited. A tiny sprout came up. It grew into a sunflower."

Part 3 — My Oral Story (creating)

Tell a true story about something that happened to you (a trip, a funny moment, a surprise). Use at least 4 linking words and 3 brilliant words. A grown-up writes it down while you speak. Then you print the first sentence and illustrate it.

🏠Homework

  1. Word of the Day. Each morning this week, choose a brilliant word. Use it 3 times before bedtime. Keep a list on the fridge.
  2. Bedtime Retell. Each night, tell a grown-up about your day using First, Then, After that, Finally.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Who decides what a word means? Could you make up a word and get everyone to use it?
  2. Why does English have so many words that mean almost the same thing — like big, huge, giant, enormous, and gigantic?
  3. What's the most beautiful-sounding word you know? What makes it beautiful?
Lesson 6 of 11

What Makes a Sentence?

Discover the secret recipe of every sentence: a WHO, a DOING part, a capital letter, and an end mark.

B3.1B3.3B3.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

“The giant purple dinosaur.” Is that a sentence? It has a capital letter and a period... but something feels unfinished. What's missing — and why does your brain feel itchy until it knows?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B3.1 explain that a sentence is a complete thought with a WHO/WHAT part and a DOING part
  • B3.1 tell the difference between a complete sentence and a sentence fragment
  • B3.3 begin every sentence with a capital letter and end it with an end mark
  • B3.2 identify the naming part (noun) and the action part (verb) in a simple sentence

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B3.1 asks children to identify and construct simple and compound sentences; B3.3 asks them to use a capital letter at the beginning of a sentence and the appropriate punctuation mark at the end. The concept of a "complete thought" is the heart of writing.

The sentence recipe

WHO or WHAT (the naming part / subject) + DOING or BEING (the action part / predicate) = a complete thought. Plus a capital letter at the start and an end mark (. ? !) at the end.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: say "The giant purple dinosaur…" and stop. Watch your child wait for more. That itch is what a fragment feels like!
  2. Read the lesson. Use two colours: blue for the WHO part, red for the DOING part.
  3. Sentence-building with cards (Classwork) — silly sentences are encouraged.
💬 You can say

"A sentence is like a sandwich. The WHO is the bread, the DOING is the filling. Without both, it's not a sandwich!"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often think a sentence is "a line of writing" or anything ending with a period. Also, they often think longer = more of a sentence. "Dogs bark." is a complete sentence! "The big brown dog in the yard" is not.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

given 6 word groups, your child can sort sentences from fragments and fix the fragments by adding what's missing.

💡 Teaching tip

When your child writes, ask: "Read me your sentence. Does it tell WHO and what they DID?"

📚The Lesson

Sentences are everywhere: in books, signs, messages and in your own talking! But what makes a group of words a sentence?

The Secret Recipe

A sentence is a complete thought. It needs two parts:

  1. WHO or WHAT the sentence is about — the naming part
  2. What they DO (or what they ARE) — the action part
🧍 WHO / WHAT
The frog+🏃 DOING
jumped into the pond=✅ The frog jumped into the pond.

Fragments: broken sentences

A fragment is a piece of a sentence. It's missing a part, so it feels unfinished. - "The giant purple dinosaur." ← WHO, but no DOING! What did it do? - "Ran across the field." ← DOING, but no WHO! Who ran? - "The giant purple dinosaur ran across the field." ✅ Complete!

Capital letter at the start, end mark at the finish

Every sentence starts with a capital letter, like a big "GO!" sign. Every sentence ends with an end mark, like a stop sign: - . a period — for telling - ? a question mark — for asking - ! an exclamation mark — for strong feelings

Short sentences are still sentences!

"Birds fly." "I laughed." "Babies cry." These are tiny — but they have a WHO and a DOING. They're complete! Long doesn't mean complete.

📖 Silly Sentence Soup

The hungry shark ate a pickle.

My grandma danced on the roof.

A tiny ant lifted a school bus.

The moon sang a lullaby.

Can you find the WHO and the DOING in each one?

🤯 Did You Know?

The longest sentence ever published in a famous English novel has around 13,955 words (in The Rotters' Club by Jonathan Coe)! And one of the shortest complete sentences in English is just one word: "Go." — the WHO ("you") is hidden but understood!

🧠 Brain moment

When you hear half a sentence, your brain automatically tries to guess the ending. That's why fragments feel "itchy" — your brain is waiting for the missing piece!

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Sentence or fragment? (a) The cat slept. (b) Under the big table. (c) My brother. (d) We ate ice cream.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Fix each fragment: "Jumped over the log." "The shiny red bicycle." Add the missing part.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

"Go!" and "Sit." have only one word. How can they be complete sentences? Where's the hidden WHO?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Build complete sentences using WHO cards and DOING cards, then fix fragments.

Materials

  • 10 blue cards (WHO): The dog, My mom, A robot, The baby, I, A dragon, The teacher, My friend, An owl, The king
  • 10 red cards (DOING): jumped on the bed, ate spaghetti, flew to the moon, sang loudly, fell asleep, laughed, built a castle, sneezed, swam in the lake, read a book
  • paper, pencils

Steps

  1. Mix up both piles. Pick one blue and one red. Read your (maybe silly!) sentence out loud.
  2. Copy 5 favourite sentences. Start with a capital, end with a period.
  3. Fragment Hospital: The grown-up reads word groups. Is it healthy (a sentence) or broken (a fragment)? "Heal" the broken ones!
  4. Walk the sentence: Say a sentence. Take one step per word. Clap at the end for the period!

Observation recording

WHO partDOING partMy complete sentence

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What two parts does every sentence need? What goes at the beginning? What goes at the end?

Part 2 — Colour code (applying)

Copy these into your notebook. Underline the WHO in blue and the DOING in red: 1. The puppy chased its tail. 2. Aisha found a shiny rock. 3. Big grey clouds covered the sun.

Part 3 — My Sentence Book (creating)

Make a 4-page mini book. On each page, write one complete sentence about your favourite animal and draw a picture. Check each one: capital letter? WHO? DOING? end mark?

🏠Homework

  1. Sentence Spotting. Find 3 sentences on cereal boxes, signs or books. Point to the capital and the end mark. Find the WHO and the DOING.
  2. Dinner Fragments Game. At dinner, a grown-up says fragments like "The fork…" and you finish the sentence as silly as you like.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Do people in other languages make sentences the same way? (In some languages, the doing word comes FIRST!)
  2. Could you tell a whole story in sentences with just two words each?
  3. Why do we need periods? What would reading be like without them?
Lesson 7 of 11

Four Kinds of Sentences: Tell, Ask, Command, Exclaim!

Meet the four sentence types — telling, asking, commanding and exclaiming — and the punctuation that goes with each.

B3.1B3.3B1.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

“You ate the whole cake.” “You ate the whole cake?” “You ate the whole cake!” The words are exactly the same. So why does each one make you feel something different?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B3.1 identify and write telling (declarative), asking (interrogative), commanding (imperative) and exclaiming (exclamatory) sentences
  • B3.3 choose the right end mark: period, question mark, or exclamation mark
  • B1.4 read each kind of sentence aloud with the right voice
  • B3.3 explain how an end mark changes the meaning of a sentence

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B3.1 names four sentence types by their official names: declarative, imperative, interrogative, and exclamatory. Grade 1 children can learn these — the grown-up names make kids feel powerful! Use kid names first, then the official ones.

  • Telling → declarative → tells a fact or idea → .
  • Asking → interrogative → asks a question → ?
  • Bossy/Command → imperative → tells someone to do something → . or !
  • Wow! → exclamatory → shows strong feeling → !

How to teach it

  1. Hook: read "You ate the whole cake" three ways, with big acting.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Play "Punctuation Actions" (Classwork): each mark has a movement.
  4. Read Don't Let the Pigeon Drive the Bus! — it's full of all four types.
💬 You can say

"Punctuation is like a secret code that tells the reader's voice what to do."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often put question marks on any sentence with "I wonder" ("I wonder where he is?") — actually that's a telling sentence. Also, many children overuse exclamation marks!!!!! Teach "one is enough — save them for real excitement."

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can write one of each type about a topic, with correct end marks, and read them aloud with matching expression.

💡 Teaching tip

Question words often start asking sentences: who, what, where, when, why, how, can, do, is, are. Make a "question word" card.

📚The Lesson

Sentences have different jobs, just like people! There are four kinds of sentences. Each one has a kid name and a grown-up name — you can learn both!

1. Telling sentences — declarative

A telling sentence tells you something: a fact, an idea or an opinion. It ends with a period (.). - "Polar bears live in the Arctic." - "I like strawberries."

2. Asking sentences — interrogative

An asking sentence asks a question. It ends with a question mark (?). Many start with a question word: who, what, where, when, why, how, can, do, is, are, will. - "Where do polar bears sleep?" - "Can I have a snack?"

3. Command sentences — imperative

A command sentence tells someone to DO something. It's a bit bossy! It usually ends with a period (.) or, if it's urgent, an exclamation mark (!). The WHO ("you") is hidden. - "Please close the door." - "Stop!"

4. Wow sentences — exclamatory

A wow sentence shows a strong feeling — excitement, surprise, fear, or anger. It ends with an exclamation mark (!). - "What a huge polar bear!" - "I can't believe it snowed in June!"

Your voice follows the marks

  • A period . → your voice goes down and stops.
  • A question mark ? → your voice goes up at the end.
  • An exclamation mark ! → your voice gets strong and excited.
📖 The Surprise Box

Mom put a big box on the table.

"What's inside?" asked Nia.

"Open it and see," said Mom.

Nia peeked inside. A tiny kitten looked up at her.

"A kitten! I can't believe it!" Nia shouted.

Can you find all four kinds of sentences?

🤯 Did You Know?

For hundreds of years, old typewriters did NOT have an exclamation mark key! To make one, people typed a period, pressed backspace, and typed an apostrophe on top of it. The exclamation mark key only became common in the 1970s.

🤯 Did You Know?

The ampersand (&) used to be taught as the 27th letter of the English alphabet! Children would finish the alphabet song with "…X, Y, Z, and per se and" — which slowly got squished into the word "ampersand."

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Name the kind of sentence: (a) Is it raining? (b) Wash your hands. (c) It is raining. (d) Wow, look at that rainbow!

⭐⭐ Stretch

Change "The dog is hungry." into an asking sentence, a command sentence, and a wow sentence.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think command sentences hide the word "you"? Could a command ever be polite? Could a question ever be bossy? ("Would you PLEASE clean your room?")

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Recognize and create all four kinds of sentences and match each with its end mark and voice.

Materials

  • 3 big cards: . ? ! · sentence strips (grown-up writes 12 sentences with NO end marks) · a toy microphone (optional)

Steps

  1. Punctuation Actions: Period = stomp once. Question mark = shrug with hands up. Exclamation mark = jump! The grown-up reads sentences; you do the action.
  2. Sort the strips into 4 piles: telling, asking, command, wow. Add the missing end mark with a marker.
  3. Interview: Use the microphone to interview a family member. Ask 5 asking sentences. Write their answers as telling sentences.
  4. Robot Commands: Give a family "robot" 4 command sentences. The robot does ONLY exactly what you say!

Observation recording

Telling (.)Asking (?)Command (. or !)Wow (!)

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Name the four kinds of sentences (kid names and grown-up names) and the end mark for each.

Part 2 — Fix the marks (applying)

Add the correct end mark and write why: 1. Where is my backpack 2. Watch out for the puddle 3. My backpack is blue 4. Hooray, we won

Part 3 — Four-Sentence Comic (creating)

Draw a 4-box comic about a surprise. Box 1: a telling sentence. Box 2: an asking sentence. Box 3: a command. Box 4: a wow sentence!

✏️ My four-sentence comic

🏠Homework

  1. Question Jar. Write 5 asking sentences you wonder about (Why is the sky blue? How do fish sleep?). Put them in a jar. Find the answer to one this week.
  2. Punctuation Hunt. Find all 3 end marks in a book or magazine. Read those sentences with the right voice.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. What if there were a new punctuation mark to show that someone is joking? What would it look like? (Some people have actually invented one!)
  2. Why do questions make your voice go up at the end?
  3. Which kind of sentence do you think grown-ups say to kids the most? Which do kids say the most?
Lesson 8 of 11

Joining Ideas: and, but, so, or

Use joining words to glue two sentences into one stronger compound sentence.

B3.1B3.2B1.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

“I wanted to go outside. It was raining.” Two sentences, two separate ideas. What ONE tiny word could you put in the middle to show how these two ideas are connected — and how does that word change the whole meaning?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B3.1 identify the difference between a simple sentence (one idea) and a compound sentence (two ideas joined)
  • B3.2 use the conjunctions and, but, so, and or to join ideas
  • B3.2 explain what each joining word means (and = more, but = different, so = because of that, or = a choice)
  • B1.5 use compound sentences when I speak to make my ideas flow

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B3.1 asks children to construct simple and compound sentences; B3.2 asks them to use common conjunctions. Conjunctions are thinking words: but shows contrast, so shows cause and effect, or shows choice. Using them well means your child is thinking logically.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: try each joining word in the hook sentence. "I wanted to go outside, but it was raining." "...so I stayed in"? Discuss meaning.
  2. Read the lesson; make the "FANBOYS-lite" cards: and, but, so, or.
  3. Play "Sentence Train" (Classwork).
💬 You can say

"A joining word is like a bridge between two islands. The kind of bridge you choose tells people how the islands are connected."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children tend to use only "and" and chain everything together ("…and…and…and…"). Also, they may join ideas that don't go together with so ("I like cats, so it is Tuesday"). Always ask: "Does that make sense? Does the joining word match the connection?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

given two simple sentences, your child can choose the best conjunction and explain why; they use but or so spontaneously in speech.

💡 Teaching tip

In Grade 1, commas before conjunctions are not required — focus on meaning.

📚The Lesson

A simple sentence has one complete idea. - "I have a dog." - "My dog is fluffy."

A compound sentence joins two complete ideas together with a joining word. Joining words are called conjunctions.

I have a dog+and+my dog is fluffy.

The four joining words

- and — adds MORE of the same kind of idea. ➕ "I ate pizza, and my sister ate pasta." - but — shows something DIFFERENT or surprising. ↔️ "I wanted to swim, but the water was too cold." - so — shows what HAPPENED BECAUSE of the first idea. ➡️ "I was thirsty, so I drank some water." - or — gives a CHOICE. 🤔 "We can play outside, or we can build a fort."

Joining words change meaning!

- "It was sunny, and we went to the beach." (it all went well!) - "It was sunny, but we stayed home." (surprise! why?) - "It was sunny, so we went to the beach." (the sun is the reason) Same first idea — totally different stories!

📖 Robo's Big Day

Robo the robot wanted to bake a cake, but he didn't know how.

He could ask his friend Zara, or he could read a recipe.

He read the recipe, and he gathered the eggs and flour.

He forgot to turn on the oven, so the cake stayed gooey.

Robo laughed, and he tried again!

🤯 Did You Know?

The word "and" is one of the most common words in the English language — it's usually in the top five, along with the, of, a, and to. You probably say it hundreds of times a day!

🧠 Brain moment

Words like but and so show that your brain understands how ideas connect — cause and effect, and surprise. Scientists call this reasoning. Every time you use because or so correctly, you're doing the same kind of thinking scientists do!

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Choose and, but, so, or or: (a) I was tired, ___ I went to bed. (b) I like apples, ___ I don't like pears. (c) Do you want milk ___ juice?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Finish each sentence 2 ways: "The dog barked, but ___." "The dog barked, so ___." How are your endings different?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think "and" is so much more common than "but"? Is a story with lots of "buts" more interesting? Why?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Build compound sentences with conjunction cards and test how meaning changes.

Materials

  • 4 "joining word" cards (and, but, so, or) in bright colours
  • 12 simple sentence strips (e.g., I found a shell. The sun came out. I lost my hat. We went to the store. The ice cream melted. I was scared.)
  • toy train cars or boxes (optional)

Steps

  1. Sentence Train: Each sentence strip is a train car. A joining word card is the hook between cars. Build trains that make sense!
  2. Read each train aloud. Does it make sense? Change the joining word. Does it still make sense?
  3. Joining Word Roulette: Grown-up says a first half ("I went to the zoo…"), you flip a card and must finish with that word.
  4. Copy 4 best compound sentences, circling the conjunction.

Observation recording

First ideaJoining wordSecond ideaDoes it make sense?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a compound sentence? What does each joining word mean: and, but, so, or?

Part 2 — Join them (applying)

Join each pair with the best conjunction: 1. I have a cat. I have a fish. 2. It was dark. I turned on the light. 3. I wanted a cookie. The jar was empty. 4. We can read. We can draw.

Part 3 — My Day in Compound Sentences (writing)

Write 4 compound sentences about your day. Use each joining word once. Illustrate one.

🏠Homework

  1. Conjunction Count. Listen to a grown-up read a story. Every time you hear "but" or "so," give a thumbs-up. How many did you catch?
  2. But-So Story. With your family, tell a round-robin story: each person adds a sentence starting with "But…" or "So…" (e.g., "A cat wanted fish. But the fish was in a bowl. So the cat…").

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Could you tell a whole story with only one enormous sentence, using lots of joining words? Would it be fun to listen to?
  2. Why is “but” sometimes a sad word and sometimes an exciting word?
  3. Do animals understand cause and effect — “I did this, so that happened”?
Lesson 9 of 11

Naming Words & the Mighty “I”

Explore nouns — naming words for people, places, animals and things — plus singular and plural, special names, and why “I” is always a capital.

B3.2B3.3B2.6
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Why do we write one mouse, two MICE — but one house, two HOUSES (not “hice”)? And why do we always write “I” with a capital, even in the middle of a sentence, when we don't do that for “you” or “me”?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B3.2 identify nouns: words that name a person, place, animal or thing
  • B3.2 change singular nouns to plural nouns using -s or -es, and know some special plurals (child → children)
  • B3.2 use the pronoun “I” correctly in sentences
  • B3.3 use capital letters for names of people and places, days, months, and the word “I”

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B3.2 asks children to understand common singular and plural nouns and using the pronoun "I". B3.3 covers capitalization. Plural -s/-es is also a spelling pattern (B2.5, B2.6) — so this lesson connects sentence knowledge and spelling.

Rules for Grade 1 plurals

  • Most nouns: add -s (cat → cats)
  • Nouns ending in s, x, z, ch, sh: add -es (box → boxes, bus → buses, dish → dishes, lunch → lunches) — because you can hear an extra syllable!
  • Irregular (just learn them): child → children, man → men, woman → women, mouse → mice, tooth → teeth, foot → feet, person → people, sheep → sheep, fish → fish

How to teach it

  1. Hook: Say "One mouse, two ___" and "One house, two ___." Enjoy the confusion.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Noun hunt around the house with sticky notes (Classwork).
  4. The "-es" test: say the plural aloud and clap syllables: box-es (2 claps) needs -es.
💬 You can say

"A noun is a naming word. If you can put 'a,' 'the,' or 'some' in front of it, it's probably a noun!"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often write "i" in lowercase, and write "me and my friend went" — in Grade 1, just focus on "I" as a capital and using "I" at the start of a sentence (I went…). Also watch for "mouses," "foots" — these are smart errors (they know the rule!); celebrate the logic, then teach the exception.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can find 5 nouns in a sentence set, make regular plurals correctly in writing, and always capitalizes "I" and their own name.

💡 Teaching tip

"Common nouns" (dog, city) vs. "proper nouns" (Rex, Toronto) — use the phrase "special names get capitals."

📚The Lesson

Everything in the world has a name! Words that name things are called nouns. A noun can name: - 👩 a person — teacher, baby, grandpa, doctor, Aisha - 🏠 a place — park, kitchen, school, Canada, Niagara Falls - 🐸 an animal — frog, moose, spider, whale - ⚽ a thing — ball, spoon, book, snowflake, bicycle

Noun test: Can you put a, the, or some in front of it? "a frog," "the park," "some spoons" — yes! They're nouns.

One or more? Singular and plural

Singular means ONE. Plural means MORE THAN ONE. - Most words just add -s: one cat → two cats, one tree → many trees - Words that end in s, x, z, ch, or sh add -es: one box → two boxes, one lunch → two lunches, one wish → three wishes Say them out loud — you can hear an extra part: box-es, wish-es!

Rule-breakers! 🙃

Some plurals don't follow the rules. You just have to learn them: WORDS: child → children | mouse → mice | tooth → teeth | foot → feet | man → men | person → people | sheep → sheep | fish → fish | goose → geese

Special names get capitals

Some nouns are the special name of ONE person, place, pet or thing. They're called proper nouns, and they ALWAYS start with a capital letter: - people and pets: Maya, Grandma Lee, Rex - places: Toronto, Lake Ontario, Canada - days and months: Monday, December

The Mighty "I"

When you talk about yourself, you use the word I. "I like tacos." "Mom and I went shopping." The word I is ALWAYS a capital letter, no matter where it is in the sentence. It's the only English word like that!

🤯 Did You Know?

English is one of the only languages in the world that capitalizes the word for "I." In French, it's je; in Spanish, yo; in German, ich — all lowercase! Nobody knows for certain why English does it. One idea: a small "i" all by itself was easy to lose or mistake for a mark on the page, so writers made it big and tall so readers wouldn't miss it.

🤯 Did You Know?

Some animal groups have amazing plural names: a group of crows is a murder, a group of owls is a parliament, and a group of flamingos is a flamboyance!

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Find the nouns: "The girl gave her dog a bone in the park."

⭐⭐ Stretch

Make these plural: fox, frog, bench, tooth, bus, child. Which ones follow the rules? Which are rule-breakers?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If one mouse is two mice, why isn't one house two "hice"? Invent your own rule-breaker plural for a made-up animal (one zorp, two ___?).

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Hunt for nouns, sort them, and practise plurals and capitals.

Materials

  • sticky notes, markers, a bag of small objects (buttons, blocks, spoons), 4 labels: PERSON · PLACE · ANIMAL · THING

Steps

  1. Noun Hunt: Walk around your home. Write a sticky note for 10 nouns and stick them on the objects!
  2. Sort: Bring the sticky notes back and sort them under PERSON, PLACE, ANIMAL, THING.
  3. Plural Machine: Put one object down. Say "one ___." Add more. Say the plural. Clap to check if it needs -es.
  4. Capital Check: Write your full name, your street, your city, and today's day. Circle every capital letter.

Observation recording

PersonPlaceAnimalThing
Singular (one)Plural (more)-s, -es, or rule-breaker?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a noun? What is the difference between singular and plural? Which nouns need capital letters?

Part 2 — Fix it! (editing)

Fix the mistakes: "i saw three foxs and two mouses in toronto on monday."

Part 3 — All About I (writing)

Write 5 sentences about yourself that start with "I" — for example, "I can ride a bike." Remember: capital I every time! Draw a self-portrait.

🏠Homework

  1. Plural Detective. Find 5 plural nouns on food packages in your kitchen (like "cookies," "peaches"). Which ones use -es?
  2. Name Map. Draw a map of your neighbourhood and label 5 proper nouns: street names, stores, parks — all with capitals!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why does English have rule-breakers? Who decided “mice” instead of “mouses”?
  2. Is “love” a noun? Can you touch it? What about “Tuesday”?
  3. If you could name a brand-new animal, what would you call it — and what would the plural be?
Lesson 10 of 11

Action Words Travel in Time

Verbs are action words — and they have a secret power: they can tell us WHEN something happens.

B3.2B2.6B1.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

If you say “I jump,” “I jumped,” and “I will jump,” your body could be doing the exact same thing — but your words have sent the jump to three different times. How can one tiny change in a word work like a time machine?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B3.2 identify verbs (action words) in sentences
  • B3.2 use verbs to show past (yesterday), present (today/now) and future (tomorrow) time
  • B2.6 add -ed to show the past, and hear its three sounds (/t/, /d/, /ed/)
  • B3.2 use some irregular past-tense verbs correctly (went, ate, saw, ran)

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B3.2 asks children to understand the past, present, and future verb tenses. The -ed ending also appears in B2.6 (morphology), where Grade 1 children learn "the three sounds of -ed": jumped (/t/), played (/d/), painted (/ed/).

Grade 1 tenses

  • Past (already happened): walked, played, jumped. Irregular: went, ate, saw, ran, came, sat, made, said, had.
  • Present (happening now or usually): walk/walks, am walking.
  • Future (hasn't happened yet): will walk, am going to walk.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: do the jump three ways, pointing behind you (past), at the floor (present), and ahead (future).
  2. Read the lesson; make a timeline on the floor with tape: YESTERDAY · TODAY · TOMORROW.
  3. Play "Time Machine Verbs" (Classwork).
💬 You can say

"Verbs are time travellers. The ending tells you when the action happened."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Grade 1 children say "I goed," "I runned," "I eated" — this shows they've learned the -ed rule and are over-applying it! It's a sign of smart learning. Model the correct form naturally: "Oh, you WENT to the park? What did you do after you went?" No need to correct harshly.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can change a sentence into all three times orally, and correctly uses at least 5 common irregular past verbs in speech.

💡 Teaching tip

The three sounds of -ed: have your child put a hand on their throat. Jumped ends with a /t/; played ends with a buzzy /d/; painted, wanted have an extra syllable /ed/ (after t or d).

📚The Lesson

Verbs are action words. They tell what someone or something does: run, jump, swim, eat, sing, sleep, think, laugh. Every sentence needs a verb!

Verb test: Can you do it? Can you say "I ___" or "She ___s"? "I dance." "She dances." Yes — it's a verb!

Verbs are time travellers ⏳

Verbs have a special power: they tell us when something happens.

⬅️ PAST
yesterday
I jumped→⏺ PRESENT
now / today
I jump→➡️ FUTURE
tomorrow
I will jump
  • Past — it already happened. Many past verbs end in -ed: I walked, we played.
  • Present — it's happening now or happens often: I walk, she walks, they are walking.
  • Future — it hasn't happened yet. We use will or going to: I will walk, I'm going to walk.

The three sounds of -ed 🎵

Put your hand on your throat and say these: - jumped — sounds like /t/ (jumpt) - played — sounds like /d/ (playd) - painted — sounds like /ed/ (paint-ed) — an extra beat! This happens after words ending in t or d: wanted, needed, landed. Even though they sound different, we always spell it -ed!

Rule-breakers! 🙃

Some past verbs don't use -ed. They change in special ways: WORDS: go → went | eat → ate | see → saw | run → ran | come → came | sit → sat | make → made | say → said | have → had | swim → swam

📖 Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow

Yesterday, I planted a tiny seed. I watered it and I waited.

Today, I see a little green sprout! I am so excited.

Tomorrow, I will measure it. Maybe it will grow as tall as me one day!

🤯 Did You Know?

Some languages don't change their verbs for time at all! In Mandarin Chinese, the verb for "eat" (chī) stays the same — speakers add time words like "yesterday" or special little words to show when. English puts the time right inside the verb!

🤯 Did You Know?

Little kids all over the world make the same smart mistakes, like "I goed" and "two mouses." Scientists love these mistakes — they prove that kids aren't just copying; they're figuring out the RULES of language by themselves!

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Past, present, or future? (a) I will eat lunch. (b) I ate lunch. (c) I eat lunch at noon.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Which -ed sound do you hear? Hopped, filled, melted, kicked, rained, needed. Sort them into /t/, /d/, /ed/.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If you had a real time machine, which would you visit — the past or the future? Write 3 sentences about it: one past, one present, and one future.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Move verbs through time using a floor timeline and sort -ed sounds.

Materials

  • masking tape, 3 signs: YESTERDAY · TODAY · TOMORROW, verb cards (jump, play, bake, paint, go, eat, see, run, swim, laugh)

Steps

  1. Floor Timeline: Tape a long line on the floor with the 3 signs. Pick a verb card. Stand on TODAY and say a present sentence. Jump back to YESTERDAY and say it in the past. Jump to TOMORROW and say it in the future!
  2. -ed Sound Sort: Say each past verb with a hand on your throat. Sort into /t/, /d/, /ed/ piles.
  3. Rule-breaker Memory: Make matching cards (go/went, eat/ate…). Play memory.

Observation recording

VerbPastPresentFuture
/t/ sound/d/ sound/ed/ sound

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a verb? What do past, present and future mean? What are the three sounds of -ed?

Part 2 — Change the time (applying)

Rewrite each sentence in the past: (1) I play soccer. (2) We go to the park. (3) The dog runs fast. (4) I see a bird.

Part 3 — My Week Journal (writing)

Write 3 sentences: one about something you DID yesterday, one about something you ARE doing today, and one about something you WILL do tomorrow. Draw a picture for each.

🏠Homework

  1. Bedtime Past-Tense Story. At bedtime, tell a grown-up about your day using only past-tense verbs. They listen for rule-breakers!
  2. Future Plans. Make a list of 5 things you will do this weekend, using "I will…"

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Can you talk about the future without using any future words? How would people know?
  2. Why do the most common verbs (go, eat, see, be) have the strangest past forms?
  3. If you could send a message to yourself in the future, what would you say — and which verb tense would you use?
Lesson 11 of 11

Describing Words: Adjectives & Adverbs

Paint pictures with words: adjectives describe nouns, adverbs describe how actions happen.

B3.2B1.5D2.3
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Close your eyes and picture “a dog.” Now picture “a tiny, soggy, three-legged dog that barked grumpily.” Why did the second picture appear so much more clearly — and who put it in your head?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B3.2 identify adjectives — words that describe nouns (colour, size, shape, number, feeling, texture)
  • B3.2 identify adverbs — words that describe how, when or where an action happens (quickly, quietly, soon, outside)
  • B1.5 use adjectives and adverbs to make my speaking more exact and interesting
  • D2.3 use describing words to share my feelings and opinions

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B3.2 includes common adjectives and adverbs. These are the "painting words" that bring writing and speaking to life — and are key tools for voice (D2.3).

Simple definitions

  • Adjective: describes a noun (person, place, animal, thing). Answers what kind? how many? which one? → red, huge, three, fluffy, sad, cold
  • Adverb: describes a verb (action). Answers how? when? where? → quickly, slowly, loudly, gently, soon, yesterday, outside, here. Many "how" adverbs end in -ly (a B2.6 suffix!).

How to teach it

  1. Hook: the two dogs. Draw both!
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Mystery Bag (Classwork): feel an object and describe it with adjectives only.
  4. "Adverb Charades": do an action in the manner of an adverb.
💬 You can say

"Adjectives describe things. Adverbs describe actions."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children tend to pile on adjectives ("the big huge giant large dog"). Teach: choose the ONE best word. Also: some -ly words are adjectives (friendly, lovely) — no need to go into this in Grade 1 unless your child asks.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can add 2 adjectives and 1 adverb to a plain sentence to make it more vivid, and can identify which word describes the noun and which describes the verb.

💡 Teaching tip

Use the five senses as an adjective menu: how does it look, sound, smell, taste, feel?

📚The Lesson

Some words are like paintbrushes. They add colour and detail to your sentences so the listener can see exactly what you mean.

Adjectives describe NOUNS 🎨

An adjective is a word that tells more about a noun (a person, place, animal or thing). Adjectives answer: What kind? How many? Which one? - Colour: a red apple - Size: a tiny ant, a gigantic whale - Shape: a round ball - Number: three kittens - Feeling: a grumpy bear, a proud girl - Texture (touch): a fluffy pillow, a prickly cactus - Senses: a stinky sock, a sweet peach, a noisy truck

Adverbs describe VERBS 🏃

An adverb tells more about an action. Adverbs answer: How? When? Where? - How: The turtle walked slowly. The baby slept peacefully. The mouse squeaked loudly. - When: We will go soon. I ate yesterday. - Where: The kids played outside. Come here! Many "how" adverbs end in -ly: quick + ly = quickly, soft + ly = softly, sad + ly = sadly.

Watch a sentence grow!

  • The cat ran.
  • The orange cat ran.
  • The fat orange cat ran quickly.
  • The fat orange cat ran quickly upstairs!

Each describing word adds a new detail to the picture in your mind!

📖 The Mystery Pond

On a foggy morning, Nadia tiptoed quietly to the old pond.

The water was dark and still.

Suddenly, two shiny eyes blinked slowly.

A huge, bumpy bullfrog croaked loudly — RIBBIT!

Nadia giggled happily and ran home.

🤯 Did You Know?

English has a hidden rule for putting adjectives in order that almost nobody is taught — but native speakers follow it anyway! We say "a big red ball," never "a red big ball." The order is roughly: number, opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material. Your brain already knows it!

🤯 Did You Know?

Bullfrogs are the largest frogs in North America, and their call can be heard over a kilometre away. Some people say it sounds like a cow mooing: jug-o-rum!

🧩Think Like a Language Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Find the adjectives and adverbs: "The small puppy barked happily."

⭐⭐ Stretch

Describe an ice cream cone using all five senses — one adjective for each sense.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Try saying "a green big ugly monster." Now "a big ugly green monster." Which sounds right? Why do you think your brain knows the order even though nobody taught you?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Use adjectives and adverbs to describe objects and actions precisely.

Materials

  • a "mystery bag" (pillowcase) with 5 objects of different textures (sponge, pine cone, spoon, feather, rubber ball)
  • adverb cards: slowly, quickly, sadly, angrily, sleepily, loudly, quietly, happily

Steps

  1. Mystery Bag: Reach in without looking. Describe the object using only adjectives (bumpy, cold, small…). The other person guesses.
  2. Adverb Charades: Pick a card and a simple action (brush teeth, walk, eat). Do it in the way of the adverb (brush teeth angrily!). Others guess the adverb.
  3. Sentence Stretch: Start with "The bird flew." Take turns adding one adjective or adverb until it's a super-sentence.

Observation recording

ObjectAdjectives I usedDid they guess?

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does an adjective describe? What does an adverb describe? Give 3 examples of each.

Part 2 — Stretch the sentences (applying)

Add at least one adjective and one adverb to each: 1. The dog ate. 2. A car drove. 3. The girl sang.

Part 3 — Describe a Treasure (writing)

Choose a special object from your home. Write 4 sentences describing it using adjectives for the senses and at least one adverb. Tell why it is special to you. Draw it carefully.

🏠Homework

  1. Adjective Walk. On a walk, collect 10 adjectives for things you see, hear, smell and feel. Write them in a list.
  2. Menu Madness. Look at a real restaurant menu (or food packages). Circle all the adjectives. Why do menus use so many?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Could you describe a colour to someone who has never seen colours? What words would you use?
  2. Why do food menus and toy ads use SO many adjectives?
  3. Is there anything that is impossible to describe with words?
Word Wall

Key Vocabulary

Read each card aloud together. Cover the definition and ask: “What does this word mean? Use it in your own sentence.” Revisit the cards at the start of every session in this strand.

listening
Paying attention with your brain to understand what you hear.
“I was listening so carefully that I remembered every detail.”
relevant
Connected to what is being talked about.
“My question was relevant because it was about her story.”
strategy
A clever plan or trick to help you do something.
“Making a movie in my mind is my favourite listening strategy.”
visualize
To make a picture in your mind.
“I can visualize the penguins huddling in the snow.”
non-verbal communication
Sending a message without words, using your face, hands and body.
“Her crossed arms and frown were non-verbal communication.”
gesture
A movement of your hands or arms that sends a message.
“He waved — a gesture that means hello.”
purpose
The reason for doing something, like speaking or writing.
“My purpose was to ask for help.”
audience
The people who are listening, reading or watching.
“I spoke clearly because my audience was my whole family.”
formal / informal
Formal is polite and careful talking; informal is relaxed everyday talking.
“I used formal words with the principal and informal words with my cousin.”
sentence
A group of words that tells a complete thought, with a naming part and an action part.
““Birds sing.” is a very short sentence.”
fragment
An incomplete piece of a sentence that is missing a part.
““Under the bed.” is a fragment — who or what is under the bed?”
end mark
The punctuation at the end of a sentence: period, question mark or exclamation mark.
“I put a question mark at the end of my asking sentence.”
declarative / interrogative
A telling sentence / an asking sentence.
““Is it snowing?” is an interrogative sentence.”
imperative / exclamatory
A command sentence / a sentence that shows strong feeling.
““Sit down.” is imperative. “We won!” is exclamatory.”
conjunction
A joining word like and, but, so or or.
“I used the conjunction “but” to show a surprise.”
compound sentence
Two complete ideas joined with a conjunction.
““I was cold, so I put on my hat.” is a compound sentence.”
noun
A naming word for a person, place, animal or thing.
““Moose” and “forest” are nouns.”
plural
More than one.
“The plural of “box” is “boxes.””
verb
An action word.
““Leap” is an exciting verb.”
past / present / future
Already happened / happening now / will happen later.
““I jumped” is past, “I jump” is present, “I will jump” is future.”
adjective
A word that describes a noun.
““Fluffy” is an adjective in “the fluffy kitten.””
adverb
A word that describes how, when or where an action happens.
“The turtle moved slowly — “slowly” is an adverb.”
