Lesson 1 of 11

Sound Detectives: Hearing Every Sound in a Word

Before letters, there are sounds. Learn to hear, pull apart and push together the tiny sounds — phonemes — hiding inside every spoken word.

B2.1B2.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

The word “cat” has three letters and three sounds. The word “ship” has four letters — but only THREE sounds. And “eight” has five letters but only TWO sounds! How can a word have more letters than sounds? Who's hiding in there?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.1 isolate the first, middle and last sound in a spoken word (the middle sound in “map” is /a/)
  • B2.1 blend separate sounds into a word, up to five sounds (/s/ /p/ /l/ /i/ /t/ → split)
  • B2.1 segment a spoken word into each of its sounds, up to five sounds (wish → /w/ /i/ /sh/)
  • B2.4 explain that segmenting helps me spell and blending helps me read

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.1 asks children to orally isolate, blend and segment phonemes in words with up to five sounds. A phoneme is the smallest sound unit in speech. This is done with ears, not eyes — no letters at first. Research (including Ontario's Right to Read report, 2022) is clear that phonemic awareness plus systematic phonics is how children learn to read. This lesson becomes a daily 3–5 minute warm-up for the whole year.

How to write sounds

In this guide, slashes mean a sound, not a letter: /m/ is the sound "mmm", not the letter name "em."

Pronounce sounds cleanly! (the #1 parent tip)

Say /m/ as "mmmm," NOT "muh." Say /t/ as a quick whispered "t," NOT "tuh." Adding "uh" makes blending impossible: "cuh-a-tuh" doesn't sound like "cat." Practise: /s/ = "ssss", /f/ = "ffff", /b/ = a short "b" with lips popping, barely any voice after.

The routine (use daily)

  1. Blend: You say sounds slowly with a 1-second gap; child says the word. Start with 2-sound words (/u/ /p/ → up), then 3, then 4, then 5.
  2. Segment: You say a word; child says each sound, tapping one finger per sound or pushing one counter per box.
  3. Isolate: "What's the first sound in fish? The last? The middle?"
💬 You can say

"Let's be sound detectives. Listen with your detective ears — no letters yet, just sounds."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often confuse letter names with sounds ("cat starts with see"). Gently say: "That's the letter's name. What sound does it make in this word?" Also, blends like /st/ are two sounds, not one: s-t.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can segment 4-sound words like frog, best, shrimp (sh-r-i-m-p is 5!) and blend 5 sounds, with 8 out of 10 correct on two different days.

💡 Teaching tip

Stop sounds (/b/ /d/ /g/ /k/ /p/ /t/) are harder than continuous sounds (/m/ /s/ /f/ /l/ /n/ /r/ /v/ /z/ /sh/). Start with words that begin with continuous sounds: mat, sun, fan, lip, nap.

📚The Lesson

Every word you say is made of tiny sounds, all squished together. Say "mop" slowly... m-o-p. Did you hear three sounds? These tiny sounds are called phonemes (say it: FOH-neemz). A phoneme is the smallest sound in a word.

Letters and sounds are different!

Letters are the marks we write. Sounds are what we hear and say. Sometimes one letter makes one sound. But sometimes two letters team up to make ONE sound! - cat → c-a-t → 3 letters, 3 sounds - ship → sh-i-p → 4 letters, but only 3 sounds! (sh is one sound) - eight → ei-ght... just 2 sounds: /ā/ /t/. Five letters!

Your two superpowers: BLEND and SEGMENT

Blending means pushing sounds together to make a word. It's how you read!

/f//i//sh/
→ fffiiish → fish!

Segmenting means pulling a word apart into its sounds. It's how you spell! frog → /f/ /r/ /o/ /g/ — four sounds, four boxes:

frog

Sound positions

Every word has a first sound, a last sound and middle sounds. The middle sound is often a vowel — the open-mouthed sounds a, e, i, o, u. Vowels are the "heart" of every word: every syllable needs one!

Stretch it like gum! 🍬

Say a word really slowly, stretching it like bubble gum: "sssuuunnn." Can you hear /s/ /u/ /n/? Pull the gum apart — segment. Squish it back together — blend!

Try these: How many sounds?

up (2)sun (3)stop (4)trip (4)chin (3)milk (4)split (5)crust (5)
🤯 Did You Know?

English uses just 26 letters, but it has about 44 sounds! That's why some sounds need letter teams, like sh, ch, and th. It's like a puzzle with more pieces than boxes!

🤯 Did You Know?

Newborn babies can hear the differences between the sounds of every language in the world. By about their first birthday, their brains tune in to just the sounds of the languages they hear every day. You were once a sound expert for every language on Earth!

🧠 Brain moment

The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was invented in 1443 by King Sejong the Great and his scholars. Some consonant letters were designed to show the shape of the mouth and tongue when you make that sound! For example, the letter for /g/ or /k/ (ㄱ) shows the back of the tongue lifting up to touch the roof of the mouth.

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Count the sounds (not letters!): dog, shell, jump, three.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Change one sound to make a new word. Start with cat. Change the first sound → ? Change the last sound → ? Change the middle sound → ? How many new words can you make?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Say "stop" without the /s/. Say "flake" without the /l/. Say "smile" without the /m/. What happens? (Sound-swapping is a real brain workout!)

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Practise blending and segmenting 2- to 5-sound words with Sound Boxes (Elkonin boxes).

Materials

  • paper with 5 boxes drawn in a row, 5 small counters (coins, buttons, Lego)
  • a toy "robot" or puppet (optional — robots talk in separate sounds!)

Steps

  1. Robot Talk (blending): The grown-up's robot says words in sounds: "/m/ /a/ /p/." You say the whole word: "map!" Do 10 words, getting longer: it, map, ship, frog, stamp, split.
  2. Sound Boxes (segmenting): The grown-up says a word. Say it slowly, and push one counter into one box for each sound. Then count the counters.
  3. First-Middle-Last: Name the first, middle or last sound in bed, fish, rug, sock.
  4. Silly Swap: Change the first sound of your name to /b/ (Maya → Baya!). Try everyone in your family.

Observation recording

WordHow many sounds?Blend ✓ / Segment ✓Notes

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a phoneme? What is the difference between blending and segmenting? Why do some words have more letters than sounds?

Part 2 — Sound Picture Sort (applying)

Draw 8 small pictures of things whose names have 2, 3, 4 or 5 sounds (like egg 2, sun 3, frog 4, plant 5). Sort them into groups by number of sounds.

✏️ My sound picture sort

Part 3 — Sound Riddles (creating)

Write or say 3 riddles: "I am thinking of an animal with the sounds /d/ /u/ /k/." Test them on your family!

🏠Homework

  1. Car or Bath Sound Game. Play "I Spy" using sounds: "I spy something that starts with /m/ … and ends with /p/!" Play 5 rounds each day.
  2. Robot Dinner. At dinner, ask for food in robot talk: "Pass the /m/ /i/ /l/ /k/." Everyone must blend to understand you!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why would a language need MORE sounds than letters? Could a language work with only 10 sounds?
  2. Do animals' calls have “phonemes”? Could a bird song be split into sounds like a word?
  3. If you invented an alphabet where every letter showed what your mouth does, what would the letter for /m/ look like?
Lesson 2 of 11

Alphabet Masters: 26 Letters, 52 Shapes, Endless Words

Name and print every uppercase and lowercase letter quickly — in and out of order — and discover where our letters came from.

B2.2D2.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

The letter A was once a picture of an ox's head — turn a capital A upside down and you can still see the horns! Every letter you write has a secret history. If YOU had invented letters, what pictures would you have used?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.2 name all 26 uppercase and lowercase letters quickly, in order and out of order, in different fonts
  • B2.2 know alphabetical order well enough to find what comes before and after any letter
  • D2.2 print upper- and lowercase letters starting at the right place, with the right size, direction and spacing
  • B2.2 put words in alphabetical order by their first letter

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.2 asks children to name and form upper- and lowercase letters both in and out of order and demonstrate knowledge of alphabetic order, with automaticity. "Automaticity" means instantly, without stopping to think — like knowing your own name. Letter naming speed is one of the strongest predictors of later reading success.

Letter formation basics (D2.2)

  • Most letters start at the top.
  • Lowercase letters live on "three floors": tall letters (b d f h k l t) reach the attic; short letters (a c e i m n o r s u v w x z) live on the main floor; tail letters (g j p q y) go into the basement.
  • Circle letters (a c d g o q) start at "2 o'clock" and go counter-clockwise.

Common reversals

b/d and p/q are super common until age 7–8 — they're not a sign of a problem. Trick: make a "bed" with your fists (thumbs up, left hand = b, right hand = d). "b" has the bat first, then the ball; "d" has the doorknob circle first, then the door.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: show the ox-head story and turn an "A" upside down.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Daily: 1-minute "letter sprint" (Classwork) — name random letters as fast as possible. Record the time weekly and watch it drop.
💬 You can say

"Letters have names AND sounds. Today we're mastering their names and shapes so your brain doesn't have to think about them anymore — then all your brain power goes to reading!"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children who can sing the ABC song may not know individual letters out of order — "elemeno" as one letter is very common! Test out of order.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child names all 52 letter forms in random order in under about 60 seconds with no errors, and forms all lowercase letters from the correct starting point.

💡 Teaching tip

Keep a wall alphabet at child's eye level, and point out letters in different fonts on signs and packaging.

📚The Lesson

Our alphabet has 26 letters. But every letter has two shapes: an uppercase (capital) letter and a lowercase (small) letter. That's 52 shapes to know! Plus, letters can look different in different fonts (styles of printing): a and a, g and g. A reading expert knows them all.

Where did our letters come from?

About 4,000 years ago, people in Egypt and nearby lands started using little pictures for sounds. Later, traders called the Phoenicians made a small set of letters that was easy to learn — just 22 letters! The Greeks borrowed it, then the Romans, and then it came to English. Many letters started as pictures: - A was an ox head 🐂 (called aleph) — turn A upside down to see the horns! - B was a house 🏠 (bet) - O was an eye 👁️ (ayin) - M was water 🌊 — see the waves?

Uppercase and lowercase

Why "upper case" and "lower case"? Long ago, printers made books with little metal letters. They kept the capital letters in a wooden box, called a case, on the upper shelf, and the small letters in the lower case! The names stuck.

Alphabetical order

The letters always go in the same order: alphabetical order. Dictionaries, phone lists and library shelves use it so we can find things fast. WORDS: A a | B b | C c | D d | E e | F f | G g | H h | I i | J j | K k | L l | M m | N n | O o | P p | Q q | R r | S s | T t | U u | V v | W w | X x | Y y | Z z

To put words in alphabetical order, look at the first letter of each word: apple, banana, cherry.

Letters live on three floors

When you print, lowercase letters live on three floors: - 🏠 Tall letters go up to the attic: b d f h k l t - 🟰 Short letters stay on the main floor: a c e i m n o r s u v w x z - ⬇️ Tail letters hang down into the basement: g j p q y

🤯 Did You Know?

The newest letter in our alphabet is J! For a long time, I and J were the same letter. J became its own letter only about 500 years ago. And the letter W is really "double U" — long ago it was written as two V's side by side: VV!

🤯 Did You Know?

The most common letter in English is E. The least common is usually Q or Z. That's why in the game Scrabble, E is worth 1 point and Q and Z are worth 10!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

What letter comes just before M? Just after R? Between G and I?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Put these words in alphabetical order: zebra, apple, moose, dog, kite. How did you decide?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think people put the letters in one fixed order? What would happen if every dictionary used a different order? Invent a picture history for the letter S.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Build speed and accuracy with letter names and practise correct letter formation.

Materials

  • 52 letter cards (index cards or cut paper), a timer, a tray of salt/sugar or shaving cream, lined paper

Steps

  1. Letter Sprint: Shuffle all 52 cards. Name each letter as fast as you can while the grown-up times you. Put any mistakes in a "practise pile." Do this daily for a week.
  2. ABC Line-up: Lay the lowercase cards in order on the floor. Then match each uppercase card to its partner.
  3. Salt Tray Letters: Write each tricky letter in the salt tray with your finger, saying its name and "top start, down…" directions.
  4. Font Hunt: Find the letters a and g in 3 different fonts on packages or magazines.

Choose your 3 favourite letters. For each, print the uppercase and lowercase letter carefully on lined paper, and draw 3 things that start with that letter.

Lesson 3 of 11

Short Vowels & Consonant Blends: Reading Real Words

Master the five short vowel sounds, then read and spell words with consonant blends — CVC, CCVC, CVCC and CCVCC words like “frog,” “jump,” and “stamp.”

B2.3B2.4B2.1
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Take the word “bat.” Change ONE letter at a time and you can walk all the way to “dog” in just a few steps. How? And what's the shortest path you can find?

(One path: bat → bag → bog → dog. Let your child hunt for the path with letter tiles before you show it!)

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.3 say the short sound for each vowel (a as in apple, e as in egg, i as in itch, o as in octopus, u as in up) with automaticity
  • B2.4 read and spell CVC words (map, sit, hug) by blending and segmenting
  • B2.4 read and spell words with blends: CCVC (frog, stop), CVCC (jump, best) and CCVCC (stamp, crust)
  • B2.1 hear both sounds in a blend (/s/ /t/ in stop)

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.3 and B2.4 ask children to identify, read, and spell grapheme-phoneme correspondences with automaticity and to use phonics knowledge and blending to read, and segmentation to spell. Short vowels are the foundation of hundreds of words. Blends add a consonant sound next to another (s-t, f-r, m-p) — each keeps its own sound.

Short vowel anchors (use actions!)

  • a /ă/ apple — pretend to bite an apple
  • e /ĕ/ egg — crack an egg on your head
  • i /ĭ/ itch — scratch your arm
  • o /ŏ/ octopus — wiggle arms
  • u /ŭ/ up — point up

Word patterns (C = consonant, V = vowel)

  • CVC: cat, pen, sit, hot, bug
  • CCVC: frog, stop, clap, drip, swim
  • CVCC: jump, best, milk, hand, lost
  • CCVCC: stamp, crust, blend, twist, plant

How to teach it

  1. Review short vowels with actions (2 min).
  2. Read the lesson, pointing under each word as you blend: touch each letter, say each sound, sweep your finger and say the word.
  3. Word chains with letter tiles (Classwork).
  4. Dictation: say a word; child segments, then writes one letter per sound.
💬 You can say

"Touch and say each sound, then slide and say the word."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

The short e and i sounds are the most confused (pen/pin). Also watch for children dropping the second consonant in blends ("fog" for "frog", "jup" for "jump") — go back to Sound Boxes and count the sounds.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child reads a list of 20 mixed CVC/CCVC/CVCC words with 90%+ accuracy, and spells 8 of 10 dictated words correctly.

💡 Teaching tip

Stay "decodable": only ask your child to read words made from patterns they've been taught. Guessing from pictures builds a bad habit.

📚The Lesson

The five vowels — a, e, i, o, u — are the most important letters in English. Every word needs at least one vowel sound. Each vowel has a short sound and a long sound. Today, we master the short vowels!

a🍎 applee🥚 eggi🦟 itcho🐙 octopusu☂️ up

CVC words: consonant–vowel–consonant

A consonant is any letter that isn't a vowel. When a vowel is trapped between two consonants, it usually makes its short sound. We call these CVC words. WORDS: cat | map | bed | pen | sit | pig | hot | mop | bug | sun

Read like this: touch each letter and say its sound → slide your finger under the word and blend → say the word! m → a → p → map!

Consonant blends

Sometimes two consonants sit side by side, and you can hear both sounds, blended quickly. This is a blend. - Beginning blends: stop, frog, clap, swim, grab, plum, snack, trip - Ending blends: jump, best, milk, hand, tent, lift, desk - Both! stamp, crust, blend, twist, plant

📖 The Frog on the Log

A green frog sat on a log.

The frog had a big grin.

A fat bug went past. The frog did a jump — flop!

He did not get the bug. He fell in the pond with a splash!

The frog swam back to the log. "I will get it next time," he said.

🤯 Did You Know?

The word "strengths" has only one vowel, but eight consonant letters! It's one of the longest one-syllable words in English. Try to say it: str-e-ng-th-s!

🧠 Brain moment

When you read a word by blending sounds, you're doing something amazing: turning squiggles into sounds and sounds into meaning. Scientists have found that every time you sound out a word correctly, your brain takes a "snapshot" of it. After you've read a word correctly a few times, your brain can recognize it instantly!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Read these words and sort them by vowel sound: hot, bed, cap, pig, bun, net, fox, lip, jam, cup.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Word ladder: change one letter at a time to go from cat to dog. Then try hot to cub.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Add ONE letter to the beginning or end to make a new word: top → stop. Now try lap, ten, ran, rip, and. How many new words can you make? Which added letters made blends?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Read and spell short-vowel words with blends using letter tiles and word chains.

Materials

  • letter tiles or cards (make with index cards: vowels in red, consonants in blue)
  • a whiteboard or paper

Steps

  1. Vowel warm-up: Point to each vowel; say its sound with the action.
  2. Word Chains: Build cat. Now change it to cap, then clap, then clip, then slip, then slap, then slam. Read each word.
  3. Blend Builder: Build top. Add s → stop. Build lip. Add f → flip. Build jump — which letters make the ending blend?
  4. Dictation: The grown-up says 10 words. Segment each with your fingers, then write it: sit, hop, bed, frog, jump, clap, lost, twist, stamp, drum.

🌟Keep Wondering

  2. Why do some people say words like “pen” and “pin” the same way? (It depends on where they grew up!)
  3. What's the longest word you can build using only short vowels?
Lesson 4 of 11

Letter Teams & Tricky Consonants

Discover consonant teams (sh, ch, th, wh, ck, ph, ng, nk), where to use -ck, -tch and -dge, the FLSZ rule, soft c and g, and sneaky silent letters.

B2.3B2.5B2.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Why do we write “knight” with a K and “lamb” with a B, when we don't say them? Here's a clue: 800 years ago, people DID say them! What happened to those sounds — and why are the letters still there?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.3 read and spell consonant digraphs: sh, ch, th, wh, ck, ph, ng, nk, and word families -all, -oll, -ull
  • B2.3 read soft c (/s/ before e, i, y — city) and soft g (/j/ before e, i, y — gem)
  • B2.5 choose the right spelling by position: -ck after a short vowel at the end, -tch and -dge after a short vowel, and double f, l, s, z (FLSZ)
  • B2.3 read words with silent letters: kn (knee), wr (write), mb (lamb)

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.3 lists these Grade 1 patterns: ‹-all›, ‹-oll›, ‹-ull›; consonant patterns ‹ph›, ‹nk›; soft c and soft g; silent letters kn, wr, mb. B2.5 asks children to use position-based tendencies to choose spellings — including -ck, -tch, -dge, and the FLSZ rule. This is a big lesson: spend 3–4 weeks here, one pattern group at a time.

Suggested order (1–2 patterns per few days)

  1. sh, ch, th, wh (digraphs: two letters, one sound)
  2. ck at the end after a short vowel (duck, sock)
  3. ng, nk (ring, sink)
  4. FLSZ: after a short vowel in a one-syllable word, double f, l, s, z (puff, bell, kiss, buzz) + -all, -oll, -ull (ball, doll, gull)
  5. -tch (catch) and -dge (badge) after a short vowel
  6. ph = /f/ (phone)
  7. Soft c / soft g (city, gem)
  8. Silent letters kn, wr, mb

The /k/ spelling rule (B2.5)

  • c before a, o, u and consonants: cat, cot, cup, clap
  • k before e, i, y: kid, keg
  • ck at the end right after a short vowel: back, neck, sick, rock, duck
💬 You can say

"These letters are teammates. When they stand together, they make ONE new sound."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often write "sh" as "s" or "ch" as "c." Use Sound Boxes: ship has 3 sounds, so 3 boxes — and the sh goes in ONE box together.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child reads a mixed list of 20 words with these patterns with 90% accuracy and spells duck, catch, bell, ship, ring correctly from dictation.

💡 Teaching tip

Make a "Letter Team" poster; add each team as it's learned.

📚The Lesson

Sometimes two letters hold hands and make one brand-new sound. They're a digraph ("di" means two, "graph" means written). A digraph is not a blend — in a blend you hear both sounds; in a digraph you hear one NEW sound.

The Letter Teams

  • sh — 🤫 ship, fish, shell, brush
  • ch — 🚂 chin, chop, lunch, much
  • th — 👅 thin, bath, this, that (put your tongue between your teeth!)
  • wh — 🐳 when, whip, which, whale
  • ck — 🦆 duck, sock, back, neck (only at the end, right after a short vowel)
  • ng — 💍 ring, song, king, hang
  • nk — 🦨 sink, bank, pink, skunk
  • ph — 📞 phone, graph, dolphin (sounds like /f/!)

Rules that tell you WHICH spelling to use

English has more than one way to spell some sounds. But there are clues! Where the sound is in the word — its position — helps you choose.

The FLSZ rule: In a short word with a short vowel, if the word ends in f, l, s, or z, double it! WORDS: puff | cliff | bell | hill | kiss | dress | buzz | fizz

The -all, -oll, -ull families: WORDS: ball | tall | small | doll | roll | troll | gull | dull | full | pull

-tch and -dge: After a short vowel, the /ch/ sound at the end is usually -tch, and the /j/ sound at the end is -dge. WORDS: catch | match | itch | fetch | badge | edge | fudge | bridge

Soft c and soft g 🪶

Usually c says /k/ (cat) and g says /g/ (goat) — these are the hard sounds. But when e, i, or y comes right after them, they often go soft: - c → /s/: city, cent, fancy, ice - g → /j/: gem, giant, gym, cage

Silent letters 🤫

  • kn → /n/: knee, knot, knock, know, knight
  • wr → /r/: write, wrap, wrist, wren
  • mb → /m/: lamb, thumb, climb, comb
🤯 Did You Know?

About 800 years ago, English speakers really DID say the k in "knight" (k-nee-cht) and the w in "write"! Over hundreds of years, people stopped saying those sounds, but the spellings stayed the same — like a fossil of how English used to sound.

🤯 Did You Know?

The word "ph" spelling comes from ancient Greek. Words like phone, photo, and dolphin came to English from Greek, and they kept their Greek-style spelling. A spelling can tell you where a word was born!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Sort these words by their letter team: ship, chin, bath, when, duck, ring, sink, phone.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Choose the right spelling and explain why: du_ (ck or k), ca_ (tch or ch), be_ (l or ll), _ity (c or s).

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If silent letters are silent, why do you think people never removed them from spelling? Would English be easier or harder if we spelled every word exactly how it sounds? What might we lose?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Read, sort and spell words with letter teams and position-based spellings.

Materials

  • index cards with 30 words (from the lesson lists), paper plates labelled with each team (sh, ch, th, wh, ck, ng, nk, ph), whiteboard

Steps

  1. Team Sort: Read each word card aloud and put it on the right plate.
  2. Rule Detective: Look at all the -ck words. What comes right before -ck every time? (A short vowel!) Do the same for -tch and -dge.
  3. Soft or Hard? Sort c and g words into HARD and SOFT piles. Look at the letter after c or g — what do you notice?
  4. Silent Letter Spy: Read kn, wr, mb words. Cross out the silent letter with a pencil, then read again.
  5. Dictation: Spell 10 words the grown-up says.

Pattern3 words I can read1 word I spelled

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a digraph? What is the FLSZ rule? When do c and g make their soft sounds?

Part 2 — Fix the spellings (applying)

Fix each word and explain the rule: dukk, kach, bel, sity, nee, fone.

Part 3 — Tongue Twister (creating)

Write a silly tongue twister using at least 6 words with ONE letter team (e.g., "Shelly shows shiny shells…"). Say it 3 times fast!

🏠Homework

  1. Letter Team Treasure Hunt. Find 2 words for every letter team (sh, ch, th, wh, ck, ng, nk, ph) in books, packages or signs.
  2. Silent Letter Family Quiz. Ask family members to spell knee, write, and thumb on paper. Did anyone forget the silent letter?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If English spelling is a “fossil” of old sounds, what might English sound like in 800 more years?
  2. Why do you think “th” is one of the hardest sounds for people learning English?
  3. Should we have a special letter for “sh” instead of two letters? What would it look like?
Lesson 5 of 11

The Magic of Silent E & Long Vowels

Discover how a silent e at the end of a word can change a vowel's sound — cap to cape! — plus y as a vowel and long-vowel word families like -ild, -old, -ind.

B2.3B2.4B2.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Add ONE letter to the end of “kit” — a letter you can't even hear — and suddenly it can fly in the sky. How can a silent letter change a whole word?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.3 read and spell VCe (silent e) words: cake, bike, rope, cute, Pete
  • B2.4 read word pairs that change with silent e: cap/cape, kit/kite, hop/hope, cub/cube
  • B2.3 read y as a vowel: /ī/ in my, fly, and /ē/ in happy, puppy
  • B2.5 read long-vowel families -ild, -old, -ind, -olt, -ost (child, cold, find, colt, most) and know some VCe exceptions (have, give, love)

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.3 lists VCe patterns, VCe exceptions, long vowel sounds in VCC words (-ild, -old, -ind, -olt, -ost), long vowel y = /ī/, and e = /ē/. The silent e (also called "bossy e," "magic e," or "sneaky e") is one of the most powerful patterns in English.

The pattern

Vowel + Consonant + e → the first vowel says its name (long sound); the e is silent. - a_e: cake, name, gate · i_e: bike, time, slide · o_e: bone, rope, stove · u_e: cube, cute, mule, flute · e_e: Pete, these (rare)

Exceptions (common words that break the rule)

have, give, live, love, come, some, done, gone, one, were — teach these as "heart words" (see Lesson 9).

Other long vowels in Grade 1

  • y at the end of a one-syllable word says /ī/: my, by, fly, cry, sky
  • y at the end of a two-syllable word says /ē/: happy, funny, baby, puppy
  • Open syllables: a vowel at the end of a syllable often says its name: he, me, we, go, no, hi
  • -ild, -old, -ind, -olt, -ost: the vowel says its name even without an e: child, mild, cold, gold, find, kind, colt, bolt, most, post
💬 You can say

"The silent e jumps over the consonant and gives the vowel a push — 'Say your name!'"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often read "cape" as "cap-ee" or forget the e when spelling (writing "bik" for bike). Always look for the e at the end BEFORE sounding out.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child reads mixed short/long pairs (hop/hope, pin/pine) accurately and spells 8/10 VCe words from dictation.

💡 Teaching tip

Make "magic e" flip cards: write cap on a card and fold an e flap on the right. Flip it open and read again!

📚The Lesson

You know the short vowel sounds: a (apple), e (egg), i (itch), o (octopus), u (up). But each vowel has another sound too: its long vowel sound. A long vowel says its own name!

ācakeēPeteībikeōboneūcube

Silent E: the sneaky helper

When a word ends in vowel + consonant + e, the e is silent. But it has a job: it makes the first vowel say its name! This is called the VCe pattern (vowel–consonant–e).

Watch the magic: - cap → cape 🦸 - kit → kite 🪁 - hop → hope 🙏 - cub → cube 🧊 - pin → pine 🌲 - tub → tube - not → note 🎵

Y is a sneaky vowel!

Y is usually a consonant at the start of a word (yes, yellow). But at the end of a word, Y acts like a vowel: - In short words, y says /ī/: my, by, fly, cry, sky, try - In longer words, y says /ē/: happy, funny, puppy, baby, sunny

Long vowels without an E

Some word families say the long vowel sound even without an e! WORDS: child | wild | cold | gold | told | find | kind | mind | bolt | colt | most | post | ghost

And when a word or syllable ends with a vowel, the vowel often says its name: he, me, we, go, no, so, hi.

Rule-breakers

Some very common words have a silent e but break the rule: have, give, live, love, come, some, done, one. We'll learn these "heart words" by heart!

📖 A Kite on the Lake

Jake has a white kite. It has a long tail.

Jake and his mom ride their bikes to the lake.

The wind is wild! The kite flies up high in the sky.

"Hold on!" Mom yells. Jake holds the line with both hands.

The kite dives and glides. Jake smiles. What a fine time!

🤯 Did You Know?

The word "rhythm" has no a, e, i, o, or u — but it still has vowel sounds, thanks to the sneaky y! Y is doing the vowel's job. The same happens in gym, myth, and fly.

🧠 Brain moment

Reading scientists call silent e a marker — a letter that doesn't make its own sound but gives a signal about the other letters. English has lots of markers. Learning to spot them is like learning to read secret codes!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Read each pair and draw a quick picture for each word: hat/hate, pin/pine, rob/robe.

✏️ My picture pairs

⭐⭐ Stretch

Which words need a magic e? Add it and read: bak_, cat_, tim_, sun_, hom_, dog_. Why do some NOT need an e?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

"Have," "give," and "love" have a silent e, but the vowel doesn't say its name. Why do you think English kept the e? (Hint: English words almost never end in the letter v!)

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Read and spell VCe words and long-vowel families, and see how silent e changes words.

Materials

  • magic e flip cards (fold an index card so an "e" flap covers the end), a magic wand (pencil with a star!)
  • whiteboard, 20 word cards

Steps

  1. Magic Wand: Read cap. Tap the card with the wand and flip open the e: cape! Do 10 pairs.
  2. Short or Long? Sort 20 word cards into short vowel and long vowel piles.
  3. Y Detective: Sort y-words: y says /ī/ or y says /ē/? What do you notice about the number of syllables?
  4. Dictation: Spell make, ride, home, cute, fly, happy, cold, find, like, bone.

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does a silent e do? What two sounds can y make at the end of a word? Name 3 rule-breaker words.

Part 2 — Sentence Reading (applying)

Read these sentences out loud to a grown-up. Circle all the VCe words: (1) I like to ride my bike. (2) The white mule ate a cone. (3) We made a cake at home.

Part 3 — Magic E Comic (creating)

Draw a comic where a wizard named Silent E changes things: a cub into a cube, a pin into a pine… Write a caption for each box.

✏️ My Magic E comic

🏠Homework

  1. Magic E Hunt. Find 10 silent-e words on labels, signs or in books. Read them to a grown-up.
  2. Kite Challenge. Read A Kite on the Lake every day this week. Time yourself — do you get smoother each day?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why would a language have a letter you don't pronounce? Is silent e really silent — or is it “talking” with its eyes?
  2. Why do you think y can be both a consonant and a vowel? Are there other letters that change jobs?
  3. If you could make a new rule for English spelling, what would it be?

Learn the vowel teams — ai, ay, ee, ea, ey, oa, ow, oe, ie, igh, oo, ew, ui, ue — and how position helps you choose the right one.

B2.3B2.5B2.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

“Rain” and “play” both have the /ā/ sound. So why does one use AI and the other use AY? Is it random — or is there a secret pattern that could help you spell thousands of words?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.3 read vowel teams for long a (ai, ay), long e (ee, ea, ey), long o (oa, ow, oe), long i (ie, igh)
  • B2.3 read oo in two ways (book, moon), and ew, ui, ue for /ū/ (new, fruit, blue)
  • B2.5 choose ai in the middle and ay at the end (rain / play), and know that ea can say /ē/, /ā/ or /ĕ/ (eat, great, bread)
  • B2.4 read and spell words with vowel teams in sentences

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.3 lists these long vowel teams for Grade 1: ‹ai›, ‹ay› = /ā/; ‹ee›, ‹ea›, ‹ey› = /ē/; ‹oa›, ‹ow›, ‹oe› = /ō/; ‹ie›, ‹igh› = /ī/; ‹oo›, ‹u› = /oo/ (as in book, put); ‹oo› = /ū/ (moon); ‹ew›, ‹ui›, ‹ue› = /ū/; and ‹ea› = /ē/, /ā/, /ĕ/. B2.5 adds positional spellings like ai vs. ay.

This is a large lesson. Plan 3–4 weeks, one sound family per 3–4 days: long a → long e → long o → long i → oo/ew/ui/ue → ea.

The positional rules (B2.5)

  • ai in the middle of a word (rain, tail); ay at the end (day, play) — because English words don't end in "i"!
  • oa in the middle (boat); ow often at the end (snow); oe at the end (toe)
  • igh before t (night, light)

The "when two vowels go walking" rhyme

"When two vowels go walking, the first one does the talking" works for ai, ee, oa, ie — but NOT always (bread, great, chief). Teach it as a helpful hint, not a law.

💬 You can say

"Vowel teams are partners. Look for them before you sound out — they get ONE box in your Sound Boxes."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children read each vowel separately ("ra-in"). Before reading, have them underline the team first. Also watch for "ow" (snow vs. cow — cow is in Lesson 7).

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can read a mixed list of vowel-team words with 90% accuracy, spell ai/ay words correctly by position, and explain why "day" uses ay.

💡 Teaching tip

Build a "Vowel Team Wall" with five columns: long a, long e, long i, long o, long u. Add words as you learn them.

📚The Lesson

Sometimes two vowels stand side by side and work together to make one sound. They are a vowel team. Often the first vowel "does the talking" and says its name, while the second one stays quiet.

Long A teams: ai, ay

raintailpaintsnaildayplaystaygray Notice: ai is in the middle; ay is at the end. That's because English words don't end in the letter i!

Long E teams: ee, ea, ey

treefeetsheepgreeneatleafbeachkeymonkeyhoney

Long O teams: oa, ow, oe

boatroadsoapcoatsnowgrowyellowtoehoe

Long I teams: ie, igh

pietiecriedlightnighthighrightbright igh is a team of THREE letters making one sound!

The oo, ew, ui, ue sounds

oo can make two sounds: 📘 short in book, foot, look, good and 🌙 long in moon, food, zoo, spoon. The letter u can say the short oo sound too, in put and push! The long oo (/ū/) sound can also be spelled: ew (new, grew, chew), ui (fruit, suit), ue (blue, glue, true).

Tricky EA

ea is a team that can make three sounds: - /ē/ — eat, sea, dream - /ĕ/ — bread, head, feather - /ā/ — great, break, steak Try the first sound; if it's not a real word, try the next one!

📖 The Snail and the Rain

A small gray snail sat on a green leaf.

Drip, drip! The rain began to fall. The snail did not mind. Snails like the rain!

She slid down the leaf and across the road, leaving a bright, shiny trail.

At night, the moon came out. The snail ate a sweet, cool meal of fresh leaves.

"What a great day," she said, and she went to sleep.

🤯 Did You Know?

Snails leave a slimy trail called mucus that helps them glide — and it's so good at protecting their soft bodies that a snail can crawl along the edge of a razor blade without getting hurt!

🤯 Did You Know?

There's an old joke that you could spell the word "fish" as ghoti: gh as in "enough," o as in "women," and ti as in "nation." But it doesn't really work — gh never makes the /f/ sound at the start of a word, and ti only says /sh/ in the middle of words. Position matters!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Sort by sound: boat, rain, tree, night, play, snow, pie, key, toe, leaf. (Long a? long e? long i? long o?)

⭐⭐ Stretch

Is it ai or ay? tr__n, s__, m__l, st__, p__nt, cl__. Explain your rule.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think English has so many ways to spell the same sound? (Hint: English borrowed words from many different languages!) Does it make English harder or more interesting?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Read, sort and spell vowel team words, and discover the ai/ay position rule.

Materials

  • 30 word cards (from the lesson), 5 paper bags labelled LONG A · LONG E · LONG I · LONG O · OO
  • highlighter

Steps

  1. Team Spotting: Before reading each card, highlight the vowel team. Then read the word.
  2. Bag Sort: Put each card in the right sound bag.
  3. Position Detective: Line up all ai and ay words. Where is ai? Where is ay? Say the rule in your own words.
  4. ea Experiment: Read eat, bread, great — try each ea sound until the word makes sense.
  5. Dictation: Spell 10 words: rain, day, feet, boat, snow, night, pie, moon, blue, eat.

Observation recording

Long ALong ELong ILong OOO

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a vowel team? Name 2 ways to spell long a, 3 ways to spell long e, and 3 ways to spell long o.

Part 2 — Read and Respond (comprehension)

Read The Snail and the Rain. Answer: Why did the snail not mind the rain? What did she eat? Find and list 6 vowel team words from the story.

Part 3 — Vowel Team Poem (creating)

Write a 4-line poem about rain, snow or night using at least 5 vowel team words. Illustrate it.

🏠Homework

  1. Vowel Team Wall. Add 3 new vowel team words to your Vowel Team Wall every day this week.
  2. Night Sky Observation. Look at the night sky with a grown-up. Write 2 sentences about what you see using igh, ee or oo words (bright light, the moon…).

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why do you think English words don't end in i or u very often? (Can you find any that do?)
  2. If you could fix English spelling so every sound had only one spelling, would you? What would we lose?
  3. Where do you think the word “snail” came from? How could you find out?
Lesson 7 of 11

Bossy R & Sliding Sounds

Meet the bossy r (car, her, bird, fork, burn), the vowel sounds that slide (oi, oy, ou, ow), plus au/aw, air/are/ear, and the -le ending.

B2.3B2.4B2.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Why does the “a” in “cat” sound totally different from the “a” in “car”? One letter — R — is standing right next to it. What kind of power does R have over the vowels around it?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.3 read r-controlled vowels: ar (car), or (fork), er/ir/ur (her, bird, burn), and air, are, ear (chair, care, bear)
  • B2.3 read diphthongs oi/oy (coin, boy) and ou/ow (out, cow), and au/aw (sauce, saw)
  • B2.5 choose oi in the middle and oy at the end; ou in the middle and ow often at the end
  • B2.4 read two-syllable words with consonant-le (bundle, apple, little) by splitting into syllables

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.3 lists r-controlled vowels; diphthongs ‹oi›, ‹oy› = /oi/; ‹ou›, ‹ow› = /ow/; ‹au›, ‹aw›, ‹augh› = /o/; ‹air›, ‹are›, ‹ear› = /air/; and ‹-le› words. B2.5 includes positional spellings oi vs. oy and ou vs. ow. Plan 3–4 weeks here.

Key teaching points

  • Bossy r changes the vowel before it into a new sound: ar /ar/, or /or/, and er, ir, ur all say /er/ (her, bird, fur). Children must learn which spelling a word uses — practise with word sorts.
  • Diphthongs are "sliding" vowels — your mouth moves while you say them. Say /oi/ and feel your mouth slide from "o" to "ee."
  • Position: oi/ou in the middle (coin, loud); oy/ow at the end (boy, cow).
  • -le words: count back three letters to split the syllable: bun-dle, ap-ple, lit-tle, ta-ble.
💬 You can say

"R is bossy. It changes the sound of the vowel right before it. Look for the r first!"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

The er/ir/ur spellings all sound the same — spelling them is hard even for adults. Accept phonetically logical attempts ("berd" for bird) in free writing, while practising correct spellings in dictation. Also "ow" can say /ō/ (snow) or /ow/ (cow) — try both.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child reads a list of 20 words mixing these patterns with 85–90% accuracy and can explain why "boy" uses oy.

💡 Teaching tip

Use actions: /ar/ pirate "arrr!"; /ow/ "ow, I stubbed my toe!"; /oi/ a pig's "oink" without the nk.

📚The Lesson

Bossy R 🏴‍☠️

When the letter r comes right after a vowel, it's so bossy that it changes the vowel's sound! These are called r-controlled vowels. - ar — says /ar/ like a pirate: car, star, farm, shark, park - or — says /or/: fork, corn, storm, horse, sport - er, ir, ur — all three say /er/: her, fern, bird, girl, first, fur, burn, turtle - air, are, ear — say /air/: chair, hair, care, share, bear, pear

Sliding vowels 🛝

Some vowel sounds make your mouth slide from one shape to another. These are called diphthongs (DIF-thongs). - oi / oy — say /oi/: coin, soil, point · boy, toy, joy - ou / ow — say /ow/: out, loud, cloud, mouse · cow, how, now, owl, down Position helps: oi and ou usually live in the middle of a word. oy and ow are often at the end.

The /aw/ sound

au and aw (and sometimes augh) make the sound in saw, paw, draw, straw, sauce, launch, caught.

Consonant + le

Lots of words end with a consonant + le. The le sounds like /ul/: table, apple, little, bundle, purple, turtle. To read them, split the word before the consonant-le: bun | dle, ap | ple, ta | ble.

📖 The Storm at the Farm

It was a dark night at the farm. A storm began to roar.

The horse ran into the barn. The girl held her little brown owl.

"Don't be scared," she said. "We are safe here."

Thunder was loud. The cow let out a big "Moo!"

In the morning, the sun came out. The girl and the boy found a shiny coin in the soil. "What a surprise!" they shouted with joy.

🤯 Did You Know?

The word "bird" used to be "brid" in Old English — the r and the i swapped places over time! Words change their spelling over the years, just like people change as they grow.

🤯 Did You Know?

Owls can turn their heads about 270 degrees — that's three-quarters of the way around! They can't move their eyes like we do, so they turn their whole head instead.

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Read and sort: car, fork, bird, her, fur, star, corn, girl. Which words have the /er/ sound?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Choose oi or oy: b__, c__n, t__, s__l, enj__. Choose ou or ow: c__, cl__d, h__, m__se. What's the pattern?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

"Her," "bird," and "fur" all have the same sound but three different spellings. If you had to invent ONE spelling for the /er/ sound, which would you choose? Why? What problems could your new rule cause?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Read and sort r-controlled and sliding-vowel words; split -le words into syllables.

Materials

  • 30 word cards, 6 cups labelled ar · or · er/ir/ur · air/are/ear · oi/oy · ou/ow, scissors, a toy pirate hat (optional!)

Steps

  1. Pirate Sort: Read each card like a pirate and drop it in the right cup.
  2. Mouth Mirror: Say oi and ow in front of a mirror. Watch your mouth slide!
  3. -le Scissors: Write apple, table, little, purple, bundle on strips. Cut each word into two syllables before the consonant-le. Read each part, then push them together.
  4. Dictation: car, fork, bird, burn, boy, coin, cow, cloud, saw, apple.

Observation recording

PatternWords I read correctlyWords to practise

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does "bossy r" do? What is a diphthong? Where do oi and oy usually go in a word?

Part 2 — Story Detective (reading)

Read The Storm at the Farm. Find 3 bossy r words, 3 sliding sound words, and 1 -le word. What surprise did the children find?

Part 3 — Farm Story (writing)

Write 4 sentences about a day on a farm, using at least 6 words with bossy r or sliding sounds. Draw it.

🏠Homework

  1. Sound Sort Walk. On a walk or in a store, find 2 words for ar, or, er/ir/ur, oi/oy, and ou/ow.
  2. -le Collection. Find 5 -le words at home (bottle, table, candle, puzzle…). Split each into syllables for a grown-up.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why do you think the r sound is so strong that it changes the vowel before it?
  2. Do people in different places say “car” and “park” differently? (Listen to someone from Boston or England!)
  3. If words like “bird” once had letters in a different order, what might words look like in 500 years?
Lesson 8 of 11

Word Builders: Bases, Prefixes & Suffixes

Words are made of meaning-parts called morphemes. Snap on prefixes and suffixes, build compound words, and learn the spelling-change rules.

B2.6B2.5B2.7
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

The word “unhappiness” looks huge and scary. But what if it's really just three small, friendly pieces snapped together like Lego? If you knew the pieces, could you read — and understand — a word you've NEVER seen before?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.6 explain that a morpheme is the smallest part of a word with meaning, and find the base in a word
  • B2.6 use prefixes un-, re-, in- (not), dis- and suffixes -s/-es, -ing, -ed, -er/-or, -est, -ly to read and build words
  • B2.5 use spelling rules when adding suffixes: double the last letter (hop → hopping), drop the e (bake → baking), change y to i (happy → happiest)
  • B2.6 build and split compound words (note + book = notebook)

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.6 asks children to use developing knowledge of the meanings of words and common morphemes (bases, prefixes, and suffixes) to read and spell words. The curriculum lists: prefixes un-, re-, in- (not), dis-; suffixes -ing, -er/-or, -est, -ly; the three sounds of -ed; compounding; and suffix spelling changes (doubling, e-drop, y to i) — which also appear in B2.5. Plan 3–4 weeks.

Key ideas

  • Morpheme = smallest unit of meaning. Cats = cat + s (2 morphemes). Unhappily = un + happy + ly (3).
  • Prefix = before the base, changes meaning: un- (not), re- (again), dis- (not/opposite), in- (not).
  • Suffix = after the base: -s/-es (more than one), -ing (happening now), -ed (past), -er (one who / more), -or (one who), -est (the most), -ly (in a way).

Spelling rules (teach one at a time)

  1. Doubling (1-1-1 rule): 1 syllable, 1 short vowel, 1 final consonant → double before a vowel suffix: hop → hopping, big → biggest, sit → sitter.
  2. Drop the e: before a vowel suffix: bake → baking, hope → hoped, nice → nicest.
  3. Y to i: consonant + y → change to i before most suffixes (not -ing): happy → happier, cry → cried (but crying).
💬 You can say

"Words are built from parts, like Lego. When you know the parts, you can take apart big words and figure out what they mean."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children sometimes see "prefixes" that aren't (the "re" in "read" isn't "again" + "ad"). Teach: a real prefix leaves a real base word behind when you take it off.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can split 10 words into base + affix and explain the meaning (e.g., "unkind means not kind"), and correctly spell hopping, baking, happiest after practice.

💡 Teaching tip

Make a "Word Workshop" with base words on one colour of card and prefixes/suffixes on another; build words daily.

📚The Lesson

Words aren't just made of letters and sounds. They're also made of meaning pieces, called morphemes (MOR-feemz). A morpheme is the smallest part of a word that has meaning.

  • cat — 1 morpheme (you can't break it into smaller meaning parts)
  • cats — 2 morphemes: cat + s (the s means "more than one"!)
  • unkindly — 3 morphemes: un + kind + ly

The base: the heart of the word ❤️

The base is the main part of a word. It carries the biggest meaning. In jumping, the base is jump.

Prefixes: pieces that go in FRONT

A prefix goes at the beginning of a base and changes its meaning. - un- means not: unhappy, unlock, unfair, untie - re- means again: redo, reread, refill, replay - dis- means not or opposite: dislike, disagree, disappear - in- means not: incorrect, invisible, inactive

Suffixes: pieces that go at the END

A suffix goes at the end of a base. - -s / -es — more than one: dogs, boxes - -ing — happening now: jumping, reading - -ed — in the past: jumped, played, painted - -er / -or — a person who does it: teacher, painter, actor, sailor - -er / -est — comparing: fast, faster, fastest - -ly — in a certain way: quickly, softly, sadly

Spelling change rules ✂️

Sometimes the base changes a little when you add a suffix: 1. Double it! Short words with one short vowel and one final consonant double the last letter: hop → hopping, big → biggest, run → runner. 2. Drop the e! bake → baking, smile → smiled, nice → nicest. 3. Y to i! happy → happier, cry → cried, funny → funniest. (But keep the y before -ing: crying.)

Compound words: two bases stuck together 🧩

note + book = notebooksun + flower = sunflowerrain + bow = rainbowfoot + ball = footballcup + cake = cupcakebook + shelf = bookshelf
📖 The Unstoppable Painter

Rosa was a painter. She painted slowly and carefully.

One day, her painting fell. It was ruined! Rosa was unhappy.

But Rosa did not quit. She repainted it. This time it was even brighter!

"I am the happiest painter in town," she said, smiling. "Mistakes just mean I get to try again."

🤯 Did You Know?

The English word "antidisestablishmentarianism" has 28 letters, and it's made of at least six morphemes stacked together! Long words are almost always built from smaller pieces — so if you know the pieces, big words aren't scary.

🧠 Brain moment

Scientists have found that strong readers break long words into meaningful parts super quickly, often without even noticing. The more word parts you learn, the faster your brain can read and understand brand-new words!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Split each word into its parts and tell what it means: unlock, replay, painter, quickly, biggest.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Add the suffix and spell it correctly: hop + ing, bake + ed, sad + est, happy + er, cry + ed. Which rule did you use each time?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Invent 3 new words using real prefixes and suffixes (like "unbroccoli-ly") and write what each one would mean. Could someone else figure out your word's meaning? Why?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Build, split and read words using morphemes, and practise suffix spelling rules.

Materials

  • cards in 3 colours: base words (kind, play, jump, happy, hop, bake, tie, fair, read, teach, paint, quick), prefixes (un-, re-, dis-, in-), suffixes (-s, -ing, -ed, -er, -or, -est, -ly)
  • scissors, tape

Steps

  1. Word Workshop: Build as many real words as you can by joining cards. Read each one and say what it means.
  2. Word Surgery: The grown-up writes 10 long words (unkindly, repainted, jumping, happiest). Cut them apart into morphemes!
  3. Rule Test: Add -ing to hop, bake, play, cry. Which ones change? Which rule?
  4. Compound Match-up: Match halves to make 8 compound words.

Observation recording

PrefixBaseSuffixNew wordMeaning

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a morpheme? What is a base, a prefix and a suffix? What do un-, re- and dis- mean?

Part 2 — Word Families (applying)

Make a word family from the base play: add as many prefixes and suffixes as you can (plays, played, playing, player, replay, playful…). Then do the same for kind.

Part 3 — Compound Creatures (creating)

Invent 3 compound-word creatures (like a "rainbowfish" or a "cupcakedog"). Draw each and write a sentence describing it.

✏️ My compound creatures

🏠Homework

  1. Prefix Hunt. Find 5 words with un-, re- or dis- in books, packages or signs (unlock, refill, discount…). What does each mean?
  2. Compound Word Walk. Find 10 compound words around your home (toothbrush, bedroom, doorbell…).

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Can you make a word so long nobody has ever said it before, using only real word parts?
  2. Why do you think English doubles letters before some suffixes (hopping) but not others (jumping)?
  3. If you could invent a new prefix, what would it mean? (Maybe “zap-” means “instantly”?)
Lesson 9 of 11

Heart Words: Reading Tricky Words

Some words have a tricky part you have to learn “by heart.” Sound out the regular parts, then memorize only the tricky bit.

B2.6B2.8B2.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

The word “said” should sound like “sayed” — and the word “one” should sound like “own-ee.” But they don't! If a word breaks the rules, does that mean you have to memorize the WHOLE word like a picture — or is there a smarter way?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.6 use phonics to read the regular parts of irregular words, and learn the irregular part “by heart” (in “said,” s and d are regular, ai is the heart part)
  • B2.8 recognize common high-frequency words instantly and effortlessly
  • B2.4 spell common heart words correctly in my writing
  • B2.6 explain why some words are irregular

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.6 (part 2) explains that children should apply phonological, orthographic, and morphological knowledge to decode and encode the parts of irregular words that are regular, and memorize the unexpected portions — "instead of memorizing words as whole units." This is the modern, research-based "heart word" method. B2.8 adds recognizing high-frequency words effortlessly.

The heart word method

  1. Say the word. Count the sounds (tap them).
  2. Write a line for each sound.
  3. Fill in the letters that are "regular" (follow patterns already taught).
  4. Put a ♥ over the irregular part: "You need to learn this part by heart."
  5. Spell it 3 times, saying the letters.

Example — said: /s/ /e/ /d/ → s, d are regular; the /e/ is spelled ai ♥.

Grade 1 heart words to learn (about 5 per week)

the, a, to, do, of, you, was, said, are, were, is, his, has, I, they, what, want, where, there, here, one, once, two, come, some, from, of, put, push, pull, full, could, would, should, does, goes, again, any, many, who, whole, your, their, very, know, give, have, live, love, other, mother, brother

💡 Teaching tip

Many "heart words" become regular once more patterns are taught (e.g., "he," "me," "we" are regular open syllables). Only put hearts on the truly unexpected parts.

💬 You can say

"Most of this word follows the rules! Only this little part is tricky. Let's put a heart on it and learn that part by heart."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Guessing words from the first letter ("was" read as "saw") is common. Always return to the letters in order, left to right.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child reads the current heart word list instantly (under 2 seconds per word) on 3 separate days and spells them correctly in dictated sentences.

💡 Teaching tip

Keep a "Heart Word Wall" — once a word is mastered in reading AND writing, move it to the "I know it!" side.

📚The Lesson

Most English words follow the phonics rules you've been learning. But some very common words have a tricky part that doesn't follow the rules. We call them heart words, because you have to learn the tricky part by heart.

Most of the word is still regular!

Look at the word said. Tap the sounds: /s/ /e/ /d/. - The s says /s/ ✅ regular! - The d says /d/ ✅ regular! - The ai says /e/ ♥ — that's the tricky part! We put a heart on it.

So you don't need to memorize the whole word — just the heart part!

More heart words

  • the — th is regular; the e says /u/ ♥
  • of — the o says /u/ ♥ and the f says /v/ ♥
  • was — w and s are regular... but the a says /u/ or /o/ ♥ and the s says /z/
  • one — the whole word says "wun" ♥♥♥ (a real rule-breaker!)
  • could, would, should — the oul says short oo ♥
  • what — wh and t are regular; the a says /u/ ♥
  • they — th is regular; the ey says /ā/ ♥
  • does, goes — look closely: does rhymes with buzz, goes rhymes with toes!

Why do heart words exist?

Many of our most common words are also our oldest words. They've been said for over a thousand years, and their sounds changed while their spellings stayed the same. Others came from other languages. Heart words are like very old treasure — a bit worn, but precious!

High-frequency words

High-frequency words are words that show up all the time in books. Just 100 words like the, and, a, to, said, in, he, I, of, it, was make up about half of all the words you read! When you know them instantly, reading gets MUCH faster.

thesaidwasofyoutheyonetwocomesomewhatwheretherecouldwouldshoulddoestheiryourmany
🤯 Did You Know?

Dr. Seuss wrote The Cat in the Hat using only 236 different words from a list of words new readers should know. Later, his publisher bet him that he couldn't write a book with only 50 different words. He did it — the book was Green Eggs and Ham!

🧠 Brain moment

Your brain has a special spot, on the left side toward the back, that becomes a "word recognition" area as you learn to read. Scientists sometimes call it the brain's "letterbox." It doesn't exist as a reading area in people who haven't learned to read yet — it grows because of reading practice. You are literally building your brain!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Find the heart part in each word: said, was, of, the, one.

⭐⭐ Stretch

"Could," "would," and "should" all have the same heart part. Can you find it? Write a sentence that uses all three!

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

The words "to," "too," and "two" all sound the same but mean different things. Why is it helpful that they are spelled differently? Can you think of other sound-alike words?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Learn 5–10 heart words using the heart word method, and practise instant recognition.

Materials

  • index cards, red crayon or heart stickers, a timer

Steps

  1. Heart Mapping: For 5 new heart words, say the word, tap the sounds, draw a line for each sound, write the regular letters, and draw a ♥ over the tricky part.
  2. Trace, Copy, Cover, Write: Trace the word saying each letter, copy it, cover it, write it from memory, check it.
  3. Flash Race: Mix your heart word cards. How many can you read in 1 minute?
  4. Sentence Builder: Use each heart word in a sentence that you say, then write one of them.

Observation recording

Heart wordHeart partRead it fast? ✓Spelled it? ✓

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a heart word? Why do heart words exist? What is a high-frequency word?

Part 2 — Heart Word Sentences (writing)

Write 5 sentences, each using at least two heart words. Underline the heart words. Example: "They said it was my turn."

Part 3 — Heart Word Poster (creating)

Choose your trickiest heart word. Make a poster to help a younger child learn it: show the heart part, draw a picture to remember it, and write a sentence.

✏️ My heart word poster

🏠Homework

  1. Heart Word Hunt. Choose 3 heart words. Count how many times you find each one on one page of a book. Which is most common?
  2. Fridge Flash. Put this week's heart words on the fridge. Read them every time you open the fridge!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If English spelling were changed so heart words followed the rules (“sed,” “wun,” “wuz”), would reading be easier? Would anything be lost?
  2. Why do you think the most common words are often the strangest ones?
  3. Could your brain's “letterbox” grow even bigger if you learned to read another language too?
Lesson 10 of 11

Word Collectors: Growing Your Vocabulary

Collect words like treasure: sort them into categories, find opposites and near-twins, discover words with many meanings, and figure out new words from clues.

B2.7B2.6
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

“Jog,” “sprint,” “dash,” “race,” and “run” all mean moving fast on your feet. So why would a language bother having FIVE words for almost the same thing? Wouldn't one be enough?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.7 sort words into categories and subcategories, and define a word by giving its category and an example (“Happy is a feeling. You feel happy when…”)
  • B2.7 use antonyms (opposites) and begin to use synonyms (near-twins) and shades of meaning (cool, warm, hot, scalding)
  • B2.7 understand that some words have multiple meanings (a bat, to bat; pop!)
  • B2.7 figure out the meaning of a new word using clues in the sentence and word parts, and ask when I don't understand

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.7 asks children to demonstrate an understanding of commonly used words, acquire and use explicitly taught vocabulary in various contexts, including other subject areas, and use morphological knowledge to analyze new words in context. Vocabulary is the single biggest driver of reading comprehension in later grades. The curriculum emphasizes Tier 2 words — useful words found in books and school talk (e.g., compare, enormous, curious, observe, discover).

How to teach it

  1. Hook: act out jog, sprint, dash, tiptoe, stomp. Discuss why the differences matter.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Classwork: category sorts, a "word thermometer" for shades of meaning, and multiple-meaning word hunts.
  4. Choose 3–5 Tier 2 "Words of the Week": say them, define them kid-style, use them in multiple contexts, and reward your child for using them.
💬 You can say

"When you don't know a word, you can be a detective: look at the sentence around it, look inside the word for parts you know, or just ask. Asking about words is what smart readers do."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often nod along without understanding a word. Model it yourself: "Hmm, I'm not sure what spacious means. Let's look for clues!"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can define a new word with a category + example, give antonyms for 10 everyday words, place 5 temperature words in order, and uses Words of the Week spontaneously.

💡 Teaching tip

Suggested Tier 2 words for Grade 1: observe, compare, curious, enormous, tiny, fragile, predict, discover, gather, explore, shout, whisper, delicious, exhausted, furious, brave, gentle, ancient, sparkle, protect.

📚The Lesson

Every word you learn is like a new tool in your toolbox. The more tools you have, the more you can understand, explain and imagine! All the words you know are called your vocabulary.

1. Words live in families (categories)

Your brain stores words in groups, like drawers in a dresser. A category is a group of things that belong together. - Food: apple, bread, carrot, cheese → Fruit: apple, banana · Vegetables: carrot, peas - Clothes: hat, boots, scarf, shorts → Winter clothes: hat, boots, scarf · Summer clothes: shorts, sandals

How to define a word like a pro: Say its category, then give an example or detail. "A robin is a bird. It has a red chest and sings in spring." "Happy is a feeling. You feel happy when you see your best friend."

2. Opposites: antonyms

Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: hot/cold, first/last, above/beneath, yesterday/tomorrow, add/subtract, young/old, full/empty.

3. Near-twins: synonyms

Synonyms are words with almost the same meaning: big/large, happy/glad, quick/fast, begin/start. But even near-twins have small differences!

4. Shades of meaning 🌡️

Some words can be lined up like a thermometer from a little to a lot:

freezing→cold→cool→warm→hot→scalding
Which is bigger: a whisper, a talk, a shout, or a scream? Is "enormous" bigger than "big"?

5. One word, many meanings

Some words have multiple meanings: - bat — a flying animal 🦇 OR a stick for baseball 🏏 OR to hit a ball - pop — a sound, a drink, or to burst a balloon - rock — a stone, OR to rock a baby, OR "this song rocks!" The sentence tells you which meaning!

6. Figuring out new words 🔍

When you meet a new word, be a word detective: 1. Look outside the word — read the sentence around it for clues. 2. Look inside the word — do you know any parts? (un-, re-, -ful…) 3. Ask! — "What does ___ mean?" Great learners ask all the time.

"Ted's backyard was too small, so he wanted one that was more spacious." Clue: "too small" → spacious must mean big, with lots of space!

🤯 Did You Know?

The Oxford English Dictionary contains about 600,000 words, and new words are added every year! Words like emoji, selfie, and staycation were added only recently.

🤯 Did You Know?

Some Indigenous languages in Canada can express a whole English sentence in one long word, by joining meaning-pieces together. In Inuktitut, one word can mean something like "I want to go to the store"!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Give the antonym: up, happy, first, full, loud, day.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Put in order from smallest to biggest: huge, tiny, big, enormous, small. Now from quietest to loudest: shout, whisper, talk, scream, murmur.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think English has so many synonyms? When might it really matter whether you say "walked," "marched," "tiptoed" or "stomped"? Tell a tiny story where the word choice changes everything.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Sort, scale and explore words to build deep vocabulary knowledge.

Materials

  • 30 picture or word cards (foods, animals, clothes, toys), paper strips, a paint-sample card (from a hardware store) for shades of meaning

Steps

  1. Category Sort: Sort cards into big categories. Then split each category into smaller groups (subcategories). Explain your groups.
  2. Word Thermometer: On a paint-sample strip, write shades of meaning from weakest to strongest (e.g., tired → sleepy → exhausted).
  3. Multiple Meaning Match: Draw two pictures for bat, bark, ring, fly, trunk. Say a sentence for each meaning.
  4. Word Detective: The grown-up reads 3 sentences with a new word. Use clues to guess the meaning, then check.

Observation recording

WordMeaning 1Meaning 2
New wordClue I usedWhat I think it means

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is an antonym? A synonym? What are 3 ways to figure out a new word?

Part 2 — Define Like a Pro (applying)

Define 4 words using a category + an example: robin, apple, angry, hammer.

Part 3 — My Word Collection Book (creating)

Start a Word Collection Book. For each of 5 new words from books or other subjects (science, math, gym), write the word, draw it, write what it means, and use it in a sentence.

🏠Homework

  1. Word of the Week. Choose 3 "Words of the Week" with your grown-up. Use each one at least 3 times a day. Keep a tally!
  2. Science Words. Find 3 new words in a science or nature book or show. Teach them to your family at dinner.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Could there be a feeling that doesn't have a word yet? What would you name it?
  2. Do people who know more words think differently? Can you think about something you have no word for?
  3. Why do some words, like “pop” and “bat,” end up with so many meanings?
Lesson 11 of 11

Smooth Reading: Fluency with Expression

Put it all together: read words accurately, at a comfortable pace, with expression that shows you understand. Fluent reading sounds like talking!

B2.8D3.2B1.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

A robot and a storyteller read the exact same words. One puts you to sleep, the other makes you laugh, gasp and lean in. The words are identical — so what is the storyteller doing that the robot isn't?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • B2.8 read simple words and high-frequency words accurately and automatically
  • B2.8 read sentences and short paragraphs at a comfortable pace (not too fast, not too slow)
  • B2.8 read aloud with expression — changing my voice for punctuation and characters
  • D3.2 perform a reading for an audience with expression

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

B2.8 asks children to read simple words, short sentences, and paragraphs fluently, with accuracy and appropriate pacing to support comprehension, and read aloud with expression. Fluency is "the bridge between word recognition and comprehension" (the curriculum's words). When decoding is effortless, the brain is free to think about meaning.

The three parts of fluency

  1. Accuracy — reading the words correctly (first and most important!)
  2. Rate — a comfortable, conversational pace (NOT racing)
  3. Prosody — expression: phrasing, pausing at punctuation, emotion, character voices

Proven methods

  • Repeated reading: read the same short passage 3–4 times over a week. Each time gets smoother.
  • Echo reading: you read a sentence with expression; your child echoes it.
  • Choral reading: read together at the same time.
  • Reader's theatre: perform a short script.

Grade 1 benchmarks (rough guide)

By June, many Grade 1 readers read around 50–60 words correct per minute in grade-level text — but accuracy and understanding matter far more than speed. Never make reading a race.

💬 You can say

"Good readers sound like they're talking. Let's make the words sound like a real person saying them."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Some children speed up and skip words to "be fluent." Praise accuracy and meaning first. Also, "robot reading" (word… by… word) is a normal stage — it smooths with repetition.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

on a fresh decodable passage, your child reads with 95%+ accuracy, pauses at periods, raises their voice for questions, and can retell what they read.

💡 Teaching tip

Record your child reading a passage on Monday and again on Friday. Listen together — the improvement is incredibly motivating!

📚The Lesson

You've learned sounds, letters, letter teams, word parts and heart words. Now it's time to put it all together and read like a storyteller! Reading smoothly, correctly and with feeling is called fluency.

The three secrets of fluent reading

  1. 🎯 Accuracy — read every word correctly. If you make a mistake, fix it!
  2. 🚗 Pace — not too fast (zoom!), not too slow (robot…reading…), but just right, like talking.
  3. 🎭 Expression — make your voice match the meaning: excited, sad, spooky, bossy or silly!

Punctuation is your map 🗺️

  • Period (.) → stop. Your voice goes down. Take a tiny breath.
  • Comma (,) → a small pause, like a speed bump.
  • Question mark (?) → your voice goes up at the end.
  • Exclamation mark (!) → strong feeling! Make your voice big.
  • Quotation marks (" ") → someone is talking — use their voice!

Phrasing: read in chunks

Fluent readers read in phrases, not one word at a time. Robot: "The / big / brown / dog / ran / to / the / park." Fluent: "The big brown dog / ran to the park."

How to practise

  • Repeated reading: read the same passage 3 or 4 times. Each time gets smoother!
  • Echo reading: your grown-up reads a line; you copy their expression.
  • Scoop it: draw a scoop under each phrase with your finger as you read.
📖 The Brave Little Mouse

A little mouse lived under a big oak tree.

One night, she heard a sound. "Who is there?" she whispered.

A deep voice said, "It is I, the Owl!"

The mouse shook, but she stood tall. "Please do not eat me," she said bravely. "I can help you!"

The Owl laughed. "How could a tiny mouse help me?"

"You will see," said the mouse. And one day, she did!

Read it 3 times: first to get the words right, second to get the pace smooth, third with BIG expression — a whisper for the mouse, a deep voice for the Owl!

🤯 Did You Know?

Actors and audiobook narrators practise a passage many times before recording it. Some famous audiobook narrators give dozens of different voices to characters in one book — all performed by one person!

🧠 Brain moment

When you read aloud with expression, you actually understand and remember the story better. Your brain has to think about what the characters feel to choose the right voice — that's comprehension in action!

🧩Think Like a Word Scientist

⭐ Warm-up

Read "I have a surprise" three ways: happy, sneaky, and scared. Which punctuation mark would you put at the end for each?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why is reading too fast a problem? Why is reading too slow a problem? What's "just right" and how do you know?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

The mouse said "I can help you!" What do you think happened "one day"? How would your expression show the mouse's feelings in your new ending?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Improve accuracy, pace and expression through repeated reading, and perform for an audience.

Materials

  • The Brave Little Mouse passage (or a decodable book), a timer, a phone to record (with permission), paper crowns or masks for characters

Steps

  1. Echo Read: The grown-up reads each line with expression; you echo it.
  2. Read 1 (accuracy): Read the whole passage. The grown-up marks any words you missed. Practise those words.
  3. Read 2 (pace): Read again, scooping phrases with your finger.
  4. Read 3 (expression): Record yourself with character voices!
  5. Listen back: What did you do well? What would you change?
  6. Reader's Theatre: Perform the story with a family member — one is the mouse, one is the Owl.

Observation recording

Reading #Words read correctlySmoothness (⭐–⭐⭐⭐)Expression (⭐–⭐⭐⭐)

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What are the three secrets of fluent reading? What does each punctuation mark tell your voice to do?

Part 2 — Reading Log (reflecting)

Each day this week, read a short book or passage aloud 2–3 times. Record the title, how many times you read it, and one thing that got better.

DayTitleTimes readWhat got better

Part 3 — Performance Night (creating)

Choose a favourite short book or poem. Practise it all week. On Friday, perform it for your family (or a video call with relatives) with full expression. Afterward, write or say: What strategy helped you most?

🏠Homework

  1. Record and Compare. Record yourself reading the same page on Monday and Friday. Play both for your family. Can they hear the difference?
  2. Bedtime Reading Swap. Take turns with a grown-up reading pages of a bedtime book. Copy their expression, then challenge them to copy yours!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Does reading silently in your head have expression? Can you hear a voice when you read silently?
  2. Why do we enjoy hearing the same story many times, even when we know how it ends?
  3. If an animal could read aloud, what kind of voice would a cat, an elephant, or a mouse have?
Word Wall

Key Vocabulary

Read each card aloud together. Cover the definition and ask: “What does this word mean? Use it in your own sentence.” Revisit the cards at the start of every session in this strand.

phoneme
The smallest sound in a spoken word.
“The word “ship” has three phonemes: /sh/ /i/ /p/.”
blend
To push sounds together to read a word (or two consonants side by side that you can both hear).
“I can blend /f/ /r/ /o/ /g/ to read “frog.””
segment
To break a word into each of its sounds, to spell it.
“I segmented “stamp” into five sounds.”
vowel
The letters a, e, i, o, u (and sometimes y) that make open sounds. Every syllable needs one.
“The vowel in “bug” is u.”
consonant
Any letter that is not a vowel.
““B,” “t,” and “s” are consonants.”
uppercase / lowercase
Capital letters / small letters.
““A” is uppercase and “a” is lowercase.”
alphabetical order
Putting words in the order of the alphabet, A to Z.
“The dictionary lists words in alphabetical order.”
digraph
Two letters that make one sound together, like sh, ch, th.
““Ch” in “lunch” is a digraph.”
silent e
An e at the end of a word that you don't hear but that makes the vowel say its name.
“Silent e changes “kit” into “kite.””
long vowel
A vowel sound that says the letter's name.
“The “a” in “cake” is a long vowel.”
vowel team
Two or more letters that work together to make one vowel sound.
““Ai” in “rain” is a vowel team.”
r-controlled vowel
A vowel followed by r that makes a new sound (ar, or, er, ir, ur).
““Ar” in “star” is an r-controlled vowel.”
diphthong
A sliding vowel sound where your mouth moves, like oi, oy, ou, ow.
““Oy” in “boy” is a diphthong.”
morpheme
The smallest part of a word that has meaning.
““Dogs” has two morphemes: dog + s.”
prefix
A word part added to the front of a base that changes its meaning.
“The prefix “un-” turns “kind” into “unkind.””
suffix
A word part added to the end of a base.
“Adding the suffix “-ing” makes “jumping.””
compound word
Two words joined to make one new word.
““Sunflower” is a compound word.”
heart word
A word with a tricky part you have to learn by heart.
“In “said,” the “ai” is the heart part.”
synonym / antonym
A word with almost the same meaning / a word with the opposite meaning.
““Glad” is a synonym for happy; “sad” is an antonym.”
fluency
Reading accurately, at a good pace, with expression.
“My fluency got better after I read the story three times.”
