Lesson 1 of 11

Stories or Facts? Kinds of Texts

Discover the two big families of texts — literary (stories and poems) and informational (facts) — and the genres inside each.

C1.2C2.2C1.1
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

A story about a bear and a book of facts about bears are both about bears. But you'd never read them the same way. Why not? What's different inside your brain when you read a story versus facts?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C1.2 tell the difference between literary texts (stories, poems) and informational texts (facts, how-to, reports)
  • C1.2 name some genres: fairy tale, fable, poem, adventure, animal fact book, recipe, letter
  • C2.2 explain my purpose for reading: for fun (enjoyment) or to find information
  • C1.1 read and understand a short story and a short information text

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C1.2 asks children to identify simple literary and informational text forms and their genres; C2.2 asks them to identify purposes for engaging with texts, including enjoyment or finding information. Knowing what kind of text you're reading tells your brain how to read it.

Two big families

  • Literary texts (made-up or imaginative, to entertain or share feelings): stories, fairy tales, fables, folktales, poems, picture books, comics.
  • Informational texts (true facts, to teach or explain): animal fact books, how-to/recipes, reports, maps, signs, letters, news.

How to teach it

  1. Gather 8–10 texts from home and the library: storybooks, a nonfiction book, a recipe, a poem, a flyer, a comic.
  2. Read the lesson, including both short texts.
  3. Classwork: sort the pile into the two families and discuss clues.
💬 You can say

"Before we read, let's ask: Is this a story or facts? Am I reading for fun or to learn something?"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often think a book with a real animal must be nonfiction, or that "nonfiction" means "not true." Clarify: fiction = made up; non-fiction = true facts. A talking bear is a clue to fiction!

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can sort 8 unfamiliar texts into literary or informational and give a clue for each (talking animals, "once upon a time," photographs, headings, a table of contents).

💡 Teaching tip

At the library, visit both sections: the picture book section and the nonfiction section (organized by number — the 590s are animals!).

📚The Lesson

Everything you read is a text — a book, a sign, a poem, a comic, a recipe, even a birthday card! Texts come in two big families.

Family 1: Literary texts 🧚

Literary texts come from someone's imagination. They tell stories or share feelings. They're mostly for enjoyment. Clues: characters, a problem, talking animals, magic, "Once upon a time…", rhyming lines.

Genres (kinds) of literary texts: - Fairy tale — magic, royalty, good vs. evil (Cinderella) - Fable — a short story with animals that teaches a lesson (The Tortoise and the Hare) - Poem — words arranged in lines, often with rhythm and rhyme - Adventure — exciting journeys and danger - Comic — pictures in boxes with speech bubbles

Family 2: Informational texts 📚

Informational texts give true facts. They teach, explain, or tell you how to do something. Clues: real photographs, headings, labels, a table of contents, a glossary, numbers and diagrams.

Genres of informational texts: - Fact book — all about one topic (Owls) - How-to / procedure — steps in order, like a recipe - Letter or card — a message to someone - Map or sign — information to help you find your way or stay safe

Why does it matter?

Your purpose for reading changes how you read. For a story, you relax, imagine, and wonder what happens next. For facts, you slow down, look at pictures and labels, and hunt for answers. You can even jump to the part you need!

📖 Bear Wants a Nap

Bear yawned a big yawn. "I am so sleepy," he said.

But Squirrel was chattering. Bird was singing. The river was splashing.

"Shhh!" said Bear. Nobody listened.

So Bear found a cozy cave, curled up, and whispered, "Goodnight, everyone. See you in spring."

📖 Black Bears in Winter

Black bears live in forests across Canada.

In fall, they eat lots of berries and nuts to get fat.

In winter, they sleep in a den for up to seven months. This is called hibernation.

During hibernation, a bear does not eat, drink, or go to the bathroom!

Which one is literary? Which one is informational? What are your clues?

🤯 Did You Know?

A hibernating black bear's heart can slow from about 40–50 beats a minute down to as few as 8–10 beats a minute! And mother bears give birth to tiny cubs — about the size of a chipmunk — in the middle of winter, while in the den.

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

Literary or informational? (a) A book called All About Sharks with photographs. (b) A story about a shark who wants to be a ballerina. (c) A recipe for pancakes. (d) A poem about the moon.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Can a text be BOTH? Think about a story about a real bear that also teaches true facts. Is it literary or informational — or both?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think people invented stories at all, when they could just share facts? What can a story do that facts can't?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Sort real texts into literary and informational families and identify their genres.

Materials

  • 8–10 real texts (storybook, nonfiction book, poem, recipe, comic, flyer, map, birthday card, magazine)
  • two baskets or big paper labelled 🧚 LITERARY and 📚 INFORMATIONAL

Steps

  1. Look at each text. Look for clues (photos? characters? headings?).
  2. Put it in the right basket. Say your clue out loud.
  3. For each text, name its genre.
  4. Choose one of each. Read a page of each together. Talk: How did you read differently?

Observation recording

TextLiterary or informational?GenreMy clue

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a literary text? What is an informational text? Name 3 genres of each.

Part 2 — Two Bears (comparing)

Reread Bear Wants a Nap and Black Bears in Winter. Write or tell: How are they the same? How are they different? What did you learn from the facts that the story didn't tell you?

Part 3 — Two Texts, One Topic (creating)

Choose an animal. Make TWO tiny texts about it: a 3-sentence story (with a character and a problem) and 3 true facts (with a labelled drawing).

🏠Homework

  1. Library Mission. At the library, borrow one literary book and one informational book about the same topic. Read both this week.
  2. Home Text Count. Count how many literary and informational texts are in your home (look at shelves, the fridge, the mailbox). Which family wins?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Can a made-up story teach you something true?
  2. Why do so many fables use animals instead of people to teach lessons?
  3. If you wrote a book about your own life, would it be literary or informational?
Lesson 2 of 11

Get Your Brain Ready: What Do I Already Know?

Before reading, good readers wake up what they already know and set a purpose — and it makes a huge difference.

C2.1C2.2C2.7
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

If a friend told you about “the best day ever at the sugar shack,” and you'd never heard of a sugar shack, you'd be lost. But if you'd been to one, you'd smell the syrup already! Why does knowing a little make understanding SO much easier?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C2.1 think about what I already know about a topic before I read, from my life and from other books
  • C2.2 set a purpose: “I'm reading to enjoy the story” or “I'm reading to find out…”
  • C2.7 explain how activating what I know helped me understand a text
  • C2.1 notice when a text teaches me something that changes what I thought I knew

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C2.1 asks children to activate prior knowledge, including knowledge gained from personal and text experiences. C2.7 asks them to identify strategies that helped them comprehend — including this one. Research shows background knowledge is one of the strongest predictors of reading comprehension.

The KWL chart

  • K — What do I already Know?
  • W — What do I Want to find out?
  • L — What did I Learn?

How to teach it

  1. Hook: talk about a place or activity your child knows well (e.g., a family tradition, a sport). Then pick something they don't know (e.g., curling, a sugar shack). Notice the difference.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Complete a KWL chart before, during and after reading the passage (Classwork).
💬 You can say

"Before we read, let's open the file in your brain for this topic. What's already in there?"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Some prior knowledge is wrong! That's fine — reading can fix it. Celebrate when your child says "I thought ___, but now I know ___." That is real learning.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child spontaneously says "This reminds me of…" or "I already know…" before reading, and can fill in a KWL chart independently with support for writing.

💡 Teaching tip

Build background knowledge on purpose: nature walks, museum visits, documentaries, and conversations are all reading instruction!

📚The Lesson

Your brain is like a giant library with millions of files. Every time you learn something, it gets stored in a file. When you read, your brain opens the right file to help you understand. Using what you already know is called activating prior knowledge. Prior means "before" — it's what you knew before you started reading!

How to wake up your brain before reading

  1. Look at the title and pictures. What is this about?
  2. Ask: What do I already know about this? Have I seen it, done it, or read about it before?
  3. Set a purpose: Am I reading to enjoy a story, or to find out something?
  4. Wonder: What do I want to find out?

The KWL chart

K
What I Know→W
What I Want to know→L
What I Learned
📖 The Sugar Shack

In early spring, when days are warm and nights are still freezing, the sap starts to run in maple trees.

People make a small hole in each tree and hang a bucket or attach a tube. Drip, drip, drip — clear sap flows out.

The sap looks like water and tastes only a tiny bit sweet. It is boiled for hours in a sugar shack until most of the water turns to steam.

What's left is thick, golden maple syrup!

Many families visit sugar shacks to eat pancakes and pour hot syrup on snow to make maple taffy.

The Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe peoples were making maple sugar long before anyone else here. Many families still gather sap every spring.

Before you read, what did you know about maple syrup? What did you learn?

🤯 Did You Know?

It takes about 40 litres of sap to make just 1 litre of maple syrup! And Canada makes about three-quarters of all the maple syrup in the world — most of it in Quebec.

🧠 Brain moment

Scientists did an experiment: kids who knew a lot about soccer understood a soccer story better than kids who were better readers but knew nothing about soccer! What you know matters as much as how well you read words.

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

Before reading a book called Life in the Ocean, what would you already know? Write 3 things.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why do you think the sap only runs when days are warm and nights are freezing? Use what you know about weather and trees.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Is it possible to understand a story about something you've never seen or done? How? (Think about stories set in space or in the past!)

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Use a KWL chart to activate prior knowledge, set a purpose, and record new learning.

Materials

  • a nonfiction library book on a topic of your child's choice (or The Sugar Shack passage)
  • a big paper folded into 3 columns: K · W · L, sticky notes

Steps

  1. K: Before reading, write or draw everything you already know on sticky notes.
  2. W: Write 2–3 questions you want to answer.
  3. Set your purpose out loud: "I am reading to find out…"
  4. Read together. Stop when you find an answer to a W question.
  5. L: Write or draw what you learned. Did any K notes turn out wrong? Move them to a "Fixed my thinking!" spot.

Observation recording

K — What I KnowW — What I Want to knowL — What I Learned

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does "prior knowledge" mean? What are the three parts of a KWL chart?

Part 2 — Sugar Shack Questions (comprehension)

Answer from the text: (1) When does sap run? (2) What happens when sap is boiled? (3) Which peoples made maple sugar first? (4) How do you make maple taffy?

Part 3 — Thinking Changes (reflecting)

Write 2 sentences: "I used to think ___. Now I know ___." Use something you learned this week in any subject.

🏠Homework

  1. Family Expert Interview. Ask a family member what they know about a topic you'll read about next week. Add their ideas to your K column.
  2. Sweet Science. If you can, taste real maple syrup and compare it to "pancake syrup." Read both labels. What's different?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. How did the first person figure out that tree sap could become syrup?
  2. Can knowing too much about something make a story boring? Or does it make it better?
  3. Where in your body do you think memories are stored — and how does your brain find the right one so fast?
Lesson 3 of 11

Predict Like a Detective

Use the title, pictures, text features and clues from the story to predict what will happen — then read on to check.

C2.3C1.3
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Weather forecasters predict tomorrow's weather — and sometimes they're wrong. Detectives predict who did it — and sometimes they're wrong. If predictions are often wrong, why do good readers bother making them?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C2.3 make a prediction using what I know, the title and pictures, and clues from the text
  • C2.3 check my prediction as I read and change it when I find new clues
  • C1.3 use text features like the title, cover and illustrations to help me predict
  • C2.3 explain the clue that led to my prediction (“I think… because…”)

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C2.3 asks children to make predictions using background knowledge, text features, and evidence from the text. Predicting keeps readers actively engaged — they read to find out if they were right.

The sentence frame

"I think ___ will happen because ___." The "because" is the crucial part: it's the evidence.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: discuss weather forecasts and detectives.
  2. Read the lesson. Use the passage in parts, stopping at each ✋ to predict.
  3. Use a picture book with a surprising ending for Classwork (e.g., The Paper Bag Princess, This Is Not My Hat).
💬 You can say

"A good prediction isn't about being right. It's about using clues. When a new clue appears, smart detectives change their minds."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children sometimes make wild guesses with no evidence ("A dragon will come!"), or feel bad when wrong. Praise the reasoning: "You used the clue about the dark clouds — great thinking, even though the author surprised us!"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child makes predictions with a "because" clue, and revises predictions mid-story without prompting.

💡 Teaching tip

Authors love to trick readers with surprise endings — talk about why an author might want to surprise you.

📚The Lesson

A prediction is a smart guess about what will happen next, based on clues. Detectives predict. Weather forecasters predict. And great readers predict all the time!

Where do clues come from?

  • 📕 The title and cover — The Monster Under the Bed... probably a bit spooky!
  • 🖼️ The pictures — a character with a worried face, dark clouds, a wobbly bridge
  • 🧠 What you already know — in fairy tales, things often happen in threes!
  • 📖 Clues in the words — "Mia heard a strange scratching sound..."

Say it like a detective

"I think ___ will happen because ___." The word because shows your evidence — the clue that proves your thinking.

Check and change

As you read, check: Was I right? If new clues appear, change your prediction! That's not failing — that's thinking.

📖 The Scratching Sound (Part 1)

Mia was reading in bed. The house was quiet.

Then she heard it. Scratch… scratch… scratch.

It came from under her bed.

Mia's heart went thump. She pulled the blanket up to her nose.

✋ STOP. Predict! What is making the sound? What is your clue?

📖 The Scratching Sound (Part 2)

Mia grabbed her flashlight. She took a deep breath and peeked under the bed.

Two shiny eyes blinked back at her. Then she heard a tiny squeak.

✋ STOP. Change or keep your prediction?

📖 The Scratching Sound (Part 3)

It was Pip, her little brother's hamster! He had escaped from his cage and was nibbling on Mia's sock.

Mia laughed. "Pip! You scared me!"

She scooped him up and carried him back to his cage. Then she read her book — with the light on.

🤯 Did You Know?

Your brain predicts all day long, even when you're not reading! When you walk down stairs, your brain predicts where the next step will be. That's why missing a step makes your stomach jump — your brain's prediction was wrong!

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

What clue in Part 1 made the story feel scary? Find two clues.

⭐⭐ Stretch

The author told us about the "shiny eyes" and the "squeak" before telling us it was a hamster. Why do you think she did that?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Can you predict the ending of a story you've already read before? What if a story had NO clues at all — would it be more fun or less fun to read?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Make, check and revise predictions while reading a picture book.

Materials

  • a picture book your child hasn't read (ideally one with a twist), sticky notes, a pencil

Steps

  1. Cover Clues: Look only at the cover and title. Write a prediction on a sticky note: "I think… because…"
  2. Stop and Predict: The grown-up reads and stops at 3 exciting moments. Each time, make a new prediction on a sticky note.
  3. Check: After reading, look at each sticky note. Put ✅ (right), 🔄 (changed), or 😲 (surprised!).
  4. Talk: Which clues helped the most?

Observation recording

When I predictedMy predictionMy clue (because…)✅ 🔄 or 😲

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a prediction? What 4 places can clues come from? Why is it OK to change a prediction?

Part 2 — Predict and Prove (applying)

Look at the cover of a new book (don't read it yet!). Write 2 predictions with "because" clues. Then read the book and write whether you were right.

Part 3 — Write a Cliffhanger (creating)

Write the start of a mystery story (3–4 sentences) that stops at an exciting moment. Include 2 clues. Ask a family member to predict the ending!

🏠Homework

  1. TV/Book Predictions. While watching a show or reading a bedtime story with your family, pause once and everyone predicts what happens next. Who was closest?
  2. Weather Detective. Look at the sky each morning for 3 days and predict the weather. Check in the evening. What clues helped?

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why do we enjoy being surprised by a story, even when it proves our prediction wrong?
  2. Can animals make predictions? How does a squirrel “know” winter is coming?
  3. If you could see the future, would stories still be fun?
Lesson 4 of 11

Movie in My Mind: Visualize, Reread & Ask Questions

Learn to notice when your understanding breaks down — and fix it by visualizing, rereading and asking questions.

C2.4C1.1C2.7
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Have you ever read a whole page, got to the bottom, and realized you have NO idea what it said? Your eyes read every word… so where did your brain go? And how do you get it back?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C2.4 visualize — make a movie in my mind — while I read or listen
  • C2.4 notice when something doesn't make sense and reread to fix it
  • C2.4 ask questions before, during and after reading (I wonder… Why did…?)
  • C2.7 name which fix-up strategy helped me understand

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C2.4 asks children to use strategies such as rereading, visualizing, and asking questions to monitor their understanding. The key skill is noticing confusion — good readers know when they don't understand. C1.1 asks them to comprehend short texts using words, grammar, sentence structure and background knowledge.

The "click and clunk" idea

When reading makes sense, it "clicks." When it stops making sense, it "clunks." Teach your child to notice clunks and use a fix-up strategy: 1. Reread the sentence. 2. Visualize — can I see it? 3. Ask a question — what's confusing me? 4. Look at the pictures. 5. Ask for help.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: talk about "zoning out." It happens to adults too!
  2. Read the lesson. Close eyes and visualize the passage while you read it aloud.
  3. Classwork: Draw-what-you-hear and a planted "clunk" sentence.
💬 You can say

"Good readers notice when their brain goes 'Huh?' That's not a problem — it's a signal to use a fix-up strategy."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children who decode well sometimes "word-call" — they read words perfectly but don't understand. Always pair reading with talk: "What just happened? What do you see in your mind?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child stops and rereads on their own when something doesn't make sense, and can describe their mental image in detail.

💡 Teaching tip

Plant a silly mistake in a sentence you read aloud ("The cat barked at the moon") and see if your child catches it.

📚The Lesson

When you read, your brain can make a movie! You see the characters, hear the sounds, smell the smells. Making pictures in your mind is called visualizing. It's one of the most powerful reading superpowers.

Visualize with all five senses

Read this slowly and close your eyes between sentences:

📖 The Campfire

The fire crackled and popped. Orange sparks floated up into the dark sky.

The smoke smelled like wood and marshmallows.

Dad held a stick with a gooey, golden marshmallow on the end.

Far away, a loon called across the lake — a long, lonely sound.

We wrapped ourselves in scratchy wool blankets and looked up at a million stars.

What did you see? Hear? Smell? Feel? Taste?

Click or clunk? 🔊

When reading makes sense, it clicks. When it stops making sense, it goes clunk! A good reader notices the clunk. This is called monitoring your understanding — like a lifeguard watching the pool.

Fix-up strategies 🛠️

When you hear a clunk, fix it! 1. Reread — go back and read the sentence again, slowly. 2. Visualize — try to see it in your mind. 3. Ask a question — "What does this word mean? Who is talking?" 4. Look at the pictures for clues. 5. Read on a little — sometimes the next sentence explains. 6. Ask someone for help.

Questions keep your brain awake 🤔

Good readers ask questions before ("What's this about?"), during ("Why did he do that?"), and after ("What would I have done?"). Some questions are answered in the text; others make you think bigger!

🤯 Did You Know?

The common loon is on Canada's one-dollar coin — that's why people call it the "loonie"! Loons can dive as deep as 60 metres underwater to catch fish, and their haunting call can travel across a whole lake.

🧠 Brain moment

Brain scientists using scanners found that when people read a word like "kick," the part of the brain that controls leg movement lights up a little, as if they were really kicking! Reading really does make a movie in your brain.

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

Draw what you visualized from The Campfire. Label something for each sense.

✏️ My campfire picture

⭐⭐ Stretch

Find the "clunk": "Sam put on his mittens because it was a hot summer day." What's wrong? Which fix-up strategy helped you notice?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Two people read the same sentence: "A dog ran across the park." Will they visualize the exact same dog? Why or why not? Does that mean one of them is wrong?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Practise visualizing and catching "clunks" with fix-up strategies.

Materials

  • paper, crayons, a short passage or picture book (don't show pictures)

Steps

  1. Draw What You Hear: The grown-up reads a descriptive paragraph without showing pictures. Draw what you visualize. Then compare with the book's picture.
  2. Clunk Catcher: The grown-up reads 6 sentences; 3 have a silly "clunk" (e.g., "The fish climbed up the tree"). Clap when you hear a clunk and fix it.
  3. Question Cards: Make 3 cards: BEFORE, DURING, AFTER. As you read a story together, ask one question from each card.
  4. Fix-up Bookmark: Make a bookmark listing the 6 fix-up strategies with little pictures.

Observation recording

SentenceClick or clunk?How I fixed it

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does "visualize" mean? What is a "clunk"? Name 4 fix-up strategies.

Part 2 — Five Senses Chart (applying)

Read a short story. Fill in: I could SEE… HEAR… SMELL… FEEL… TASTE…

SenseWhat I imagined

Part 3 — Question Log (thinking)

While reading a book this week, write 3 questions: one before, one during and one after. Circle any questions the book answered.

🏠Homework

  1. Sound Visualizing. Listen to a story or audiobook with your eyes closed for 10 minutes. Draw your favourite scene afterward.
  2. Campfire Night. If you can, have a real (or pretend!) campfire. Write 2 sentences using all five senses.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Do people who are born blind visualize stories? What might their “movie” be made of?
  2. Why is a book sometimes better than the movie version?
  3. Where do the pictures in your mind come from if you've never seen the thing you're reading about?
Lesson 5 of 11

Pictures Talk Too: Illustrations, Images & Text Features

Discover how pictures, labels, captions, titles, symbols and diagrams work WITH the words to tell us more.

C1.4C1.3C3.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

In some picture books, the words say one thing while the pictures show something totally different — and that's what makes them hilarious. How can a book “lie” in its words but tell the truth in its pictures?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C1.4 explain how illustrations, photos and graphics add to what the words say
  • C1.4 notice when pictures tell something the words don't (or even disagree with the words!)
  • C1.3 name text features — title, labels, captions, headings, symbols, diagrams — and explain how they help readers
  • C3.2 use picture clues to infer what a character feels or what's really happening

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C1.4 asks children to demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between simple illustrations, images, and graphics and the text. C1.3 includes text features, including illustrations, symbols, and titles. In picture books, the pictures are often half the story.

Great books for this lesson

  • This Is Not My Hat or I Want My Hat Back by Jon Klassen — pictures tell the truth the words hide!
  • Rosie's Walk by Pat Hutchins — the words never mention the fox chasing Rosie.
  • Any nonfiction book with photographs, labels, captions and diagrams.

How to teach it

  1. Read a picture book first with only words (hide pictures), then with pictures. Discuss.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Classwork: text feature scavenger hunt in a nonfiction book.
💬 You can say

"Illustrators are storytellers too. Let's read the pictures as carefully as the words."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children sometimes rely on pictures to guess words — in decoding, redirect to the letters. But for comprehension, pictures are a fantastic resource. Keep these two uses separate.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can explain one thing a picture told them that the words didn't, and can name and explain 4 text features in a nonfiction book.

💡 Teaching tip

Make a text features "museum" — cut examples from old magazines and label them.

📚The Lesson

In a picture book, there are two storytellers: the author who writes the words, and the illustrator who makes the pictures. Sometimes they're the same person!

Pictures add information

Words might say: "Grandma made soup." But the picture shows Grandma's apron, a steaming pot, a cat sleeping on the counter, and snow outside the window. The picture tells us more!

Sometimes pictures tell a secret

In some books, the words say one thing and the pictures show another. In Rosie's Walk, the words only say Rosie the hen went for a walk. But the pictures show a fox sneaking behind her, getting bonked every time! The joke is only in the pictures.

Text features: helpers on the page

Informational texts have special helpers called text features. They help you find and understand information quickly. - 📕 Title — tells the topic - 🔠 Headings — tell what each section is about - 🖼️ Photographs — show what real things look like - 🏷️ Labels — name the parts of a picture - 💬 Captions — sentences under a picture that explain it - 📊 Diagrams — drawings that show how something works or its parts - 🔣 Symbols — small pictures that stand for something (⚠️ = danger, ♻️ = recycle) - 📑 Table of contents — a list of what's inside and where

A labelled diagram

🦋
Butterfly — labels: antennae wings head thorax abdomen legs (6)
Caption: A monarch butterfly has four wings and six legs, like all insects.
🤯 Did You Know?

The monarch butterfly migrates up to 4,000 kilometres from Canada to the mountains of Mexico every fall — and the butterflies that make the trip have never been there before! Scientists are still studying how they find the way.

🤯 Did You Know?

Illustrator Jerry Pinkney, an African-American artist, won the Caldecott Medal for The Lion & the Mouse, a picture book with almost no words at all — the pictures tell the whole story!

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

What's the difference between a label and a caption?

⭐⭐ Stretch

Look at a picture in a storybook. Find 3 things the picture tells you that the words don't say.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Could you tell a whole story with only pictures and no words? What would be easy to show? What would be hard to show? (Try showing "yesterday" or "I'm thinking about my grandma" with only a picture!)

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Find text features in real nonfiction and explore how pictures add to meaning.

Materials

  • a nonfiction book with text features, a storybook where the pictures tell extra (e.g., Rosie's Walk), sticky notes

Steps

  1. Words Only: The grown-up reads a picture book page without showing the picture. Draw what you imagine. Then look at the real picture — what extra did it show?
  2. Text Feature Scavenger Hunt: Find and flag with sticky notes: title, heading, photo, label, caption, diagram, table of contents, symbol.
  3. Feature Detective: For each one, say how it helps a reader.

Observation recording

Text featurePageHow it helps a reader

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Name 6 text features. What does an illustrator do?

Part 2 — Picture Power (analyzing)

Choose a page from a picture book. Write: What do the words say? What does the picture show? What does the picture add?

Part 3 — My Labelled Diagram (creating)

Draw a labelled diagram of something you know well (your bike, a tree, your pet, a snowman). Add a title, at least 5 labels, and a caption.

✏️ My labelled diagram

🏠Homework

  1. Symbol Hunt. Find 5 symbols in your home or neighbourhood (♻️ ⚠️ 🚻 ♿ 🔥). What does each stand for? Why use a symbol instead of words?
  2. Wordless Book. Borrow a wordless picture book (e.g., Journey by Aaron Becker). Tell the story aloud to a family member.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why do you think many books for grown-ups have no pictures? Do grown-ups stop needing them?
  2. If you illustrated your favourite story, what would you draw differently?
  3. Can a picture ever be more truthful than words?
Lesson 6 of 11

First, Next, Last: Sequence & the Main Idea

Put events in order, spot the most important information, and find the main idea — the one big thing a text is about.

C1.3C3.3C2.6
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

If you mixed up the pages of “Goldilocks” — she runs away screaming, THEN tastes the porridge, THEN meets the bears — would it still be the same story? Why does ORDER matter so much?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C1.3 identify text patterns like sequence and chronological (time) order and explain how they help me understand
  • C3.3 retell the important events of a story in order: beginning, middle, end
  • C3.3 identify the most important information in an informational text
  • C2.6 find the main idea of a simple text and tell it in one sentence

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C1.3 includes text patterns such as sequencing and chronological order. C3.3 asks children to analyze texts by identifying and sequencing important information and events. C2.6 asks them to identify important information, including the main idea. These are the foundations of summarizing.

Key ideas

  • Sequence: order of events or steps (first, next, then, last).
  • Beginning–Middle–End: characters & setting → problem & events → solution.
  • Main idea: what the whole text is MOSTLY about. Details support it.

The "umbrella" metaphor

The main idea is the umbrella; the details are the raindrops underneath that it covers.

How to teach it

  1. Hook: retell Goldilocks with scrambled events. Let your child fix it.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Classwork: cut up a comic strip or story and resequence it; find a main idea using the umbrella.
💬 You can say

"When you retell, don't tell me EVERYTHING — tell me the most important parts in order."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children's retells are often either too short ("A bear came.") or include every tiny detail. Teach "Somebody–Wanted–But–So–Then" for stories. For main ideas, children often pick an interesting detail instead of the big idea — use the umbrella test: "Does this cover ALL the sentences?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child retells a new story with beginning, middle and end in order, and chooses the main idea from 3 options with a reason.

💡 Teaching tip

Use real-life sequences: brushing teeth, a recipe, a day at the park.

📚The Lesson

Stories and information texts are like a train: each car comes in a special order. If the cars get mixed up, the train doesn't make sense!

Sequence: putting things in order

Sequence means the order that things happen. Stories often go in chronological order — the order of time, from first to last. Clue words help: first, next, then, after that, later, finally, at the end.

Stories have a beginning, middle and end

  • Beginning — Who are the characters? Where are they (the setting)?
  • Middle — What is the problem? What happens?
  • End — How is the problem solved?

Somebody – Wanted – But – So – Then 🧩

A magic way to retell ANY story in one breath: - Somebody: Goldilocks - Wanted: to find food and a place to rest - But: the house belonged to three bears - So: she ate their porridge, broke a chair and fell asleep in a bed - Then: the bears came home, and she ran away!

The main idea ☂️

The main idea is what a text is mostly about — the ONE big idea. The details are the smaller facts that support it. Think of an umbrella: the main idea is the umbrella; the details are the raindrops it covers.

📖 Busy Beavers

Beavers are amazing builders.

They cut down trees with their strong orange teeth.

They drag branches and mud to the river to build dams.

The dam makes a pond where they build a home called a lodge.

The lodge has an underwater door to keep them safe from wolves.

Which sentence tells the main idea? (Hint: which sentence is the umbrella?)

🤯 Did You Know?

The biggest beaver dam ever found is in Wood Buffalo National Park in Alberta. It's about 850 metres long — longer than eight hockey rinks in a row! It's so big it can be seen from space.

🤯 Did You Know?

A beaver's teeth never stop growing! They're orange because they have iron in them, which makes them extra strong — perfect for chewing through trees.

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

Put these in order: "The chick hatched." "The hen laid an egg." "The chick grew into a hen." "The egg cracked."

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why did the beavers need an underwater door? Which detail explains it? Does that detail fit under the main idea's umbrella?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Some stories start at the END and then go back to tell how it happened. Why might an author tell a story out of order? Could it make the story more exciting?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Sequence events in stories and procedures, and find main ideas.

Materials

  • a comic strip cut into boxes (or photocopied story pictures), scissors, glue, an umbrella drawing on paper, a familiar story

Steps

  1. Comic Scramble: Mix up the comic boxes. Put them in order and glue them down. Retell using first, next, then, finally.
  2. SWBST Retell: Retell a familiar story (e.g., The Three Little Pigs) using Somebody–Wanted–But–So–Then.
  3. Umbrella Test: The grown-up reads 5 sentences about one topic. Choose which sentence is the umbrella (main idea) and which are the raindrops (details).
  4. Life Sequence: Act out a routine (making a sandwich) in the WRONG order. Laugh, then fix it!

Observation recording

SomebodyWantedButSoThen

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is sequence? What happens in the beginning, middle and end of a story? What is a main idea?

Part 2 — Story Map (analyzing)

Choose a book you read this week. Draw a 3-part story map: Beginning (characters, setting), Middle (problem), End (solution).

✏️ My story map

Part 3 — My Own Main Idea (writing)

Choose a topic you know a lot about. Write one main-idea sentence and 3 detail sentences that fit under its umbrella.

🏠Homework

  1. Photo Story. Take (or find) 4 photos of something your family did. Mix them up and have a family member put them in order. Then retell the event.
  2. Main Idea at Dinner. After a family member tells about their day, say the main idea in one sentence: "So your day was mostly about ___."

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Could a story have two main ideas? Or no main idea at all?
  2. Why do you think beavers learned to build dams? Who taught the very first beaver?
  3. If you could change the order of events in your favourite story, what would happen?
Lesson 7 of 11

Reading Between the Lines: Inferring & Connecting

Authors don't tell you everything! Use clues plus what you know to infer — and connect stories to your life, other texts and the world.

C3.2C2.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

“Jamal stomped into the house, slammed the door, and threw his backpack on the floor.” The author never said how Jamal felt. So how do you KNOW? Where did that knowledge come from?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C3.2 make an inference using clues from the text and what I already know (clues + my brain = inference)
  • C3.2 figure out how a character feels or why they did something, even when the author doesn't say it
  • C2.5 make text-to-self connections (“This reminds me of when I…”)
  • C2.5 make text-to-text and text-to-world connections

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C3.2 asks children to make simple inferences, using stated and implied information and ideas. C2.5 asks them to identify connections between texts and their own lives, other texts, and the world. Inference is where true comprehension lives.

The formula

Clues in the text + What I know = Inference

Three kinds of connections

  • Text-to-self: "This reminds me of my life."
  • Text-to-text: "This reminds me of another book/show."
  • Text-to-world: "This reminds me of something happening in the world."

How to teach it

  1. Hook: act out Jamal's entrance. Ask how he feels and how they know.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Play "Mystery Bag" inference games (Classwork).
  4. Read This Is Not My Hat by Jon Klassen — a masterclass in inference.
💬 You can say

"The author left clues like breadcrumbs. You follow them and figure out what they didn't say."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Connections can drift off-topic ("This reminds me that I have a dog… and my dog is called…"). Ask: "How does that connection help you understand the story?" A good connection explains a character's feelings or actions.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child infers feelings/motives with a reason ("He's scared because his hands are shaking and I shake when I'm scared") and makes connections that deepen understanding.

💡 Teaching tip

Inference happens constantly in daily life — "Why do you think the neighbour's car is covered in snow?" (They didn't go anywhere today.)

📚The Lesson

Authors don't tell you everything! Sometimes they leave clues and trust YOU to figure out the rest. When you use clues and your own knowledge to figure out something the author didn't say, you are making an inference.

🔍 Clues in the text+🧠 What I know=💡 Inference

Try it!

"Jamal stomped into the house, slammed the door, and threw his backpack on the floor." - Clues: stomped, slammed, threw - What I know: People do those things when they're upset. - Inference: Jamal is angry or upset!

"Lila's eyes filled with tears as she hugged her grandma at the airport." - Clues? What do you know? Inference? Is Lila happy or sad? Could she be both?

📖 The Empty Bowl

When Leo woke up, the sun was shining.

He ran to the kitchen. Max's food bowl was empty, and the back door was open.

There were muddy paw prints across the clean floor.

Mom was holding the leash and looking out the window. "Max!" she called.

Leo pulled on his boots.

What happened? Who is Max? Why did Leo pull on his boots? The author never told you — but you know!

Making connections 🔗

Your brain understands new stories by connecting them to things you know. - 🙋 Text-to-self: "Leo's dog ran away. My cat got out once and I was so worried!" - 📚 Text-to-text: "This reminds me of a book where a dog got lost too." - 🌍 Text-to-world: "Lots of pets go missing, so people put tags on their collars." A good connection helps you understand the story better — like knowing how worried Leo must feel!

🤯 Did You Know?

Dogs have up to 300 million smell sensors in their noses; people have about 6 million. A lost dog can sometimes follow its own scent trail home from surprisingly far away!

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

Infer how the character feels: "Ava's cheeks turned red and she hid behind her mom when everyone sang Happy Birthday."

⭐⭐ Stretch

Infer the season and place: "Kai zipped up his parka, pulled on his mitts, and grabbed his sled."

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Can two people make different inferences from the same clues? Can they both be reasonable? Try it with Lila at the airport.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Practise making inferences from clues and making meaningful connections.

Materials

  • a "mystery bag" filled with 4–5 objects belonging to a pretend person (e.g., swim goggles, sunscreen, a towel, a map)
  • a picture book (ideally This Is Not My Hat or another with hidden feelings)

Steps

  1. Who Owns This Bag? Pull out one object at a time. After each, infer: Who owns it? Where are they going? Change your inference as new clues appear.
  2. Feelings Detective: In a picture book, find 3 moments where a character's feelings are shown but not told. Infer the feeling and point to the clue.
  3. Connection Chain: After reading, make one text-to-self, one text-to-text, and one text-to-world connection. Explain how each helps you understand.

ClueWhat I knowMy inference
Connection typeMy connectionHow it helped me understand

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is an inference? What's the "inference formula"? What are the 3 kinds of connections?

Part 2 — The Empty Bowl (inferring)

Answer with evidence: What happened to Max? How does Leo feel? What will happen next? Use "I think… because the text says…"

Part 3 — Show, Don't Tell (writing)

Write 3 sentences about a character who is excited, but DON'T use the word "excited." Show it with clues! Ask your family to infer the feeling.

🏠Homework

  1. Inference at Home. Look for inference clues at home: muddy boots at the door, an empty cookie jar, a wet umbrella. What happened? Make 3 inferences.
  2. Movie Feelings. While watching a show, pause and infer how a character feels based on their face, body and actions.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why don't authors just tell us everything? Would stories be better or worse if they did?
  2. Do animals make inferences? How does your pet know you're about to go for a walk?
  3. Could a computer ever make inferences as well as a person?
Lesson 8 of 11

Word Music: Rhyme, Alliteration & Onomatopoeia

Hear the music in writing: rhyme, alliteration, onomatopoeia, repeated patterns, and word choice that gives a text its voice.

C3.1C1.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Why can you remember the words to songs and nursery rhymes from when you were tiny — but not what you had for lunch last Tuesday? What's the secret power hiding in rhythm and rhyme?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C3.1 identify rhyme, alliteration and onomatopoeia in poems and stories
  • C3.1 explain how these devices make a text fun, memorable or exciting
  • C1.5 identify simple elements of style: voice, word choice, word patterns (repetition) and sentence structure
  • C1.5 describe how an author's style helps communicate meaning

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C3.1 asks children to identify simple literary devices, including rhyme, alliteration, and onomatopoeia, and describe how they help communicate meaning. C1.5 asks them to identify elements of style — voice, word choice, word patterns, and sentence structure. This is where children start to see that writers make deliberate choices.

Definitions

  • Rhyme: words that end with the same sound (cat/hat, light/night).
  • Alliteration: several words starting with the same sound (Silly Sally sang songs).
  • Onomatopoeia: words that sound like what they mean (buzz, crash, sizzle, splash).
  • Repetition/pattern: repeated words or lines ("Brown Bear, Brown Bear, what do you see?").
  • Voice: the personality you can "hear" in the writing.

Great books

Some Smug Slug (Pamela Duncan Edwards), Click, Clack, Moo (Doreen Cronin), Chicka Chicka Boom Boom, any Dr. Seuss, Mr. Brown Can Moo! Can You?, Brown Bear, Brown Bear (Bill Martin Jr.).

💬 You can say

"Writers are like musicians. They choose words for how they SOUND, not just what they mean."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children may think any similar-looking words rhyme (e.g., "cat/can"). Rhyme is about the END sound. Also, alliteration is about sounds, not letters: "cute kitten" is alliteration (/k/), "circus cat" is not (/s/ vs /k/).

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child finds examples of all three devices in a new poem and explains why an author used one ("The crash makes it feel loud and exciting").

💡 Teaching tip

Poetry is best read aloud — and performed! Keep a family poetry book where everyone copies favourite poems.

📚The Lesson

Writers are like musicians. They choose words for how they sound, not just what they mean. These word-music tricks are called literary devices.

🎵 Rhyme

Rhyme is when words end with the same sound: cat, hat, flat · night, light, bright · moose, goose, loose. Rhymes make poems bouncy and easy to remember.

🐍 Alliteration

Alliteration is when several words close together start with the same sound: "Seven slippery snakes slid silently south." · "Big brown bears bounce balls." It's fun to say — like a tongue twister!

💥 Onomatopoeia

Onomatopoeia (on-oh-mat-oh-PEE-ah) is a word that sounds like the noise it names: buzz, crash, splash, sizzle, hiss, pop, boom, crunch, moo, tick-tock, drip. It helps you hear the story!

🔁 Repetition and patterns

Many books repeat words or lines: "Brown Bear, Brown Bear, what do you see?" Repeating creates a pattern that helps you predict and join in!

🎤 Voice and style

Every writer has a voice — a personality you can hear in their writing. Some are silly, some are gentle, some are dramatic. Voice comes from word choice and sentence length: short, punchy sentences feel fast and exciting. Long, flowing sentences feel calm and dreamy. - "Run! Hide! It's coming!" (fast and scary) - "The soft snow fell slowly, covering the sleepy town in a white blanket." (calm and peaceful)

📖 Storm Song

Drip, drop, the raindrops fall,

Plip, plop, on the garden wall.

Whoosh! goes the wind, wild and wide,

Boom! goes the thunder — run inside!

Crash! Flash! The lightning bright,

Then hush… the storm says goodnight.

Can you find rhyme? Alliteration? Onomatopoeia?

🤯 Did You Know?

Onomatopoeia is different in every language! In English, a dog says "woof." In Japanese, it's "wan wan." In Spanish, "guau guau." In Korean, "meong meong." A rooster says "cock-a-doodle-doo" in English, but "cocorico" in French and "kikeriki" in German!

🤯 Did You Know?

Poet Amanda Gorman, who read a poem at a U.S. presidential inauguration at age 22, had trouble saying the "r" sound as a child. She practised by singing songs full of r's — like "Aaron Burr, Sir" from the musical Hamilton! Word music helped her find her voice.

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

Sort these: buzz, cat/hat, silly snakes slither, splash, night/light, big bouncy balloons.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why do you think so many picture books for little kids rhyme? What does rhyme do for a listener's brain?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If a cat said "meow" in English and "nyan" in Japanese, what does a cat REALLY say? Why would different languages hear the same sound differently?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Find, sort and create literary devices, and perform a poem.

Materials

  • 3–4 poems or rhyming picture books, 3 colours of highlighter/crayon, kitchen objects that make noise (pot, spoon, crinkly bag, whisk)

Steps

  1. Device Detectives: Read Storm Song and another poem. Colour-code: rhyme = blue, alliteration = green, onomatopoeia = orange.
  2. Kitchen Sound Lab: Make sounds with kitchen objects. Invent an onomatopoeia word for each (a whisk might say "swish-swish")!
  3. Alliteration Name Game: Make an alliteration sentence for each family member ("Dad dances during dinner").
  4. Poetry Performance: Perform Storm Song with sound effects!

Observation recording

ObjectThe sound it madeMy onomatopoeia word
Rhymes I foundAlliteration I foundOnomatopoeia I found

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Define rhyme, alliteration and onomatopoeia and give 2 examples of each.

Part 2 — Style Detective (analyzing)

Compare two sentences: "The dog ran." and "Zoom! The dizzy dog dashed down the driveway!" Which devices did the second use? How does it change the feeling?

Part 3 — My Sound Poem (creating)

Write a 4–6 line poem about weather, animals or food. Use at least 2 rhymes, 1 alliteration and 3 onomatopoeia words. Illustrate it and perform it!

🏠Homework

  1. Sound Walk. Go for a walk and collect 10 sounds. Write an onomatopoeia word for each.
  2. Family Poetry Night. Everyone reads or recites a favourite poem or nursery rhyme. Vote for the best performance!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why do human brains love rhythm and rhyme so much? Do babies like rhymes before they understand words?
  2. Could you write a poem that doesn't rhyme and still sounds like music?
  3. What would the sound of silence be as onomatopoeia?
Lesson 9 of 11

Who's Telling the Story? Point of View & Perspective

Discover who is telling the story, imagine the story told by someone else, and notice how a text's perspective can influence you.

C1.6C3.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

In “The Three Little Pigs,” the wolf is the bad guy. But what if the WOLF told the story? Could the exact same events make you feel sorry for him? How is that possible?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C1.6 identify the narrator's point of view: a character telling (I, me) or an outside narrator (he, she, they)
  • C1.6 retell a story from another character's point of view
  • C3.5 identify the perspective in a text — both what's said directly (explicit) and what's hinted (implicit)
  • C3.5 describe how a text's perspective could make readers feel or think a certain way

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C1.6 asks children to identify the narrator's point of view and suggest an alternative point of view. C3.5 asks them to identify explicit and implicit perspectives and describe how these perspectives could influence an audience. This is the start of critical literacy: every story is told by someone, from somewhere.

Key books

  • The True Story of the Three Little Pigs by Jon Scieszka (told by the wolf!)
  • They All Saw a Cat by Brendan Wenzel (one cat, seen by many animals)
  • Voices in the Park by Anthony Browne
  • Duck! Rabbit! by Amy Krouse Rosenthal

Key vocabulary

  • Narrator: the voice telling the story
  • First person: narrator is a character — uses I, me, we
  • Third person: narrator is outside the story — uses he, she, they
  • Perspective: how someone sees or feels about something
💬 You can say

"Every story is told by someone. Let's ask: Who is telling it? Whose side do they want us on? Who DON'T we hear from?"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children think the narrator's view is simply "the truth." Gently question: "Would the other character agree?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can identify first vs. third person in a new text and retell a familiar story convincingly from another character's perspective.

💡 Teaching tip

Retell family events from different family members' perspectives — even the dog's!

📚The Lesson

Every story has a narrator — the voice telling the story. Asking "Who is telling this story?" is one of the smartest questions a reader can ask!

First person: "I" am telling it

When a character in the story is telling it, they use words like I, me, my, we. This is called first-person point of view. "I opened the door and I saw a giant cake. My mouth dropped open!"

Third person: someone outside is telling it

When the narrator is NOT in the story, they use words like he, she, they, it, and characters' names. This is called third-person point of view. "Maya opened the door. She saw a giant cake. Her mouth dropped open!"

Same story, different teller 🔄

A story can change completely depending on who tells it!

📖 The Big Game (told by Omar)

I was the goalie. The ball came flying at me and I jumped as high as I could.

I missed it. The other team scored. Everyone groaned.

I felt terrible. I wanted to hide under the bench.

📖 The Big Game (told by Omar's coach)

Omar made a huge jump for the ball. It was a really tough shot — nobody could have stopped it.

I was so proud of how hard he tried. After the game, I told him, "That was the bravest jump I've seen all season!"

Same moment. Two different points of view. How does the second one change how you feel about Omar?

Perspective: whose side?

A perspective is how someone sees or feels about something. Sometimes a text says its perspective clearly (explicit): "Recess is the BEST part of school!" Sometimes it's hidden (implicit) in the words and pictures the author chooses — like showing the wolf with a scary face and the pigs with sweet smiles.

Perspectives can influence us — they can make us feel sorry for someone, angry at someone, or want to buy something. A smart reader asks: Whose voice is missing? What would they say?

🤯 Did You Know?

In the picture book They All Saw a Cat, a cat walks through the world and is seen by a child, a dog, a fox, a fish, a bee, a bird, a flea and a bat. Each animal "sees" the cat totally differently — the bee sees it in dots, the bat "sees" it with sound! Scientists say this is really how different animals experience the world.

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

First or third person? (a) "I love my new puppy." (b) "Leo loves his new puppy." (c) "We went to the beach."

⭐⭐ Stretch

Retell Goldilocks in 3 sentences from Baby Bear's point of view. Use "I."

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Is there any story that could be told from only ONE point of view? Think about a story where someone's voice is missing. Why might an author leave a voice out?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Identify points of view and retell a story from a new perspective.

Materials

  • a familiar fairy tale book, The True Story of the Three Little Pigs (if available), paper bag puppets or stuffed animals

Steps

  1. Pronoun Hunt: Read 2 pages from 2 different books. Hunt for I/me/we or he/she/they. Decide: first or third person?
  2. Hot Seat: Pretend to be a character (e.g., the wolf). The grown-up interviews you: "Why did you blow down the house?" Answer from the wolf's perspective!
  3. Puppet Retell: Use puppets to retell a fairy tale from the villain's point of view.
  4. Missing Voice: Choose a story. Whose voice is missing? Give that character one sentence.

Observation recording

BookWho tells it?First or third person?Clue words

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a narrator? What is the difference between first-person and third-person point of view? What is perspective?

Part 2 — Compare Perspectives (analyzing)

Reread both versions of The Big Game. How did Omar feel? How did the coach feel? Which version made you feel better about Omar? Why?

Part 3 — The Other Side (creating)

Rewrite a fairy tale from a different character's point of view. Use first person (I, me). Write 5–6 sentences and illustrate the most important part.

🏠Homework

  1. Family Perspectives. Ask 2 family members to describe the same event (a trip, a holiday dinner). How were their stories different? Why?
  2. Pet's Point of View. Write or tell about one day in your house from your pet's (or a houseplant's!) point of view.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Is there ever a story that is told from no one's point of view — just the plain truth?
  2. If your toys could tell stories about you, what would they say?
  3. How do we know which perspective to believe when two people disagree?
Lesson 10 of 11

Stories That Carry Culture

Explore how texts carry culture through symbols, values and traditions — including texts by First Nations, Métis and Inuit creators, and how they connect past and present.

C1.7C3.4C3.7C2.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

A Métis sash, a Haudenosaunee wampum belt, a Christmas tree, a Diwali lamp, and a Chinese red envelope — none of these are words, but each one tells a story. How can an object hold a story inside it?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C3.4 identify cultural elements in texts — symbols, values, foods, clothing, celebrations, languages — and explain how they add meaning
  • C1.7 read, listen to and view texts by First Nations, Métis and Inuit creators and talk about what they show about their cultures, communities and lives
  • C3.7 identify how texts by Indigenous creators share history, cultural experiences and events, and connect to life today
  • C2.5 connect cultural elements in texts to my own family's traditions

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C3.4 asks children to identify cultural elements represented in various texts, including symbols and values. C1.7 asks them to read, listen to, and view texts by diverse First Nations, Métis, and Inuit creators. C3.7 asks them to identify how texts by First Nations, Métis, and Inuit creators communicate about historical periods, cultural experiences, and events, and how they relate to current lived experiences. This lesson needs 2–3 real books by Indigenous creators — plan library holds ahead of time.

Recommended texts (choose at least two)

  • Fiddle Dancer — Anne Patton & Wilfred Burton (Métis): the sash, fiddle and jigging
  • Sweetest Kulu — Celina Kalluk (Inuk): Arctic animals give gifts to a newborn
  • Nibi's Water Song — Sunshine Tenasco (Anishinaabe): water protection, today
  • Fry Bread — Kevin Noble Maillard (Seminole): food, family and history
  • We Are Grateful: Otsaliheliga — Traci Sorell (Cherokee): seasons of gratitude
  • When We Were Alone — David A. Robertson (Cree): a grandmother gently explains residential schools (preview first; many Grade 1–2 classes use it)
  • A short online video of an Elder or storyteller from a First Nation near you

How to teach it

  1. Hook: gather a few meaningful objects from your own family's culture and share their stories.
  2. Read the lesson together.
  3. Read an Indigenous-authored book; use the "Look, Think, Connect" frame in Classwork.
💬 You can say

"When we read books by First Nations, Métis and Inuit authors, we're learning from people telling their own stories — that's the most respectful way to learn."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Avoid treating Indigenous cultures as costumes or crafts (no "headdress" crafts, etc.). Use the specific nation's name. Keep the present tense: these cultures are living today.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child can name a symbol from a text and explain what it means to that culture, name the author's Nation, and make a respectful connection to their own family's traditions.

💡 Teaching tip

Many public libraries in Ontario have "Indigenous Voices" or "First Nations, Métis & Inuit" collections — ask a librarian.

📚The Lesson

Culture is the way a group of people lives: their language, food, music, clothing, celebrations, beliefs and stories. Texts often carry culture inside them, like a treasure chest!

Cultural elements in texts

When you read, look for: - 🍞 Food — bannock, dumplings, jollof rice, pierogi - 👗 Clothing — a Métis sash, a sari, a kimono, a kufi - 🎉 Celebrations — Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year, Christmas, a powwow - 🗣️ Language — words from another language in the text - 🔣 Symbols — objects or pictures that stand for bigger ideas - 💛 Values — what the culture thinks is important (family, sharing, respect, gratitude)

Symbols: objects that hold stories

A symbol is something that stands for a bigger idea. - The Métis sash (ceinture fléchée) is a colourful woven belt. Long ago it was used as a rope, a towel, even a first-aid kit! Today, it's a symbol of Métis pride. Its colours have meanings: red is often said to stand for the blood of Métis ancestors, blue for depth of spirit, green for growth, white for connection to the earth, and yellow for prosperity (the colours can differ by region and family). - The Haudenosaunee Hiawatha Belt is a wampum belt made of purple and white shell beads. It shows five nations joined together in peace — like a treaty you can hold in your hands. - The inukshuk (inuksuk) is a figure made of stacked stones by Inuit people. Inuksuit can show travellers the way, mark a good fishing or hunting place, or say "someone was here." The word means something like "in the likeness of a person."

Stories that connect past and present

Books by First Nations, Métis and Inuit creators often share history — sometimes hard history — and show how it connects to life today. In Nibi's Water Song, a girl today searches for clean water, connecting to the long tradition of Anishinaabe women caring for the water. In Fry Bread, bread connects family members across many generations.

📖 My Kokum's Bannock

Every Sunday, my Kokum (that's "grandma" in Cree) makes bannock.

She mixes flour, baking powder, and water in her big blue bowl.

"My kokum taught me this," she says, "and her kokum taught her."

While it bakes, she tells me stories about when she was little, picking berries by the lake.

We eat the bannock warm, with butter and saskatoon berry jam.

It tastes like sharing. It tastes like family.

What cultural elements can you find? What values does this text show?

🤯 Did You Know?

The inuksuk became famous around the world when an inuksuk design, named Ilanaaq, was chosen as the emblem of the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics. Ilanaaq means "friend" in Inuktitut.

🤯 Did You Know?

The Métis Red River jig is a dance with super-fast footwork done to fiddle music. Some jigs have "changes" — the music shifts and dancers must switch steps without missing a beat!

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

Find 3 cultural elements in My Kokum's Bannock. What values does it show?

⭐⭐ Stretch

The text says the bannock "tastes like sharing. It tastes like family." Can food really taste like sharing? What does the author mean?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think it matters WHO tells a culture's stories? What might go wrong if someone from outside a culture told its stories without asking?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Explore cultural elements and symbols in texts by Indigenous creators and connect them to your own family's culture.

Materials

  • 1–2 books by First Nations, Métis or Inuit creators, paper, crayons
  • 1–3 meaningful objects from your own family's culture

Steps

  1. Author Check: Before reading, find the author's name and their Nation or community (often on the back flap).
  2. Look, Think, Connect: While reading, stop 3 times. Look at a cultural element. Think: What does it mean? Connect: Does my family have something similar?
  3. Symbol Share: Show your family's objects. Tell the story behind each one. What value does it show?
  4. Symbol Drawing: Draw a symbol from the book and one from your family. Write what each stands for.

Observation recording

Cultural element in the bookWhat it meansMy family's connection

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is culture? What is a symbol? Name 2 symbols from First Nations, Métis or Inuit cultures and what they mean.

Part 2 — Book Response (responding)

After reading a book by an Indigenous creator, write: The author is ___ from the ___ Nation. The book is about ___. A cultural element I noticed was ___. It connects to today because ___.

Part 3 — My Family's Story Object (creating)

Choose one object that carries a story in your family. Draw it and write 3–4 sentences: What is it? Where did it come from? What does it mean to your family?

🏠Homework

  1. Family Recipe. Cook a family recipe with a grown-up. Ask: Who taught you this? Where did it come from? Write or record the story.
  2. Symbols Around Us. Find 3 cultural symbols in your community (at a place of worship, a cultural centre, a flag, a mural). Draw one.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If your family had a symbol, like a sash or a belt, what would it look like and what would each colour mean?
  2. Why do families pass recipes and stories down instead of just writing them in a book?
  3. What stories will your grandchildren tell about you?
Lesson 11 of 11

My Thinking, My Feelings: Responding to Texts

Share your thoughts and feelings about books — including big ideas like fairness, inclusion and accessibility — and reflect on the thinking skills that help you understand.

C3.6C3.8C2.7C1.1
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Two kids read the same book. One loved it; the other thought it was boring. Can they both be right? Is there such a thing as a “correct” feeling about a book?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • C3.6 express my thoughts and feelings about ideas in a text, including ideas about diversity, inclusion and accessibility
  • C3.6 give reasons for my opinion about a text (“I liked… because…”)
  • C3.8 identify thinking skills that helped me understand a text (predicting, visualizing, inferring, connecting)
  • C2.7 choose the reading strategies that work best for me

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

C3.6 asks children to express personal thoughts and feelings about ideas presented in texts, such as ideas about diversity, inclusion, and accessibility. C3.8 and C2.7 ask them to identify thinking skills and strategies that helped them understand. This lesson is a capstone for Strand C — revisit it often with new books.

Key ideas

  • Diversity: people are different in many ways — that's a strength.
  • Inclusion: making sure everyone gets to join in and belong.
  • Accessibility: making places, things and activities usable by everyone, including people with disabilities (ramps, Braille, captions, sign language).

Great books for this lesson

Last Stop on Market Street (Matt de la Peña), All Are Welcome (Alexandra Penfold), Just Ask! (Sonia Sotomayor), We're All Wonders (R.J. Palacio), The Day You Begin (Jacqueline Woodson), Hair Love (Matthew A. Cherry).

💬 You can say

"There's no wrong feeling about a book — but good readers explain WHY they feel that way, using the text."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children may say "I liked it" and stop. Push for "because" and evidence. Also, for accessibility, children may say things like "She can't walk, that's sad" — guide toward "What does she need so she can join in? Who could help make that happen?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child gives an opinion with 2 reasons from the text, and names at least 2 reading strategies they used and how each one helped.

💡 Teaching tip

Start a "Book Talk" ritual: after each read-aloud, each person gives a thumbs up/sideways/down and one reason.

📚The Lesson

After you read, your brain isn't done! Great readers respond — they think about how the text made them feel, what they think about its ideas, and what they learned. There's no single "right" feeling about a book. But good readers always explain why.

Say it with reasons

- "I loved this book because the ending surprised me." - "I felt sad when the girl was left out because I know how that feels." - "I didn't agree with the character because she wasn't fair to her friend." Use evidence — point to the part of the book that made you feel that way!

Big ideas in books 🌈

Many books help us think about how to treat each other: - Diversity means people are different in many ways: how they look, where they come from, what languages they speak, what they believe, how their bodies and brains work. Differences make the world richer! - Inclusion means making sure everyone can join in and belong. - Accessibility means making things usable by everyone, including people with disabilities: ramps and elevators, Braille, sign language, captions on videos, large print.

📖 The Reading Garden

Mr. Tran's class wanted a reading garden at school.

"We need benches," said Priya. "And shade," said Jonah.

Sofia uses a wheelchair. "The path is bumpy gravel," she said. "I can't get to the benches."

The class thought hard. They asked the principal for a smooth, wide path.

On opening day, everyone rolled, walked and skipped to the garden.

Sofia read her book under the maple tree. "Now it's a garden for everyone," she said.

How did the class include Sofia? What would have happened if they hadn't asked her?

Thinking about my thinking 🧠

Good readers also think about how they understood. Which strategies helped you? - 🔮 Predicting · 🎬 Visualizing · 🔗 Connecting · 🕵️ Inferring · ❓ Asking questions · 🔁 Rereading · 🧠 Using what I know Thinking about your own thinking has a big name: metacognition!

🤯 Did You Know?

Louis Braille went blind as a young child. At just 15 years old, he invented a reading system of raised dots that people read with their fingertips. Braille is still used all over the world today — you can find it on elevator buttons and many signs!

🤯 Did You Know?

The curb cut — the little ramp where a sidewalk meets the street — was designed for wheelchair users. But it helps everyone: people with strollers, bikes, suitcases and wagons. Designers call this the "curb-cut effect": when you include some people, you often help everyone!

🧩Think Like a Reading Detective

⭐ Warm-up

How did The Reading Garden make you feel? Give one reason from the text.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Look around your home or neighbourhood. Find one place that would be hard for someone using a wheelchair, or someone who can't see or hear. How could it be made more accessible?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Can you love a book but disagree with what a character did? Can you dislike a book but still learn something important from it? Explain with an example.

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Respond to a text with feelings and reasons, and reflect on the strategies you used.

Materials

  • a picture book about inclusion or accessibility (see Parent Guide), strategy cards (make 7 small cards with the strategy icons from the lesson)

Steps

  1. Read together. Before reading, pick 2 strategy cards you plan to use.
  2. Feeling Stops: At 3 moments, show a feeling face (😊 😢 😠 😮) and say why.
  3. Accessibility Audit: Walk through your home. Where could someone with a disability need help? Draw one improvement.
  4. Strategy Reflection: Sort your strategy cards: "Helped a lot," "Helped a little," "Didn't use."

Observation recording

Moment in the bookMy feelingWhy (evidence)
StrategyHow it helped me

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What do diversity, inclusion and accessibility mean? What is metacognition?

Part 2 — Book Review (responding)

Write a book review of a book you read this month: Title and author · What it's about (2 sentences) · How it made me feel and why · Stars out of 5 · Who would like it?

Part 3 — My Reading Toolbox (reflecting)

Draw a toolbox. Inside, draw your 3 favourite reading strategies. For each, write one sentence about when it helped you this year.

✏️ My reading toolbox

🏠Homework

  1. Braille Discovery. Find Braille in your community (elevators, public washrooms, bank machines). Feel it with your fingertips. How hard is it to tell the dots apart?
  2. Family Book Club. Choose a book to read together. Each person shares a feeling and a reason at dinner.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Is there a book that EVERYONE in the world would love? What would it have to be like?
  2. Why do some books make us cry even though we know the story isn't real?
  3. What is one thing that would make your community a better place for everyone?
Word Wall

Key Vocabulary

Read each card aloud together. Cover the definition and ask: “What does this word mean? Use it in your own sentence.” Revisit the cards at the start of every session in this strand.

text
Anything that communicates a message: a book, poem, sign, video, or comic.
“A cereal box is a kind of text.”
literary text
A text from someone's imagination, like a story or poem.
“Fairy tales are literary texts.”
informational text
A text that gives true facts.
“I read an informational text about beavers.”
genre
A kind or category of text, like fable, poem or fact book.
“My favourite genre is adventure.”
prior knowledge
What you already know before you read.
“My prior knowledge about snow helped me understand the story.”
prediction
A smart guess about what will happen, based on clues.
“My prediction was that the hamster made the noise.”
evidence
Clues or facts that prove your thinking.
“I used evidence from the text to support my answer.”
visualize
To make pictures in your mind while reading.
“I visualized the campfire sparks.”
text features
Parts of a text that help readers, like titles, labels, captions, diagrams.
“The labels were my favourite text feature.”
illustrator
The person who makes the pictures in a book.
“The illustrator showed the fox sneaking behind Rosie.”
sequence
The order in which things happen.
“I retold the story in the right sequence.”
main idea
What a text is mostly about.
“The main idea is that beavers are amazing builders.”
inference
Figuring out something the author didn't say, using clues plus what you know.
“My inference was that Jamal was angry.”
connection
A link between a text and your life, another text, or the world.
“I made a connection between the story and my trip to the lake.”
rhyme
Words that end with the same sound.
““Moon” and “spoon” rhyme.”
alliteration
Words close together that start with the same sound.
““Silly snakes slither” is alliteration.”
onomatopoeia
A word that sounds like the noise it names.
““Sizzle” is onomatopoeia.”
narrator
The voice telling the story.
“The wolf was the narrator of that book.”
point of view
Who is telling the story: first person (I) or third person (he, she, they).
“The story was told in first-person point of view.”
symbol
Something that stands for a bigger idea.
“The Métis sash is a symbol of pride.”
inclusion
Making sure everyone can join in and belong.
“The class practised inclusion by asking Sofia what she needed.”
accessibility
Making things usable by everyone, including people with disabilities.
“The ramp improved accessibility at the library.”

Finding ideas, gathering facts, planning, printing, drafting true stories, how-to texts and opinions, editing like a pro, then publishing and presenting to a real audience.
