Lessons
Lesson 1 of 9

Why Do Writers Write? Topic, Purpose & Audience

Every piece of writing starts with three questions: What am I writing about? Why? Who will read it?

D1.1D2.3
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

A note to your best friend, a sign for your bedroom door, and a letter to the Prime Minister are all writing. Would you write them the same way? What changes — and why?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D1.1 identify the topic (what it's about) of a text I plan to write
  • D1.1 identify the purpose: to tell a story, to teach, to explain how, to persuade, to share feelings
  • D1.1 identify the audience: who will read it, and how that changes my writing
  • D2.3 understand that my own thoughts and feelings make my writing special

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D1.1 asks children to identify the topic, purpose, and audience for various simple texts they plan to create. These three questions ("the Writer's Compass") are the start of every piece of writing for the rest of the year — and for life.

The Writer's Compass 🧭

  • Topic: What am I writing about?
  • Purpose: Why am I writing? (to entertain, to inform/teach, to explain how, to persuade, to express feelings)
  • Audience: Who will read it?

How to teach it

  1. Hook: show 3 real texts (a sticky-note reminder, a greeting card, a formal letter). Discuss who each was for and why.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Classwork: write three very short texts about the SAME topic for three audiences.
  4. Put a "Writer's Compass" poster above your writing space.
💬 You can say

"Before you write, ask the Compass questions. The answers tell you what words to choose and how to write."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Grade 1 writers often think their audience is "the teacher." Give them REAL audiences: grandparents, a neighbour, the mail carrier, a younger cousin, the local library. Real audiences create real motivation.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

before writing, your child can state the topic, purpose and audience without prompting, and their writing changes appropriately for different audiences.

💡 Teaching tip

This year, try to send at least one piece of writing a month to a real person outside your home.

📚The Lesson

Writers write for lots of reasons: to tell stories, to share facts, to say thank you, to make people laugh, to change people's minds. Every piece of writing starts with three big questions. Let's call them the Writer's Compass. 🧭

1. TOPIC — What am I writing about?

The topic is the subject: my dog, volcanoes, my trip to the farm, why we need a class pet.

2. PURPOSE — Why am I writing?

  • 😂 To entertain — a funny story, a poem
  • 🧑‍🏫 To inform — teach facts about a topic
  • 🛠️ To explain how — give steps, like a recipe
  • 🙏 To persuade — convince someone of your opinion
  • 💌 To express feelings — a thank-you card, a diary

3. AUDIENCE — Who will read it?

Your audience changes how you write! - For a little cousin, use simple words and big pictures. - For your best friend, you can be silly and use jokes. - For the mayor, use your best, most polite writing.

Same topic, three audiences

Topic: I lost my tooth! - To Grandma (feelings): "Dear Grandma, I lost my first tooth today! I was brave. I miss you. Love, Sami" - To the Tooth Fairy (persuade): "Dear Tooth Fairy, Please give me an extra coin. I brushed every night and flossed too!" - For a class poster (inform): "Kids lose their baby teeth between ages 5 and 12. New adult teeth grow in their place."

Your voice makes it special

Only YOU have your ideas, your memories, and your way of saying things. That's your voice. Readers can "hear" you in your writing when you share your real thoughts and feelings.

🤯 Did You Know?

Children have written real books! Dav Pilkey made his first comics as a kid when his teacher sent him to sit in the hallway — and those comics grew into Dog Man and Captain Underpants. And in 2022, a five-year-old girl in England, Bella J. Dark, set a world record as the youngest girl ever to publish a book — a story called The Lost Cat!

🤯 Did You Know?

A long time ago, before the Internet, people wrote so many letters that the Canadian post office delivered mail twice a day in many cities!

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

What is the purpose of each? (a) A birthday card. (b) A recipe. (c) A sign that says "Save the bees!" (d) A funny comic.

⭐⭐ Stretch

You want a later bedtime. How would you write to your parents to persuade them? How would you write about it in a diary? Why are they different?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Can one piece of writing have TWO purposes at once — like being funny AND teaching facts? Think of an example. Is that harder or easier to write?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Write three short texts on one topic for three different audiences and purposes.

Materials

  • 3 pieces of paper (one card, one note, one mini-poster), markers, pencils
  • a "Writer's Compass" poster (draw a compass with TOPIC, PURPOSE, AUDIENCE)

Steps

  1. Choose one topic you love (your pet, a favourite food, snow).
  2. Text 1: a card to a grandparent to share feelings.
  3. Text 2: a mini-poster to teach a younger kid 2 facts.
  4. Text 3: a note to persuade your family to do something related to the topic.
  5. Read all three aloud. How did your words change?

Observation recording

TextPurposeAudienceHow I changed my writing

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What are the three parts of the Writer's Compass? Name 5 purposes for writing.

Part 2 — Match It (applying)

For each audience, write one sentence about "the rain": (1) a baby, (2) a scientist, (3) your best friend.

Part 3 — A Real Letter (creating)

Write a real letter to someone outside your home (a relative, neighbour, or a favourite author). Plan with the Compass first. Then mail or deliver it!

🏠Homework

  1. Text Collector. Collect 5 real texts from your mailbox or fridge (flyers, cards, bills, notes). For each, name the purpose and audience.
  2. Mail It. Send your letter. Keep watch for a reply!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Why do people still write letters and cards by hand when they could send a text message?
  2. If you could write to anyone in the world — alive or from history — who would it be, and what would you say?
  3. Can you write something with NO audience at all? Is a diary written for nobody — or for your future self?
Lesson 2 of 9

Idea Treasure Hunt: Where Do Ideas Come From?

Never say “I don't know what to write” again! Learn simple strategies to find ideas in your life, your heart, your memories and your learning.

D1.2D1.5
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Authors write hundreds of books. Where do they keep finding ideas? Is there a secret idea store — or are ideas hiding somewhere much closer, maybe even inside you right now?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D1.2 generate ideas for writing using strategies: heart map, list, sketch, talking it out, looking at photos
  • D1.2 find ideas in my own life experiences and in what I'm learning in other subjects
  • D1.5 identify which idea strategies work best for me
  • D1.2 keep a Writer's Notebook of ideas to use later

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D1.2 asks children to generate ideas about given and chosen topics, using simple strategies and drawing on various resources, including their own lived experiences and learning from other subject areas. D1.5 asks them to identify the strategies that helped them develop ideas. The #1 obstacle for young writers is "I don't know what to write" — this lesson removes it.

Idea strategies

  1. Heart Map: draw a big heart, fill it with people, places, things and memories you love.
  2. Lists: "Things that make me laugh," "Times I was brave," "Things I know a lot about."
  3. Sketch first: draw, then write about the drawing.
  4. Talk it out: tell the story out loud before writing.
  5. Photos and objects: family photos, souvenirs.
  6. Learning from other subjects: "What did I learn in science that I could teach someone?"

How to teach it

  1. Hook: share where a favourite author got an idea.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Make a Heart Map and 3 idea lists in a real notebook — the "Writer's Notebook" your child will use all year.
💬 You can say

"Your life is full of stories. Small moments are the best ones — like the time the dog stole your sandwich."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often pick huge topics ("My summer") and then write a list of events. Teach "zoom in" on ONE small moment: "the moment I jumped off the dock."

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

when asked to write, your child can independently open their Writer's Notebook and choose an idea, and can name the strategy that helped them find it.

💡 Teaching tip

Keep the Writer's Notebook out all year. Whenever something funny, scary or exciting happens, say, "That's a story! Put it in your notebook."

📚The Lesson

Ideas are everywhere — you just need to know how to find them! The best writers are idea collectors. They notice small moments and save them.

Ideas come from YOU

  • 🏠 Your life: trips, family, pets, friends, favourite places
  • ❤️ Your feelings: a time you were proud, scared, excited, or silly
  • 🧠 Your learning: facts from science, math, art or reading that you could teach
  • 🌍 The world around you: things you notice on a walk or at the store
  • 💭 Your imagination: "What if my cat could talk?"

Strategy 1: The Heart Map ❤️

Draw a giant heart. Fill it with the people, places, things and memories you love most. Every picture is a story waiting to be written!

Strategy 2: Idea Lists 📝

Make lists with titles like: - Times I was brave - Things that make me laugh - Things I know a LOT about - Places I love - "What if…?" questions

Strategy 3: Sketch it, then write it ✏️

Draw a picture of a memory. Add details. Then look at your picture and ask: What happened? What did I feel? What did people say?

Strategy 4: Talk it out 🗣️

Tell your story out loud to someone first. Talking warms up your writing brain!

Zoom in on a small moment 🔍

Don't write about "My whole summer." Zoom in like a camera to ONE moment: "The moment the big wave knocked me over at the beach." Small moments make BIG stories.

🤯 Did You Know?

Beatrix Potter first wrote The Tale of Peter Rabbit as a letter to a sick five-year-old boy named Noel, to cheer him up. Later, it became one of the best-selling books of all time!

🤯 Did You Know?

Robert Munsch, the Canadian author of Love You Forever and The Paper Bag Princess, makes up stories out loud for audiences first. He tells them again and again, changing them each time, before ever writing them down. Some of his stories were told for years before they became books!

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Name 3 small moments from this week that could be stories.

⭐⭐ Stretch

"My trip to Grandma's" is a big topic. Zoom in! Choose ONE small moment from a visit to someone special.

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Robert Munsch tells stories out loud before writing them. Beatrix Potter wrote a letter. Which idea strategy works best for YOU? Why do you think different writers need different strategies?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Create a Writer's Notebook full of ideas using three strategies.

Materials

  • a real notebook (the Writer's Notebook), crayons, markers, family photos (optional)

Steps

  1. Decorate the cover of your Writer's Notebook with things you love.
  2. Heart Map: On page 1, draw a big heart and fill it with at least 10 things you love.
  3. Idea Lists: On page 2, make 3 lists (5 items each): Times I was brave · Things I know a lot about · What if…?
  4. Photo Talk: Look at 3 family photos. Tell the story of one out loud to a grown-up.
  5. Star it: Put a ⭐ next to the 3 ideas you most want to write about.

Observation recording

StrategyNumber of ideas it gave meDid I like it? (⭐–⭐⭐⭐)

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

Name 4 strategies for finding writing ideas. What does "zoom in" mean?

Part 2 — Small Moment Story (writing)

Choose one ⭐ idea. Sketch it first. Then write 3–5 sentences about that ONE moment. Include what you saw, felt and said.

✏️ My sketch

Part 3 — My Idea Strategy (reflecting)

Which strategy helped you most? Write: "The strategy that helped me most was ___ because ___."

🏠Homework

  1. Idea Catcher. Carry a small notepad for 3 days. Every time something interesting happens, jot or draw it. Bring back at least 5 new ideas.
  2. Family Story Swap. Ask a family member to tell you a story from when they were your age. Add it to your Writer's Notebook as an idea.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Can you ever run out of ideas? Is there a limit to how many stories a person has?
  2. Do dreams count as ideas? Could you write a story from a dream?
  3. Why do small moments often make better stories than big events?
Lesson 3 of 9

Young Researchers: Gathering & Sorting Facts

Gather facts about a topic from one good source, write them as notes, and sort them into groups ready for writing.

D1.3D1.4A2.3
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Scientists who study animals spend months watching and writing notes before they write a single page about what they learned. Why not just start writing right away? What goes wrong if you skip the research?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D1.3 gather information about a topic from one source (a book, a video, or an expert)
  • D1.3 record facts as short notes or labelled drawings, in my own words
  • D1.4 sort facts into groups (like “what it looks like,” “where it lives,” “what it eats”)
  • D1.4 put my groups in an order that makes sense for an information text

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D1.3 asks children to gather information and content relevant to a topic, using a single source. D1.4 asks them to sort and sequence ideas and information, taking into account the text form. Together these create the first research report of your child's life!

How to teach it

  1. Let your child choose an animal (or another topic) they're curious about.
  2. Borrow ONE good nonfiction book at their level, or choose a short kids' documentary.
  3. Read the lesson.
  4. Over 2–3 sessions: read the source together, take notes (drawings + key words), sort notes into groups.
  5. In Lesson D5 or later, they can turn this into an "All About" book.

Note-taking for 6-year-olds

  • Key words + drawings (not copying sentences!)
  • One fact per sticky note
  • Say the fact in your own words first, then write 2–3 key words
💬 You can say

"Researchers don't copy — they read, think, then write the fact in their own words."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children want to copy whole sentences from the book. Close the book, then ask "What did you learn?" and write that. Also watch for "facts" that are opinions ("Pandas are cute").

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child produces 8+ fact notes in their own words and sorts them into 3 sensible groups with headings.

💡 Teaching tip

A "fact sort" on a big paper with 3 hula-hoop circles (or drawn circles) makes sorting visual and fun.

📚The Lesson

A researcher is someone who finds out information about a topic. Scientists, journalists, and authors all do research before they write. Now it's your turn!

Step 1: Choose a topic you're curious about 🤔

Pick something you really WANT to know more about — an animal, a place, a job, a machine.

Step 2: Find ONE good source 📚

A source is where you get your information. For your first research project, use ONE great source: - a nonfiction book from the library - a kids' science video (with your grown-up) - an expert you can interview (a vet, a farmer, a grandparent)

Step 3: Take notes — in your own words ✏️

Notes are short words and drawings that help you remember facts. Don't copy the book! Read a part, close the book, and ask yourself: "What did I learn?" Then write a few key words and draw a small picture. Example note: 🐙 "8 arms — can taste with arms!"

Step 4: Sort your facts into groups 🗂️

Put facts that go together in the same group. For an animal, you might use:

👀 What it looks like🏡 Where it lives🍽️ What it eats🤯 Amazing facts

Step 5: Put your groups in order

Decide which group comes first, next and last. Usually we start with what it looks like and end with the most amazing facts — save the best for last!

📖 Octopus Notes

🐙 has 8 arms

🐙 can change colour in less than a second

🐙 has 3 hearts!

🐙 lives in the ocean, in dens and cracks in rocks

🐙 eats crabs and clams

🐙 can squeeze through a hole the size of a coin

🐙 has blue blood

🐙 squirts ink to escape

Can you sort these notes into groups?

🤯 Did You Know?

An octopus's arms have so many nerve cells that each arm can taste and touch by itself — and can even keep reaching for food for a short time after it's been separated from the body! About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, not its head.

🤯 Did You Know?

Jane Goodall began studying chimpanzees in Tanzania in 1960. She took careful notes every day for decades. Her notes proved that chimpanzees make and use tools — something scientists thought only humans could do!

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Sort the octopus notes into 3 groups: What it looks like · Where it lives & what it eats · Amazing facts.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Which of these is a fact and which is an opinion? "Octopuses have 3 hearts." "Octopuses are creepy." "Octopuses are the coolest animal." How does a researcher use opinions?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do you think it's important to put facts in your OWN words instead of copying? What might happen if everyone just copied?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Research a topic from one source and sort your notes into groups.

Materials

  • one nonfiction book or kids' video about your topic, sticky notes, a large paper with 3–4 circles or boxes, crayons

Steps

  1. Before: Write your topic and 3 questions you wonder about.
  2. Read/watch one section at a time. Close the book. Say what you learned. Write ONE fact per sticky note with key words and a tiny drawing.
  3. Collect at least 8 notes.
  4. Sort: Make 3 or 4 groups on the big paper. Give each group a heading.
  5. Order: Number your groups 1, 2, 3, 4 in the order you'll write them.

Observation recording

Group headingFacts in this groupOrder (1, 2, 3…)

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a researcher? What is a source? Why do we take notes in our own words?

Part 2 — Fact Paragraph (writing)

Choose one of your groups. Write a heading and 3 sentences using the facts in that group.

Part 3 — Fact Poster (creating)

Make a poster about your topic with a title, a big labelled drawing, and one fact from each group.

✏️ My fact poster

🏠Homework

  1. Expert Interview. Ask someone who knows about your topic 3 questions. Add their answers to your notes.
  2. Teach It. Teach your family 5 facts you learned — without looking at your notes!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If you could research anything in the world for a whole year, what would you choose?
  2. Could an octopus be smarter than a dog? How would a scientist find out?
  3. Are there questions that no one in the world knows the answer to yet? Could YOU be the one to find out?
Lesson 4 of 9

Beautiful Printing: Letters, Spaces & Lines

Print letters and words with the right formation, size, placement on the line, and finger spaces so readers can read your wonderful ideas.

D2.2B2.2
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Scientists have discovered that kids who learn to print letters by hand learn to READ them faster than kids who only type them. Why would moving a pencil help your brain read?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D2.2 form each letter starting at the right place and moving in the right direction
  • D2.2 size letters correctly: tall letters, short letters, tail letters
  • D2.2 place letters on the line and leave finger spaces between words
  • B2.2 print uppercase and lowercase letters fluently from memory

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D2.2 asks children to print letters and words with appropriate formation patterns, size, placement, and spacing. Handwriting isn't just neatness: research (e.g., Karin James, Indiana University) found that printing letters by hand activates reading areas of the brain more than typing or tracing.

Grip and posture

  • Sit with feet flat, back straight, paper slightly tilted.
  • Tripod grip: pencil held between thumb and index finger, resting on the middle finger. Short pencils (golf pencils) naturally encourage this.

Formation groups (lowercase)

  • Magic c letters (start at 2 o'clock, go around): c, a, d, g, o, q
  • Tall stick letters: l, t, b, h, k, f
  • Down-up-and-over: n, m, r, h, b, p
  • Diagonal letters: v, w, x, y, k, z
  • Others: e, s, i, j, u

How to teach it

  1. Hook: discuss the brain research.
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Practise 2–3 letters per day for 5 minutes as part of Word Lab, saying the formation aloud.
  4. Use multi-sensory practice: sky-writing, sand trays, playdough letters.
💬 You can say

"Start at the top! Tall letters touch the sky, short letters touch the fence, tail letters dig into the ground."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Starting letters from the bottom, making circles clockwise, and floating letters above the line are common. Correct gently at the moment it happens. Don't demand perfection — aim for readable.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child prints a 2-sentence dictation where all letters are formed from the correct start point, sit on the line, and have clear finger spaces.

💡 Teaching tip

Short, daily practice (5 min) beats long weekly sessions. Stop before hands get tired.

📚The Lesson

Your ideas are amazing — and your readers want to read them! Printing clearly means forming letters so other people can read your writing easily.

Hold your pencil like a pro ✏️

Pinch the pencil with your thumb and pointer finger, and let it rest on your middle finger. This is called the tripod grip — like a camera stand with three legs. Keep your other hand flat on the paper to hold it still.

Letters live on a line 📏

Think of your paper like a house: - ☁️ The top line is the sky. - 🟰 The dotted middle line is the fence. - 🌱 The bottom line is the grass. - ⬇️ Below the grass is the ground.

  • Tall letters (b d f h k l t) touch the sky.
  • Short letters (a c e i m n o r s u v w x z) touch the fence.
  • Tail letters (g j p q y) dig into the ground.
  • ALL letters sit on the grass — no floating!

Start at the top! ⬇️

Almost every letter starts at the top. Circle letters like c, a, d, g, o start like the letter c: at "2 o'clock," go up and around to the left.

Finger spaces 👆

Put a finger space between words so they don't squish together. Squished: Ilikepizza. 😵 · Spaced: I like pizza. 😊

Capitals and lowercase

Use a capital letter only at the start of a sentence, for names, and for "I." Everywhere else, use lowercase. wHaT dO yOu tHiNk? is hard to read!

🤯 Did You Know?

Scientist Karin James scanned children's brains and found that when kids printed letters by hand, the reading areas of their brains lit up more than when they typed or traced letters. Printing helps your brain learn letters!

🤯 Did You Know?

Before printing presses, every single book was copied by hand! Monks called scribes could spend more than a year copying one book with a feather pen, called a quill.

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Sort these letters into tall, short and tail letters: b, a, g, t, o, y, h, m, p.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Why do you think we leave finger spaces? Write a sentence with no spaces and ask someone to read it. What happened?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If scribes spent a year copying one book, how many books do you think existed long ago? How did the printing press change the world?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Practise correct letter formation, sizing, line placement and spacing using multi-sensory activities.

Materials

  • lined paper (with dotted middle line), a short pencil, playdough, a tray of salt or sand, a popsicle stick (spacer)

Steps

  1. Warm-up: Squeeze playdough for 1 minute to strengthen hand muscles.
  2. Sky Writing: Write letters in the air with your whole arm, saying the directions.
  3. Salt Tray: Write your tricky letters in the salt tray with your finger.
  4. Playdough Letters: Roll "snakes" and form 5 letters.
  5. Line Practice: Print 3 letters from each group on lined paper. Circle your best one of each.
  6. Spacing Sentence: Copy "The big dog ran to the park." using a popsicle stick as a spacer.

Observation recording

LetterStart at the top? ✓Right size? ✓On the line? ✓

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is the tripod grip? Where do tall, short and tail letters go? Why do we need finger spaces?

Part 2 — Best Printing (applying)

Print the whole alphabet in lowercase and uppercase, in your very best printing. Circle the 3 letters you're proudest of. Put a star on 1 letter to practise more.

✏️ My alphabet in best printing (do this in your notebook)

Part 3 — Copy a Poem (creating)

Choose a short poem (4 lines). Copy it in your best printing. Decorate the border. Give it to someone as a gift!

🏠Homework

  1. Daily 5-Minute Printing. Each day, practise 3 letters you find tricky, 5 times each, saying the directions aloud.
  2. Real-World Writing. Write the family grocery list this week in your best printing.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Will people still write by hand in 100 years? Should they?
  2. Why do some people have neat handwriting and others messy? Can handwriting show personality?
  3. If you invented a brand-new letter shape, what would it look like and how would you write it?
Lesson 5 of 9

Personal Narratives: Telling True Stories About Me

Write a true story about a small moment in your life — with a beginning, middle and end, feelings, details, and “I” as the narrator.

D2.1D1.4D2.4D2.3
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Your life has already been full of adventures, surprises, disasters and triumphs. If a stranger read ONE true story from your life, which would you want them to read — and why that one?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D2.1 draft a personal narrative about a small moment in my life
  • D1.4 sequence my story with a beginning, middle and end using time words (first, then, finally)
  • D2.4 identify that my personal narrative is written in first person (I, me, my)
  • D2.3 show my voice by including my thoughts and feelings

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D2.1 asks children to draft short, simple texts, including personal narratives. D2.4 asks them to identify point of view, including first person, used in their texts. D1.4 covers sequencing ideas, and D2.3 covers personal voice. The personal narrative is the heart of Grade 1 writing.

The shape of a personal narrative

  1. Beginning: who, where, when ("Last summer, I was at the lake with my dad.")
  2. Middle: what happened, step by step, with feelings and details
  3. End: how it ended and how you felt or what you learned

How to teach it

  1. Choose a "small moment" from the Writer's Notebook.
  2. Plan: fold paper into 3 (beginning, middle, end). Sketch each part.
  3. Tell it out loud across your fingers (thumb = beginning, fingers = events, pinky = end).
  4. Draft: write 1–3 sentences for each part. Spend 2–3 sessions on drafting.
💬 You can say

"Tell me the story first. Now, let's write it just the way you told it."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Grade 1 writers often write "bed-to-bed" stories (woke up… ate breakfast… went to bed). Coach: "Zoom in on the most exciting part and tell me more about just that." Also, spelling can stall writing — encourage phonetic spelling of new words ("Write the sounds you hear") and correct only taught patterns later during editing.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child writes a 5–8 sentence narrative with a clear beginning, middle and end, uses time words, includes at least one feeling, and can tell you it's in first person because it uses "I."

💡 Teaching tip

A drafting session should feel like play, not a test. Save correcting for the editing lesson (D8).

📚The Lesson

A personal narrative is a true story about something that happened to you. You're the main character, and you're also the storyteller!

First person: "I" am the narrator

In a personal narrative, you tell the story using I, me, my, we. This is called first person. "I jumped into the lake. My heart was pounding!"

Beginning, middle and end

🌅 BEGINNING
Who? Where? When?→⛰️ MIDDLE
What happened? How did I feel?→🌇 END
How did it end? What did I learn?

Time words keep your story in order

First, … Then, … Next, … Suddenly, … After that, … Finally, …

Add your voice: feelings and details

Great narratives make the reader feel like they were THERE. - Feelings: "I was so nervous my knees were shaking." - Senses: "The water was icy cold and smelled like fish." - Talking: "'You can do it!' Dad shouted." - Thoughts: "I thought, 'What if I sink?'"

📖 The Day I Jumped (a mentor text)

Last summer, I stood at the end of the dock at my uncle's cottage. The lake looked dark and deep.

My cousins were already splashing in the water. "Jump, Amir! Jump!" they yelled.

My knees were shaking. I thought, "What if I sink like a rock?"

I held my nose, closed my eyes, and counted. One… two… THREE!

SPLASH! The water was freezing! I bobbed up in my life jacket, spitting and laughing.

Finally, I climbed out and did it again — five more times!

Now I know that being brave means being scared and doing it anyway.

Can you find the beginning, middle and end? The feelings? The time words? The first-person words?

🤯 Did You Know?

Christopher Paul Curtis, who grew up in Flint, Michigan, and has lived in Windsor, Ontario, won the Newbery Medal for Bud, Not Buddy. He says many of his characters and stories came from his own family's memories — and from the stories his grandfathers told.

🧠 Brain moment

Writing about your own experiences helps your brain organize memories. Scientists have found that people who write about their experiences often remember them more clearly and understand their own feelings better.

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Find 5 first-person words in The Day I Jumped.

⭐⭐ Stretch

The last sentence says, "Being brave means being scared and doing it anyway." Why do you think the author ended this way? What does it add?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

If Amir's cousin wrote about the same day, how would the story change? Would it still be a personal narrative? Why?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Plan and draft a personal narrative about one small moment.

Materials

  • your Writer's Notebook, paper folded into 3 sections, pencil, crayons

Steps

  1. Choose one small moment from your Writer's Notebook.
  2. Tell it across your fingers: thumb (beginning), 3 fingers (events), pinky (end).
  3. Sketch your 3 parts on the folded paper.
  4. Draft: Write 1–3 sentences under each sketch. Use time words. Spell words the best you can by saying the sounds.
  5. Add voice: Add one feeling and one thing someone said.
  6. Check: Did you use "I"? Circle every "I."

Observation recording

PartWhat happensA feeling or detail I added

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is a personal narrative? What point of view does it use? What goes in the beginning, middle and end?

Part 2 — My Narrative Draft (writing)

Write your full personal narrative (5–8 sentences). Use at least 3 time words, 2 feelings, and 1 thing someone said.

Part 3 — Author's Checklist (reflecting)

Check your draft: ☐ Beginning tells who, where, when · ☐ Middle has events in order · ☐ End tells how it finished · ☐ I used "I" · ☐ I shared a feeling. Which part are you proudest of?

🏠Homework

  1. Story at Dinner. Tell your narrative out loud to your family at dinner. Ask: "What part did you like best? What do you want to know more about?"
  2. Family Narrative. Ask a grown-up to tell you their own "brave moment" story. Listen for beginning, middle and end.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Is a memory exactly what happened, or does our brain change memories over time?
  2. If you wrote one true story every day for a year, what would you learn about yourself?
  3. Why do we love hearing true stories about other people's lives?
Lesson 6 of 9

How-To Writing: Procedures That Work

Write clear step-by-step instructions that a reader can actually follow — then test them!

D2.1D1.4D1.1
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

If you wrote instructions for making a peanut butter sandwich and a robot followed them EXACTLY — every word — would it work? Or would the robot end up with peanut butter on its head?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D2.1 draft a procedural text with a title, materials list and numbered steps
  • D1.4 put steps in the right order, using time words and command sentences
  • D1.1 think about my audience: what does someone who has never done this need to know?
  • D2.1 test my instructions and improve them

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D2.1 lists procedural texts as one of the three required Grade 1 forms. Procedures teach precise thinking: every step matters, and order matters. D1.4 asks for sequencing appropriate to the text form.

Features of a procedure

  • Title: "How to…"
  • Materials / You need: a list
  • Steps: numbered, in order, starting with command verbs (Get… Put… Spread…)
  • Picture for each step (optional but helpful)
  • Ending: "Enjoy!" or a tip

The famous "Exact Instructions" game

Have your child write or say instructions for making a sandwich. You follow them exactly — silly literally. ("Put the peanut butter on the bread" → place the closed jar on the bread bag.) Children LOVE this and immediately understand the need for precision.

💬 You can say

"Pretend your reader has never, ever done this before. What do they need to know?"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Missing steps are the most common problem ("Make the sandwich. Eat it."). Testing reveals the gaps. Also watch for steps that aren't commands ("I get the bread") — model command sentences ("Get two slices of bread").

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child writes a 5+ step procedure with materials; another person can follow it successfully after one round of revision.

💡 Teaching tip

Connect to B3 (command sentences are imperative!) and A9 (the fruit kebab recipe).

📚The Lesson

A procedure is a text that tells how to do something, step by step. Recipes, game rules, Lego instructions and science experiments are all procedures!

The parts of a procedure

  1. Title: tells what you'll make or do — "How to Plant a Bean Seed"
  2. Materials: a list of everything you need — "You need: a cup, soil, a bean seed, water"
  3. Steps: numbered and in order
  4. Pictures: show what each step looks like
  5. Ending: a tip or "Enjoy!"

Steps start with bossy verbs! 🫡

Each step is a command sentence (remember imperative sentences?). It starts with an action word: Get… Put… Pour… Mix… Fold… Cut… Wait… Push…

Be exact! 🎯

Your reader can't read your mind. Tell them exactly what to do. - Not exact: "Put some water in." - Exact: "Pour a small cup of water on the soil."

📖 How to Plant a Bean Seed

You need: 1 clear plastic cup · soil · 1 dry bean · water · a sunny window

1. Fill the cup with soil almost to the top.

2. Poke a hole in the soil with your finger, as deep as your first knuckle.

3. Drop the bean into the hole.

4. Cover the bean with soil and pat it gently.

5. Pour a little water on the soil until it is damp, not soggy.

6. Put the cup by a sunny window.

7. Water it a little every two days and watch for a sprout!

Tip: Use a clear cup so you can see the roots grow!

🤯 Did You Know?

A bean seed usually sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks. Inside every seed is a tiny baby plant, called an embryo, with its own packed lunch of food to help it grow until it can make food from sunlight!

🤯 Did You Know?

Julia Child, a famous cook, tested some of her recipes dozens of times before putting them in her cookbook, to make sure anyone could follow them. Testing is what makes a procedure great!

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Find the problem: "How to Brush Your Teeth: 1. Brush your teeth. 2. Put toothpaste on the toothbrush. 3. Rinse."

⭐⭐ Stretch

Write the missing step: "1. Get two slices of bread. 2. ___. 3. Put the slices together. 4. Eat!"

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why do Lego instructions use almost NO words — only pictures? When are pictures better than words for instructions? When are words better?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Write, test and revise a procedure.

Materials

  • ingredients for a simple no-cook snack (e.g., bread, jam, a butter knife) OR materials for a paper airplane, paper, pencil

Steps

  1. Exact Instructions Game: Tell a grown-up how to make a jam sandwich. They must follow your words EXACTLY (and silly-literally!). Laugh, then fix your instructions.
  2. Plan: Write the title and materials list.
  3. Draft: Write numbered steps starting with bossy verbs. Draw a picture for each.
  4. Test: A family member follows ONLY your written steps.
  5. Revise: Add any missing steps or clearer words.

Observation recording

Step that didn't workWhat went wrongHow I fixed it

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What are the 5 parts of a procedure? What kind of sentence starts each step?

Part 2 — My Procedure (writing)

Write a procedure for something you're an expert at (making a snowman, building a fort, feeding your pet, a playground game). Include a title, materials, at least 5 numbered steps with bossy verbs, and pictures.

Part 3 — Plant Experiment (applying)

Follow How to Plant a Bean Seed. Record your bean's growth every 2 days for 2 weeks.

DayWhat I seeHeight

🏠Homework

  1. Procedure Hunt. Find 3 real procedures at home (a recipe, game rules, medicine instructions — read with a grown-up). What features do they have?
  2. Teach a Grown-Up. Teach a grown-up a game or trick using only your written procedure.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Could you write instructions for something that has never been done before?
  2. How do you think the very first recipe was written?
  3. If you wrote instructions for how to be a good friend, what would the steps be?
Lesson 7 of 9

Persuasive Writing: My Opinion Matters

State your opinion clearly, back it up with strong reasons, and use your voice to convince a real audience.

D2.1D2.3D1.1
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Kids aren't allowed to vote or make laws. But kids HAVE changed rules, saved parks, and started movements — using words. How could a six-year-old possibly convince grown-ups to change their minds?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D2.1 draft a persuasive text: an opinion, at least two reasons, and an ending
  • D2.3 use words that express my thoughts, feelings and opinions (I think, I believe, the best, because)
  • D1.1 choose reasons that will convince my specific audience
  • D2.3 show a strong personal voice

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D2.1 requires persuasive texts, and D2.3 asks children to use words that express their thoughts, feelings, and opinions. Persuasive writing teaches reasoning, audience awareness, and that their voice has real power.

The OREO structure 🍪

- Opinion: "I think we should get a class hamster." - Reason: "because it would teach us responsibility." - Example/Explanation: "We would feed it every day and clean its cage." - Opinion again: "That's why we should get a hamster!" Grade 1: aim for opinion + 2 reasons + ending.

Great mentor texts

I Wanna Iguana (Karen Kaufman Orloff), Don't Let the Pigeon Drive the Bus! (Mo Willems), Hey, Little Ant (Phillip & Hannah Hoose), Earrings! (Judith Viorst).

💬 You can say

"A strong opinion needs strong reasons. Why should your reader agree with you? What does THEY care about?"

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Children often give reasons that only matter to them ("because I want it"). Coach them to think about the audience: "Would Grandma care about that? What would make HER say yes?"

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child writes an opinion with 2+ audience-aware reasons using "because," and ends by restating the opinion.

💡 Teaching tip

Make it REAL: let a persuasive letter actually change a family decision (a weekend activity, dinner choice) if it's convincing!

📚The Lesson

Do you ever want to convince someone to agree with you? Maybe to get a pet, stay up later, or go to the park? When you use words to change someone's mind, you are persuading!

Opinion vs. fact

An opinion is what you think or believe. People can disagree with opinions. "Dogs are the best pets" is an opinion. A fact can be proven: "Dogs have four legs."

The OREO recipe 🍪

  • O — Opinion: Say what you think. "I think every school should have a garden."
  • R — Reasons: Tell why. "Because kids can learn how food grows."
  • E — Examples: Explain more. "We could grow carrots and tomatoes and eat them at lunch!"
  • O — Opinion again: End strong. "That's why every school needs a garden!"

Know your audience

Choose reasons that matter to YOUR reader. - To persuade Mom to get a dog: "I will walk it every day, so you won't have to." - To persuade your teacher: "Reading to a dog helps kids practise reading."

Opinion words 💬

I think · I believe · I feel · In my opinion · The best · Everyone should · You will love · Because · That's why

📖 Why We Need a Class Library Day (a mentor text)

I think our family should have a library day every Saturday.

First, reading makes our brains grow stronger. We could learn about dinosaurs, space and sharks!

Second, the library is free. We can borrow ten books and it doesn't cost a penny.

Also, it would be fun family time. We could read together on the big comfy chairs.

That's why we should go to the library every Saturday. Please say yes!

🤯 Did You Know?

Autumn Peltier, an Anishinaabe girl from Wiikwemkong Unceded Territory in Ontario, began speaking up for clean water when she was just 8 years old. At 13, she spoke at the United Nations! Kids' words can change the world.

🤯 Did You Know?

The ancient Greeks thought persuasion was so important that they taught it in school as its own subject, called rhetoric. Great persuaders used three tools: good reasons, good character (being trustworthy), and strong feelings.

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Fact or opinion? (a) Summer is the best season. (b) Ice melts in the sun. (c) Broccoli is yucky. (d) Canada has 10 provinces.

⭐⭐ Stretch

You want a later bedtime. Give one reason that would convince a child, and one reason that would convince a parent. Why are they different?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Is it fair to persuade someone using only feelings and no facts? When is persuasion helpful, and when could it be tricky or unfair (like in some ads)?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Plan and draft a persuasive text using OREO for a real audience.

Materials

  • an OREO planning sheet (4 boxes: Opinion, Reasons, Examples, Opinion again), mentor text, pencil
  • (optional) real OREO cookies for motivation!

Steps

  1. Opinion Line-up: The grown-up reads statements ("Pizza is the best food"). Stand on one side of the room if you agree, the other if you disagree. Give one reason.
  2. Choose a real issue to persuade a real audience about (a family outing, a pet, a new rule).
  3. Plan with OREO boxes.
  4. Draft your persuasive letter or poster.
  5. Deliver it to your audience and see if it works!

Observation recording

O — OpinionR — ReasonsE — ExamplesO — Opinion again

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What is an opinion? What does OREO stand for? Name 5 opinion words.

Part 2 — Persuasive Letter (writing)

Write a persuasive letter to a real person about something you really want to change. Include an opinion, at least 2 reasons with examples, and a strong ending.

Part 3 — Persuasive Poster (creating)

Make a poster to persuade people to do something good for the world (turn off lights, pick up litter, read more). Use a catchy slogan, a picture and one reason.

✏️ My poster

🏠Homework

  1. Persuasion Spotting. Find 3 examples of persuasion in real life (ads, signs, a sibling asking for something!). What reasons did they use?
  2. Family Debate. Hold a friendly family debate: "Cats or dogs?" Each person gives 2 reasons.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. Should kids be allowed to vote? What would change if they could?
  2. Is it possible to change someone's mind if they don't want to listen? How?
  3. What is one thing in the world you would change if you could convince everyone?
Lesson 8 of 9

Editing Detectives: Capitals, Punctuation & Spelling

Become an editing detective with CUPS: check Capitals, Understanding, Punctuation and Spelling to make your writing ready for readers.

D2.5B3.3B2.4
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

Here's a sentence: “let's eat grandma.” Now: “Let's eat, Grandma!” One tiny comma and a capital letter just saved Grandma's life. How can such small marks make such a GIANT difference?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D2.5 reread my draft and make simple edits to capitalization, punctuation and spelling
  • D2.5 use an editing checklist (CUPS) on my own writing
  • B3.3 fix missing capitals at the start of sentences, for names and for I, and add missing end marks
  • B2.4 use my phonics knowledge to fix spelling of words with patterns I've learned

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D2.5 asks children to make simple edits to draft texts, such as changes to capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Editing teaches children to reread their own work as a reader would — a lifelong skill.

CUPS checklist

  • Capitals — start of sentences, names, I
  • Understanding — does it make sense? (read it aloud!)
  • Punctuation — . ? ! at the end of every sentence
  • Spelling — fix words with patterns you've learned; circle words you're unsure about

How to teach it

  1. Hook: "Let's eat grandma" — lots of giggles!
  2. Read the lesson.
  3. Edit a "messy" paragraph together, then the child's own draft from D5, D6 or D7.
  4. Use a coloured pencil for editing so edits are visible and celebrated.
💬 You can say

"Editing isn't fixing mistakes because you're bad at writing. Every real author edits. It's how good writing gets great."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Don't expect perfect spelling in Grade 1 — ask your child to fix only words with patterns they've been taught (and heart words they've mastered). Circle other words ("Good try — let's look at this one together later"). Too much red ink kills the joy of writing.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child independently finds and fixes 3+ capital and punctuation errors in their own draft and corrects taught spelling patterns.

💡 Teaching tip

Reading aloud is the best editing tool: children hear where sentences end and when something doesn't make sense.

📚The Lesson

Writers write a first draft quickly, getting their ideas down. Then they go back and make it ready for readers. Checking and fixing your writing is called editing. Real authors, journalists and even famous scientists edit their work many times!

Be a CUPS detective ☕

  • C — Capitals: Does every sentence start with a capital? Do names and the word I have capitals?
  • U — Understanding: Read it aloud. Does it make sense? Are any words missing?
  • P — Punctuation: Does every sentence end with a . ? or ! mark?
  • S — Spelling: Are words spelled correctly? Use your phonics! Circle words you're not sure about.

Punctuation can change everything! 😱

  • "Let's eat grandma." 😬 (Oh no!)
  • "Let's eat, Grandma!" 😊 (Phew! Dinner with Grandma!)

Editing marks

Editors use special marks: - ≡ three lines under a letter = make it a capital - ⊙ a circle with a dot = add a period - ^ a caret = add a missing word - ○ circle = check the spelling

Practice: find the mistakes!

📖 A Messy Draft

on saturday i went to the park with my dog rex

we plaid fetch and he ran super fast

then it started to rane

we ran home and got wet

it was the best day ever

Can you find 5 capitals, 5 end marks and 2 spelling mistakes?

🤯 Did You Know?

Before computers, editors used red pencils to mark mistakes. Even famous authors get a LOT of red marks! Roald Dahl rewrote parts of his books many, many times. He once explained that by the time he neared the end of a story, he had reread and fixed the first part at least 150 times!

🤯 Did You Know?

In 1962, a spacecraft called Mariner 1 had to be destroyed just minutes after launch. One famous explanation blames a single missing symbol — a tiny mark in the instructions! Small marks can make BIG differences.

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Fix this sentence using CUPS: "my frend and i ate ice cream"

⭐⭐ Stretch

Read "The Messy Draft" and fix everything. How many mistakes did you find?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Why is it easier to find mistakes in someone else's writing than in your own? What tricks could help you see your own mistakes?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Edit a practice draft and then your own writing using CUPS.

Materials

  • a coloured pencil (the "editing pencil"), a CUPS checklist card, a draft from an earlier lesson (D5, D6 or D7), a magnifying glass (for fun!)

Steps

  1. Messy Draft Rescue: Edit the Messy Draft together using editing marks.
  2. Read Aloud: Read your own draft aloud, slowly, pointing to each word.
  3. CUPS Passes: Go through your draft 4 times, looking for ONE thing each time: first Capitals, then Understanding, then Punctuation, then Spelling.
  4. Partner Edit: Have a grown-up read your draft aloud to you. Listen for places to fix.
  5. Celebrate: Count your fixes!

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does CUPS stand for? What editing mark means "make a capital"? Why do authors edit?

Part 2 — Edit This (applying)

Edit: "yesterday me and sam saw a big moos in the forest it was huge we took a foto"

Part 3 — Edit My Own Work (applying)

Choose your personal narrative (D5) or persuasive letter (D7). Edit it using all four CUPS passes. Then write a clean copy.

🏠Homework

  1. Grown-Up Editor. Ask a grown-up if they ever edit their writing (emails, reports, messages). Ask them to show you an example!
  2. Punctuation Jokes. Find or create a sentence where punctuation changes the meaning (like "Let's eat, Grandma!"). Share it at dinner.

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. If punctuation didn't exist, how would people know where sentences end?
  2. Should spelling matter if people can still understand what you mean? Why or why not?
  3. Who edits the editors?
Lesson 9 of 9

Publish & Present: The Author's Celebration

Turn your best writing into a finished book, poster or digital piece, then present it to a real audience with expression — and reflect on what helped.

D3.1D3.2D3.3A2.6
Session 1 Hook · Objectives · LessonSession 2 Think · ClassworkSession 3 Assignment · reviewBetween Homework

✨Wonder Hook

The same story can be a hand-made book, a poster, a comic, a puppet show, a podcast or a video. Which one would make YOUR story come alive the most — and how would you decide?

🎯Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, I will be able to…

  • D3.1 produce a final text using simple techniques (neat printing, illustrations, a cover, a title, colour, layout) to achieve the effect I want
  • D3.2 present my text to an audience using strategies like reading aloud with expression, eye contact and a loud clear voice
  • D3.3 identify a strategy that helped me when presenting
  • A2.6 choose a tool to publish with — paper book, poster, audio recording, or digital slideshow

🧑‍🏫Parent Teaching Guide

Why this lesson matters

D3.1 asks children to produce final texts, using simple techniques, to achieve the intended effect. D3.2 asks them to present texts they have created using appropriate strategies, including reading aloud with expression. D3.3 asks them to identify a strategy they found helpful when presenting. Publishing is the reward that makes all the drafting and editing worthwhile.

Publishing options

  • Hand-made book: folded paper, stapled, with a cover, title, author's name, illustrations, and "About the Author" page.
  • Poster: big title, pictures, clear print.
  • Audio/video: recorded reading (with permission), maybe with sound effects.
  • Digital slideshow: one picture and sentence per slide.

Presentation strategies

Loud, clear voice · expression · eye contact · pausing · holding the book so the audience can see · standing still and tall

How to teach it

  1. Choose 1–3 pieces from the year to publish.
  2. Plan the publishing format and techniques (D3.1).
  3. Rehearse (repeated reading from W11!).
  4. Hold an Author's Celebration: invite family (in person or video call), serve a snack, have your child present, and let guests ask questions and give compliments.
💬 You can say

"You are a real author now. Real authors share their books with real readers."

⚠️ Watch for this misconception

Some children are nervous about presenting. Start small (one family member, a stuffed-animal audience), then build. Let them choose what to present.

🎯 You’ll know they’ve got it when…

your child produces a finished text with intentional choices ("I made the title big and red so it looks exciting"), presents it with expression, and names one strategy that helped.

💡 Teaching tip

Keep a year-end "Author's Portfolio" of published works — a treasure for years to come.

📚The Lesson

You've planned, drafted and edited. Now it's time for the most exciting part: publishing! Publishing means making a final, polished copy of your writing to share with real readers.

Choose how to publish

  • 📕 A book — with a cover, title page, pictures and an "About the Author" page
  • 🖼️ A poster — big and bold for everyone to see
  • 💬 A comic — pictures in boxes with speech bubbles
  • 🎙️ An audio recording — read your story aloud with sound effects
  • 💻 A slideshow — one picture and sentence on each slide

Make choices on purpose 🎨

Authors and illustrators make choices to create an effect — a feeling in the reader: - Big, bold letters in the title → exciting! - Soft colours → calm and gentle - Dark colours → spooky or serious - A picture on every page → easier for young readers - Neat printing and spaces → easy to read

Present like a pro 🎤

When you share your writing with an audience: - 🗣️ Use a loud, clear voice - 🎭 Read with expression — change your voice for feelings and characters - 👀 Look up and make eye contact with your audience - ⏸️ Pause at periods and before exciting parts - 📖 Hold your book so people can see the pictures - 🧍 Stand tall and still

After you present, reflect

What helped you most? Practising? Taking a deep breath? Looking at a friendly face? Knowing what helps you is a superpower for next time!

🤯 Did You Know?

The Governor General's Literary Awards are some of Canada's biggest book prizes — and there's a special category just for children's books. Maybe one day your book will win one!

🤯 Did You Know?

Lots of people feel nervous about speaking in front of an audience — even famous actors and singers! A good trick: take three slow, deep breaths before you begin. Breathing slowly tells your body it's safe, and your heart slows down.

🧩Think Like an Author

⭐ Warm-up

Name 3 presentation strategies.

⭐⭐ Stretch

Your story is spooky. What colours, fonts and pictures would you choose to create a spooky effect? What if your story were funny?

⭐⭐⭐ Brain-bender

Is a story still the same story if it's a book, a podcast, or a movie? What changes? What stays the same?

🛠️Classwork

Objective

Publish a final text and present it at an Author's Celebration.

Materials

  • your best edited writing, paper, stapler, markers, crayons, a device for recording (optional, with permission)
  • invitations, a snack for guests!

Steps

  1. Choose your best piece of writing from this year.
  2. Plan your publishing format and 3 techniques to create the effect you want.
  3. Publish: Make the cover, title page, neat pages with illustrations, and an "About the Author" page with a self-portrait.
  4. Rehearse: Read aloud 3 times with expression (W11!).
  5. Invite guests with a hand-written invitation.
  6. Present at your Author's Celebration. Guests give one compliment and ask one question.

Observation recording

Technique I usedThe effect I wanted

📝Assignment

Part 1 — Recall

What does "publishing" mean? Name 4 ways to publish. Name 4 presentation strategies.

Part 2 — About the Author (writing)

Write an "About the Author" page for your book: your name, age, where you live, what you love, and why you wrote this book. Draw a self-portrait.

Part 3 — Presentation Reflection (reflecting)

After your Author's Celebration, write: "The strategy that helped me most when presenting was ___ because ___. Next time, I want to ___."

🏠Homework

  1. Library Display. Ask your local library if they display children's writing — some do! Or give a copy of your book to a relative.
  2. Author Portfolio. Put all your published writing from this year into a folder. Look through it and notice how much you've grown as a writer!

🌟Keep Wondering

  1. What makes someone an “author” — having a book in a store, or writing something someone else reads?
  2. If you wrote a book that would be read 100 years from now, what would you want it to say?
  3. Why do people feel nervous in front of an audience, even when they know the audience loves them?
Word Wall

Key Vocabulary

Read each card aloud together. Cover the definition and ask: “What does this word mean? Use it in your own sentence.” Revisit the cards at the start of every session in this strand.

author
A person who writes a text.
“I am the author of my own book about my dog.”
topic
What a piece of writing is about.
“My topic is volcanoes.”
purpose
Why an author writes: to entertain, inform, explain, persuade or express feelings.
“The purpose of my letter was to say thank you.”
audience
The people who will read your writing.
“My audience is my little cousin, so I used simple words.”
brainstorm
To think of lots of ideas quickly without judging them.
“We brainstormed ten story ideas.”
small moment
One short, specific event that makes a great story.
“I wrote about the small moment when I caught my first fish.”
research
Finding information about a topic.
“I did research about octopuses using a library book.”
notes
Short words and drawings that help you remember facts.
“My notes said: “3 hearts, blue blood.””
tripod grip
Holding a pencil with your thumb and pointer finger, resting on your middle finger.
“My tripod grip helps my printing stay neat.”
draft
A first try at writing, before editing.
“My first draft had lots of great ideas.”
personal narrative
A true story about something that happened to you.
“My personal narrative is about my first day of school.”
first person
Writing using I, me, my, we.
“My story is in first person because I am telling it.”
procedure
A text that tells how to do something in steps.
“I wrote a procedure for making a paper airplane.”
materials
The things you need to do a task.
“The materials for my recipe were bread and jam.”
opinion
What you think or believe; people can disagree.
“In my opinion, winter is the best season.”
persuade
To try to change someone's mind with reasons.
“I tried to persuade my mom to get a kitten.”
reason
An explanation of why.
“My best reason was that I would feed the kitten every day.”
voice
The personality and feelings you can hear in writing.
“My writing has a funny voice.”
editing
Checking and fixing capitals, punctuation, spelling and meaning.
“Editing helped me find three missing periods.”
publish
To make a final copy and share it with readers.
“I published my story as a book with a cover.”
present
To share your work with an audience.
“I presented my book to my grandparents with expression.”
